nodes.summary: The war between Rāma’s vānara army and Rāvaṇa’s rākṣasas, culminating in the deaths of Kumbhakarṇa, Indrajit and Rāvaṇa, whom Rāma kills with the Brahmā weapon given by Agastya.

nodes.name: Sītā’s ordeal by fire
nodes.summary: After Rāvaṇa’s death Rāma publicly refuses Sītā; she has Lakṣmaṇa build a pyre and enters the fire calling Agni to witness her fidelity; Agni returns her unharmed and the gods proclaim Rāma’s divinity.
nodes.details: The Rāmopākhyāna has the repudiation and divine testimony but no fire-entry (MBh (CE) 3.275.10–36). See cmp:sita-ordeal-banishment.

nodes.name: The banishment of Sītā and her return to the earth
nodes.summary: Hearing that his subjects gossip about Sītā’s stay in Rāvaṇa’s house, Rāma has Lakṣmaṇa abandon the pregnant Sītā near Vālmīki’s hermitage; years later, asked to prove her purity again at the horse sacrifice, she calls upon the Earth, who receives her.
nodes.details: Found only in the Uttarakāṇḍa among the Sanskrit epic versions; absent from the Rāmopākhyāna.

nodes.name: The krauñca bird and the first śloka
nodes.summary: Vālmīki sees a hunter kill one of a pair of mating krauñca birds; his grief (śoka) issues spontaneously as the first verse (śloka), and Brahmā bids him compose Rāma’s story in that metre.

sources.quote: mā niṣāda pratiṣṭhāṃ tvam agamaḥ śāśvatīḥ samāḥ / yat krauñcamithunād ekam avadhīḥ kāmamohitam

nodes.name: The sacrifice for sons and the birth of the four princes
nodes.summary: Daśaratha’s sacrifice performed by Ṛśyaśṛṅga, the gods’ request that Viṣṇu be born as a man to kill Rāvaṇa, and the births of Rāma, Bharata, Lakṣmaṇa and Śatrughna as portions of Viṣṇu.

nodes.name: Rāma kills Tāṭakā
nodes.summary: On Viśvāmitra’s instruction the young Rāma kills the demoness Tāṭakā, his first deed against the rākṣasas.

nodes.name: The release of Ahalyā
nodes.summary: Passing Gautama’s hermitage, Rāma ends the curse on Ahalyā, who had been seduced by Indra.

nodes.name: Rāma and Paraśurāma
nodes.summary: On the way back from Mithilā, Jāmadagnya Rāma (Paraśurāma) challenges Dāśarathi Rāma to string Viṣṇu’s bow; Rāma does so and Paraśurāma yields.

nodes.name: Kaikeyī’s two boons
nodes.summary: Incited by Mantharā, Kaikeyī reminds Daśaratha of the two boons he granted when she saved him in battle and demands Bharata’s consecration and Rāma’s exile.

nodes.name: The death of Daśaratha
nodes.summary: Grieving for Rāma, Daśaratha recalls how he once killed an ascetic’s son and was cursed to die lamenting a son, and dies in the night.

nodes.name: Bharata and the sandals
nodes.summary: Bharata seeks Rāma at Citrakūṭa and begs him to return; Rāma refuses, and Bharata takes his gold-adorned sandals to rule in his name.

nodes.name: The mutilation of Śūrpaṇakhā
nodes.summary: Rāvaṇa’s sister Śūrpaṇakhā propositions Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa at Pañcavaṭī and attacks Sītā; Lakṣmaṇa cuts off her nose and ears, setting the war with the rākṣasas in motion.

nodes.name: The golden deer
nodes.summary: At Rāvaṇa’s command Mārīca takes the form of a jewelled golden deer near the hermitage; Sītā asks Rāma to catch it, and Mārīca, dying, cries out in Rāma’s voice to draw Lakṣmaṇa away.

nodes.name: Jaṭāyu’s fight with Rāvaṇa
nodes.summary: The vulture king Jaṭāyu attacks Rāvaṇa to free Sītā, is mortally wounded, and lives long enough to tell Rāma what happened.

nodes.name: The alliance of Rāma and Sugrīva
nodes.summary: Hanumān brings Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa to Sugrīva on Ṛśyamūka; they swear friendship before fire, Rāma promising to kill Vālin and Sugrīva to search for Sītā.

nodes.name: The killing of Vālin
nodes.summary: During Sugrīva’s second duel with Vālin, Rāma shoots Vālin from concealment; the dying Vālin reproaches him and Rāma defends the act.

nodes.name: Vibhīṣaṇa joins Rāma
nodes.summary: Rebuked by Rāvaṇa for urging Sītā’s return, Vibhīṣaṇa flies to Rāma’s camp; despite Sugrīva’s suspicion Rāma accepts him and promises him Laṅkā.

nodes.name: The death of Kumbhakarṇa
nodes.summary: Roused from sleep for the war, Kumbhakarṇa devastates the vānaras until he is killed — by Rāma in Vālmīki’s Yuddhakāṇḍa, by Lakṣmaṇa with the Brahmā weapon in the Mahābhārata’s Rāmopākhyāna.

nodes.name: The death of Indrajit
nodes.summary: Lakṣmaṇa kills Rāvaṇa’s son Indrajit after a long duel.

nodes.name: The return to Ayodhyā and Rāma’s consecration
nodes.summary: Rāma returns to Ayodhyā with Sītā and is consecrated king, as the gods consecrated Indra.

nodes.name: Rāvaṇa’s boon from Brahmā
nodes.summary: Through austerities Rāvaṇa obtains from Brahmā invulnerability to gods, demons, nāgas, yakṣas and other beings — but not to humans; Vibhīṣaṇa asks only for steadfastness in dharma.

nodes.name: Vedavatī’s curse
nodes.summary: The ascetic Vedavatī, molested by Rāvaṇa, enters the fire vowing to be reborn for his destruction; the Uttarakāṇḍa says she is reborn as Sītā.

nodes.name: Hanumān’s childhood leap at the sun
nodes.summary: The infant Hanumān leaps at the rising sun thinking it a fruit, is struck down by Indra’s thunderbolt; the wind god withdraws in grief until the gods restore the child and grant him boons.

nodes.name: The killing of Śambūka
nodes.summary: When a brahmin’s son dies prematurely, Rāma finds the śūdra Śambūka performing austerities and beheads him, after which the boy revives.

nodes.name: Lava and Kuśa sing the Rāmāyaṇa
nodes.summary: At Vālmīki’s instruction the twins sing the whole poem in Rāma’s presence during his horse sacrifice, leading to their recognition as his sons.

nodes.name: Rāma’s return to Viṣṇu’s form
nodes.summary: At the end of his reign Rāma, with his brothers, enters the Sarayū and, at Brahmā’s invitation, the radiance of Viṣṇu.

nodes.name: The dice game
nodes.summary: Duryodhana, envious of the Pāṇḍavas’ wealth, has Śakuni challenge Yudhiṣṭhira to dice in the new hall at Hāstinapura; Yudhiṣṭhira loses his wealth, kingdom, brothers, himself and Draupadī, and in the return match the Pāṇḍavas are condemned to twelve years’ exile and a thirteenth incognito.

earliestText.label: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

nodes.name: The humiliation of Draupadī in the assembly hall
nodes.summary: Draupadī, staked and lost, is dragged by her hair into the hall in a single garment; she asks whether Yudhiṣṭhira lost himself before staking her; Duḥśāsana tries to strip her and her garment is miraculously renewed; Dhṛtarāṣṭra finally grants her boons.
nodes.details: In the CE constituted text the miracle is stated without an agent (“another garment of the same kind appeared, many times over”, 2.61.41); Draupadī’s prayers to Kṛṣṇa are found only in star passages *542–*547 inserted after 2.61.40.

earliestText.label: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

nodes.name: Draupadī’s svayaṃvara
nodes.summary: At Drupada’s city the disguised Arjuna strings the great bow and hits the target to win Draupadī; Kuntī’s unwitting instruction to share leads to her marriage to all five Pāṇḍavas, justified in several ways in the text.

earliestText.label: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

nodes.name: The house of lac
nodes.summary: Duryodhana has a house of lac built at Vāraṇāvata to burn the Pāṇḍavas and Kuntī; warned by Vidura, they escape through a tunnel and are thought dead.
nodes.details: Duryodhana broods (MBh (CE) 1.129), the Pāṇḍavas are sent to Vāraṇāvata (1.130–131), Purocana’s house is fired and the townspeople find the remains (1.136–137), and the family escapes (1.138).

earliestText.label: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

nodes.name: The Kurukṣetra war
nodes.summary: The eighteen-day war between the Pāṇḍavas and the Kauravas at Kurukṣetra, narrated in the Bhīṣma-, Droṇa-, Karṇa- and Śalyaparvans, which ends in the death of almost all the warriors on both sides.
nodes.limits: The war is a narrative event; dates proposed for a “historical” war (e.g. 3102 BCE by traditional reckoning) are recorded as traditional, not as facts.

earliestText.label: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

nodes.name: Kṛṣṇa’s discourse to Arjuna (the Gītā)
nodes.summary: On the battlefield, Arjuna, seeing his kinsmen and teachers arrayed against him, lays down his bow; Kṛṣṇa teaches him on duty, action without attachment, knowledge and devotion, and reveals his universal form.

nodes.name: The destruction of the Yādavas and Kṛṣṇa’s death
nodes.summary: Thirty-six years after the war, the Yādavas, cursed through Sāmba and fulfilling Gāndhārī’s curse, kill one another at Prabhāsa with clubs grown from erakā grass; Balarāma departs in yoga and Kṛṣṇa is shot in the foot by the hunter Jarā.

earliestText.label: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

nodes.name: The birth of Kṛṣṇa
nodes.summary: Kṛṣṇa is born to Devakī and Vasudeva in Kaṃsa’s prison at Mathurā, after Kaṃsa has killed her earlier children; he is carried to Vraja and exchanged with the daughter born to Yaśodā at the same time.

nodes.name: Kṛṣṇa lifts Mount Govardhana
nodes.summary: Kṛṣṇa persuades the cowherds to honour the mountain instead of Indra; when Indra sends a deluge he uproots Govardhana and holds it up for seven days to shelter Vraja, and Indra comes to honour him.

nodes.name: Kṛṣṇa subdues the serpent Kāliya
nodes.summary: The boy Kṛṣṇa plunges into the pool of the Yamunā poisoned by Kāliya, subdues the serpent by dancing on its heads and sends it away to the ocean.

nodes.name: The killing of Kaṃsa
nodes.summary: Summoned to Mathurā for a wrestling festival, Kṛṣṇa and Balarāma kill the wrestlers, and Kṛṣṇa drags Kaṃsa down by the hair and kills him, restoring Ugrasena.

nodes.name: Nala and Damayantī
nodes.summary: Damayantī chooses Nala over the gods; possessed by Kali, Nala loses his kingdom at dice to his brother Puṣkara and abandons her in the forest; after many trials, disguised as a charioteer, he is recognised and regains his kingdom.

earliestText.label: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

nodes.name: Sāvitrī and Satyavān
nodes.summary: Sāvitrī marries Satyavān knowing he will die in a year; when Yama takes his life she follows and, winning boon after boon by her words, obtains his life back.

earliestText.label: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

nodes.name: Ugraśravas’ recitation at Naimiṣa
nodes.summary: The outer frame of the Mahābhārata: the bard Ugraśravas arrives at Śaunaka’s twelve-year sacrifice in the Naimiṣa forest and recites the epic he heard at Janamejaya’s snake sacrifice.

earliestText.label: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

nodes.name: Janamejaya’s snake sacrifice
nodes.summary: To avenge his father Parīkṣit, killed by Takṣaka, Janamejaya performs a sacrifice that draws the serpents into the fire; Āstīka stops it. During its intervals Vaiśampāyana recites the Mahābhārata.

earliestText.label: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

nodes.name: Bhīṣma’s vow
nodes.summary: To let his father Śantanu marry Satyavatī, whose father demands that her son inherit, Devavrata renounces the throne and vows lifelong celibacy, and is thenceforth called Bhīṣma.

earliestText.label: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

nodes.name: Vyāsa’s niyoga: the births of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Pāṇḍu and Vidura
nodes.summary: After Vicitravīrya dies childless, Satyavatī asks her son Vyāsa to raise offspring on his widows; Ambikā bears the blind Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Ambālikā the pale Pāṇḍu, and a servant woman Vidura.

earliestText.label: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

nodes.name: The birth and abandonment of Karṇa
nodes.summary: The unmarried Kuntī tests Durvāsas’s mantra on the Sun and bears Karṇa with armour and earrings; fearing disgrace she sets him adrift, and the charioteer Adhiratha and his wife Rādhā raise him.

earliestText.label: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

nodes.name: The births of the Pāṇḍavas
nodes.summary: Cursed never to approach his wives, Pāṇḍu asks Kuntī to use her mantra: she bears Yudhiṣṭhira by Dharma, Bhīma by Vāyu and Arjuna by Indra; Mādrī bears the twins by the Aśvins.

earliestText.label: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

nodes.name: Ekalavya’s thumb
nodes.summary: The niṣāda Ekalavya, refused by Droṇa, teaches himself archery before a clay image of him; when Arjuna sees his skill, Droṇa demands Ekalavya’s right thumb as fee, and Ekalavya cuts it off.

earliestText.label: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

nodes.name: The tournament of the Kuru princes
nodes.summary: At the public display of the princes’ skill Karṇa enters and matches Arjuna; challenged on his birth, he is made king of Aṅga by Duryodhana, and Adhiratha’s arrival exposes him to Bhīma’s scorn as a sūta’s son.

earliestText.label: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

nodes.name: Bhīma and Hiḍimbā
nodes.summary: After escaping the house of lac Bhīma kills the man-eater Hiḍimba and, with Kuntī’s consent, lives with his sister Hiḍimbā, who bears Ghaṭotkaca.

earliestText.label: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

nodes.name: The burning of the Khāṇḍava forest
nodes.summary: Kṛṣṇa and Arjuna help the fire god Agni consume the Khāṇḍava forest against Indra’s rains; Agni gives Arjuna the bow Gāṇḍīva and Kṛṣṇa the discus, and the spared Maya later builds the Pāṇḍavas’ hall.

earliestText.label: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

nodes.name: The killing of Jarāsandha
nodes.summary: Before the rājasūya, Kṛṣṇa, Bhīma and Arjuna enter Magadha disguised as brahmins and Bhīma kills Jarāsandha in a wrestling match.

earliestText.label: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

nodes.name: The rājasūya and the killing of Śiśupāla
nodes.summary: At Yudhiṣṭhira’s royal consecration Bhīṣma proposes Kṛṣṇa for the first honour; Śiśupāla protests and insults Kṛṣṇa, who beheads him with his discus.

earliestText.label: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

nodes.name: Arjuna and the Kirāta
nodes.summary: Seeking divine weapons in the Himālaya, Arjuna fights a hunter (kirāta) over a boar; the hunter is Śiva, who, pleased, gives him the Pāśupata weapon.

earliestText.label: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

nodes.name: The Yakṣa’s questions
nodes.summary: At a lake whose water kills his brothers, Yudhiṣṭhira answers the questions of a yakṣa — the god Dharma — and wins back their lives.

earliestText.label: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

nodes.name: The killing of Kīcaka
nodes.summary: At Virāṭa’s court the general Kīcaka harasses Draupadī (disguised as Sairandhrī); Bhīma meets him at night in the dancing hall and kills him.

earliestText.label: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

nodes.name: Kṛṣṇa’s embassy to the Kauravas
nodes.summary: Kṛṣṇa goes to Hāstinapura to seek peace; when Duryodhana plots to seize him he reveals his cosmic form, then leaves, taking Karṇa aside to reveal his birth.

earliestText.label: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

nodes.name: Ambā’s revenge and Śikhaṇḍin
nodes.summary: Ambā, rejected after Bhīṣma’s abduction, seeks his death, is reborn as Drupada’s daughter Śikhaṇḍinī and becomes the man Śikhaṇḍin through an exchange of sex with the yakṣa Sthūṇa.

earliestText.label: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

nodes.name: Kuntī meets Karṇa
nodes.summary: Before the war Kuntī goes to Karṇa on the bank of the Gaṅgā and asks him to join his brothers; he refuses but promises to spare all but Arjuna, so that she will still have five sons.

earliestText.label: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

nodes.name: The fall of Bhīṣma
nodes.summary: On the tenth day, with Śikhaṇḍin before him, Arjuna pierces Bhīṣma with arrows; Bhīṣma falls and lies on a bed of arrows awaiting the winter solstice.

earliestText.label: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

nodes.name: The death of Abhimanyu
nodes.summary: On the thirteenth day Abhimanyu breaks into Droṇa’s circular array, is surrounded by several warriors and killed by Duḥśāsana’s son with a mace.

earliestText.label: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

nodes.name: The death of Ghaṭotkaca
nodes.summary: In the night battle Karṇa uses Indra’s infallible spear, reserved for Arjuna, to kill Ghaṭotkaca.

earliestText.label: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

nodes.name: The death of Droṇa
nodes.summary: Told that “Aśvatthāman” is dead — an elephant of that name killed by Bhīma, confirmed by Yudhiṣṭhira — Droṇa lays down his weapons and is beheaded by Dhṛṣṭadyumna.

earliestText.label: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

nodes.name: The death of Karṇa
nodes.summary: On the seventeenth day Karṇa’s chariot wheel sinks into the earth; while he struggles to free it, Arjuna, urged by Kṛṣṇa, kills him.

earliestText.label: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

nodes.name: The mace duel and the breaking of Duryodhana’s thighs
nodes.summary: In the final mace duel, prompted by Kṛṣṇa and Arjuna, Bhīma strikes Duryodhana below the navel, breaking his thighs as he had vowed, to Balarāma’s anger.

earliestText.label: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

nodes.name: The night massacre
nodes.summary: Aśvatthāman, with Kṛpa and Kṛtavarman, enters the Pāṇḍava camp by night and kills Dhṛṣṭadyumna, the Draupadeyas and the sleeping warriors.

earliestText.label: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

nodes.name: Gāndhārī curses Kṛṣṇa
nodes.summary: Lamenting on the battlefield, Gāndhārī blames Kṛṣṇa for not preventing the slaughter and curses him and his clan to perish in thirty-six years.

earliestText.label: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

nodes.name: Bhīṣma’s instruction from the bed of arrows
nodes.summary: At Kṛṣṇa’s urging, the dying Bhīṣma instructs Yudhiṣṭhira at length on kingship, emergencies, liberation and many other topics before dying at the winter solstice.

earliestText.label: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

nodes.name: The great departure of the Pāṇḍavas
nodes.summary: Renouncing the kingdom, the Pāṇḍavas and Draupadī walk towards Mount Meru; one by one they fall, and only Yudhiṣṭhira, followed by a dog that proves to be Dharma, reaches Indra’s chariot.

earliestText.label: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

nodes.name: Śakuntalā and Duḥṣanta
nodes.summary: King Duḥṣanta meets Śakuntalā in Kaṇva’s hermitage and marries her by gāndharva rite; when she later brings their son to court he denies her until a heavenly voice confirms her, and the boy Bharata becomes heir.

earliestText.label: mid-2nd century BCE – turn of the era

nodes.name: Kṛṣṇa carries off Rukmiṇī
nodes.summary: Kṛṣṇa takes Rukmiṇī, daughter of Bhīṣmaka of Vidarbha, away from her intended marriage to Śiśupāla and defeats her brother Rukmin.

nodes.name: Ayodhyā
nodes.summary: Capital of Kosala and of the Ikṣvāku kings in the Rāmāyaṇa, Rāma’s birthplace and royal seat; traditionally identified with Ayodhya on the Sarayū (Ghaghara) in Uttar Pradesh, and with ancient Sāketa.

location.label: Ayodhya, Uttar Pradesh, India

nodes.limits: The present-day town’s identification with the epic city is traditional and widely accepted in devotion; the epic’s description is literary. Archaeological occupation of the modern site does not establish the narrative.

nodes.name: Mithilā
nodes.summary: Capital of Videha ruled by Janaka, where Rāma breaks Śiva’s bow and marries Sītā; traditionally identified with Janakpur in the Nepal Terai, within the wider Mithilā region of north Bihar and Nepal.

location.label: Janakpur, Madhesh Province, Nepal

nodes.limits: Janakpur’s identification is traditional; Sītāmaṛhī (Bihar) is separately revered as Sītā’s birthplace. The epic city is not archaeologically located.

nodes.name: Laṅkā (in the Rāmāyaṇa)
nodes.summary: Rāvaṇa’s island fortress-city beyond the southern ocean, earlier the seat of Kubera; widely identified in tradition with the island of Sri Lanka, though some scholars have proposed locations in central India.

location.label: Sri Lanka (traditional identification of the narrative Laṅkā)

nodes.limits: Kept separate from the modern island: the narrative Laṅkā is a literary place. Its identification with Sri Lanka is traditional and widely held; alternative central-Indian locations have been argued (e.g. discussed by Sankalia 1973). Coordinates are the island’s centroid, for mapping only.
openQuestions: Which central-Indian locations were proposed, by whom (M. V. Kibe, Sankalia and others), and on what textual evidence — to be checked.

nodes.name: Kiṣkindhā
nodes.summary: Cave-city of the vānara kings Vālin and Sugrīva near the Pampā lake and Ṛśyamūka hill; traditionally identified with the Hampi–Anegundi area on the Tuṅgabhadrā in Karnataka.

location.label: Anegundi, near Hampi, Vijayanagara district, Karnataka, India

nodes.limits: The Hampi identification is traditional (local sites named Ṛṣyamūka, Añjanādri, Pampā sarovara); the epic’s geography is not mapped by the text with that precision.

nodes.name: Citrakūṭa
nodes.summary: Hill in the forest south of the Yamunā where Rāma, Sītā and Lakṣmaṇa first settle in exile on Bharadvāja’s advice, and where Bharata finds them; identified with Chitrakoot on the Uttar Pradesh–Madhya Pradesh border.

location.label: Chitrakoot Dham (Karwi), Uttar Pradesh / Chitrakoot, Madhya Pradesh, India

nodes.limits: Traditional identification; pilgrimage sites at Chitrakoot commemorate the episode.

nodes.name: Pañcavaṭī
nodes.summary: Forest spot on the Godāvarī recommended by Agastya, where Rāma builds his hermitage and from which Sītā is abducted; traditionally identified with Panchavati in Nashik, Maharashtra.

location.label: Panchavati, Nashik, Maharashtra, India (Kalaram temple area)

nodes.limits: Traditional identification; coordinates are those of the Kalaram temple in the Panchavati quarter of Nashik.

nodes.name: Daṇḍaka forest
nodes.summary: The vast forest of the exile, peopled by sages and harassed by rākṣasas, stretching (in later understanding) between the Narmadā and the Godāvarī/Kṛṣṇā; the modern Dandakaranya region of central-eastern India takes its name from it.

location.label: Dandakaranya region (Bastar, Chhattisgarh, with parts of Odisha, Telangana, Andhra Pradesh, Maharashtra), India

nodes.limits: A literary forest; the modern regional name is a later application. Coordinates (Jagdalpur) mark the modern region for mapping only.

nodes.name: Hastināpura
nodes.summary: Capital of the Kuru kings and seat of the Kauravas; identified with Hastinapur in Meerut district, Uttar Pradesh, where B. B. Lal excavated Painted Grey Ware levels (1950–52).

location.label: Hastinapur, Meerut district, Uttar Pradesh, India

nodes.limits: The identification is traditional and was adopted by Lal; the excavated settlement establishes ancient occupation, not the epic narrative.

nodes.name: Indraprastha
nodes.summary: City founded by the Pāṇḍavas on the Yamunā after clearing the Khāṇḍava forest, seat of Yudhiṣṭhira’s rājasūya; traditionally identified with the area of the Purana Qila in Delhi.

location.label: Purana Qila, New Delhi, India

nodes.limits: The Purana Qila identification is traditional; excavations there found early historic occupation (incl. Painted Grey Ware sherds), which does not establish the epic city.

nodes.name: Kurukṣetra
nodes.summary: The “field of the Kurus” where the eighteen-day war is fought, also called Samantapañcaka and dharmakṣetra; identified with the Kurukshetra region in Haryana, an important pilgrimage area.

location.label: Kurukshetra, Haryana, India

nodes.limits: The region is named Kurukṣetra already in Vedic literature; specific battle sites shown to pilgrims are traditional.

earliestText.label: c. 8th–6th c. BCE (late Brāhmaṇa period; approximate)

nodes.name: Dvārakā
nodes.summary: Kṛṣṇa’s city by the western sea, to which the Yādavas move from Mathurā, and which the sea submerges after Kṛṣṇa’s death; identified with Dwarka in Gujarat (with Bet Dwarka island also associated).

location.label: Dwarka, Devbhumi Dwarka district, Gujarat, India

nodes.limits: Traditional identification; claims that offshore remains are Kṛṣṇa’s city are a separate, disputed claim (claim:dwarka-submerged).

nodes.name: Mathurā
nodes.summary: City of the Śūrasenas on the Yamunā, ruled by Kaṃsa, where Kṛṣṇa is born and kills Kaṃsa; the modern city in Uttar Pradesh, an important early centre of Vāsudeva–Kṛṣṇa worship.

location.label: Mathura, Uttar Pradesh, India

nodes.limits: The modern city’s identification is secure as a continuously named place; that it is the setting of the narrated events is a matter of tradition.

nodes.name: Vṛndāvana
nodes.summary: Forest near the Yamunā to which the cowherds move from their first settlement and where Kṛṣṇa’s childhood feats and sports with the gopīs take place; identified with Vrindavan near Mathura.

location.label: Vrindavan, Mathura district, Uttar Pradesh, India

nodes.limits: The modern town was developed as a pilgrimage centre especially from the 16th century (Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇava activity); identification with the Harivaṃśa’s forest is traditional.

nodes.name: Naimiṣa forest
nodes.summary: Forest where Śaunaka holds his twelve-year sacrifice and Ugraśravas recites the Mahābhārata (and, in Purāṇic frames, the Purāṇas); identified with Nimsar (Neemsar) on the Gomatī in Sitapur district, Uttar Pradesh.

location.label: Nimsar (Naimisharanya), Sitapur district, Uttar Pradesh, India

nodes.limits: Traditional identification; coordinates from the location link on the Wikipedia article (approximate).

nodes.name: Kāmpilya
nodes.summary: Capital of southern Pañcāla left to Drupada after Droṇa’s victory, the setting of Draupadī’s svayaṃvara in tradition; identified with Kampil in Farrukhabad district, Uttar Pradesh.

location.label: Kampil, Farrukhabad district, Uttar Pradesh, India

nodes.limits: Traditional identification of the modern village with the epic city.

nodes.name: Takṣaśilā
nodes.summary: City in Gandhāra from which Janamejaya returns to Hāstinapura after his snake sacrifice (MBh 18.5.29); identified with Taxila in Punjab, Pakistan.

location.label: Taxila, Punjab, Pakistan

nodes.limits: The identification of Takṣaśilā with Taxila is secure for the historical city; that Janamejaya’s sacrifice took place there is the epic’s own statement.

nodes.name: Virāṭanagara
nodes.summary: Capital of King Virāṭa of the Matsyas, where the Pāṇḍavas spend the thirteenth year in disguise; traditionally identified with Viratnagar (Bairat) in Jaipur district, Rajasthan.

location.label: Viratnagar (Bairat), Jaipur district, Rajasthan, India

nodes.limits: Traditional identification; Bairat is better known archaeologically for Aśokan-period remains, which do not bear on the epic.

nodes.name: Prabhāsa
nodes.summary: Coastal tīrtha where the Yādavas gather and destroy one another in drunken strife; identified with Prabhas Patan (Somnath) in Gujarat.

location.label: Prabhas Patan, Gir Somnath district, Gujarat, India

nodes.limits: Traditional identification; local sites associated with Kṛṣṇa’s death (e.g. Bhalka) are pilgrimage traditions.

nodes.name: Pampā lake
nodes.summary: Lake near Ṛśyamūka on whose western shore Śabarī lives and near which Rāma meets Hanumān and Sugrīva; identified with Pampa Sarovar near Hampi, Karnataka.

location.label: Pampa Sarovar, near Hampi, Koppal district, Karnataka, India

nodes.limits: Traditional identification.

nodes.name: Śṛṅgaverapura
nodes.summary: Town of the niṣāda chief Guha on the Gaṅgā, where Rāma crosses the river at the start of the exile; identified with Shringverpur near Prayagraj.

location.label: Shringverpur, Prayagraj district, Uttar Pradesh, India

nodes.limits: Traditional identification; excavations at Shringverpur (B. B. Lal, 1977–86) concern the ancient settlement, not the narrative.

nodes.name: The Kuru lineage
nodes.summary: The royal line descended from Kuru in the lunar dynasty, ruling from Hāstinapura, to which Śantanu, Bhīṣma, Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Pāṇḍu and both the Kauravas and Pāṇḍavas belong.
nodes.details: The epic genealogies (MBh (CE) 1.70–90) run from Dakṣa, Manu and Purūravas through Bharata and Kuru to Śantanu. Historians identify a Kuru polity of the late Vedic period in the upper Gaṅgā–Yamunā doab; the epic line is a literary genealogy.
nodes.limits: The genealogy is narrative; the historical late-Vedic Kuru state is a separate (Vedic-domain) topic.

nodes.name: The Pāṇḍavas
nodes.summary: The five legal sons of Pāṇḍu — Yudhiṣṭhira, Bhīma and Arjuna (by Kuntī) and Nakula and Sahadeva (by Mādrī), each fathered by a god — with their shared wife Draupadī and their descendants down to Parīkṣit and Janamejaya.

nodes.name: The Kauravas
nodes.summary: The hundred sons (and one daughter) of Dhṛtarāṣṭra and Gāndhārī, led by Duryodhana; also, more broadly, the Kuru side in the war.
nodes.details: The aṃśāvataraṇa makes the hundred brothers incarnations of Paulastya rākṣasas (MBh (CE) 1.61.82–83). Yuyutsu, son by a vaiśya woman, joins the Pāṇḍavas.

nodes.name: The Yādavas / Vṛṣṇis
nodes.summary: The descendants of Yadu, including the Vṛṣṇi, Andhaka and Bhoja clans of Mathurā and Dvārakā, to which Śūra, Vasudeva, Kuntī, Kṛṣṇa, Balarāma and Subhadrā belong; their genealogy fills the Harivaṃśa.
nodes.details: The Mausalaparvan narrates their mutual destruction at Prabhāsa (MBh (CE) 16.4). The Vṛṣṇis appear in early inscriptions (the material domain’s ins:mora-well) in connection with the worship of Vṛṣṇi heroes.

nodes.name: The Paulastyas (line of Pulastya)
nodes.summary: The descendants of the sage Pulastya through Viśravas: Kubera (Vaiśravaṇa) and the rākṣasa siblings Rāvaṇa, Kumbhakarṇa, Śūrpaṇakhā and Vibhīṣaṇa.

nodes.name: The vānaras of Kiṣkindhā
nodes.summary: The monkey people of Kiṣkindhā ruled by Vālin and Sugrīva, among them Hanumān, Aṅgada, Nala and Nīla, born — in the Rāmāyaṇa and Rāmopākhyāna — of gods to aid Viṣṇu’s descent.
nodes.limits: The vānaras are narrative beings; anthropological readings (e.g. as forest peoples) are scholarly interpretations not encoded here.

nodes.name: The Pāñcālas (line of Drupada)
nodes.summary: The ruling house of Pañcāla: Drupada and his children Dhṛṣṭadyumna, Śikhaṇḍin and Draupadī, allies of the Pāṇḍavas.

nodes.name: The Bhāratas (line of Bharata Dauḥṣanti)
nodes.summary: The lineage named after Bharata, son of Duḥṣanta and Śakuntalā, from which the Kurus descend and after which the epic (Bhārata, Mahābhārata) is named.

nodes.name: The identification of the Rāmāyaṇa’s Laṅkā with Sri Lanka
nodes.summary: The traditional and widely held view that Rāvaṇa’s island-city Laṅkā is the island of Sri Lanka, set against scholarly proposals that the epic’s Laṅkā lay elsewhere (notably in central India) or is a purely literary geography.
nodes.details:
For: the Rāmāyaṇa places Laṅkā across the southern ocean, reached by Hanumān’s leap and by the causeway built from the southern shore (VR (CE) 5.1; 6.15); later South Indian and Sri Lankan traditions, place-names (Rāma Setu/Adam’s Bridge, Rameswaram) and pilgrimage sites embody the identification.

Against / alternatives: several twentieth-century scholars argued that the epic’s geography south of the Vindhyas is vague and that Laṅkā may have been a hill-fort in central India (proposals discussed by H. D. Sankalia, 1973); others treat Laṅkā as a literary island not mappable onto any real place.
nodes.limits: Recorded as a debatable claim. The dataset keeps the narrative place (place:lanka-narrative) separate from any modern territory.
openQuestions: Name and check the specific central-Indian proposals (M. V. Kibe’s Amarkantak hypothesis is often cited) and their arguments.

nodes.name: Vāsudeva (deity of early inscriptions)
nodes.subtype: deity attested in inscriptions and coins
nodes.summary: Vāsudeva is the deity named in the earliest Vaiṣṇava inscriptions of the 2nd–1st centuries BCE, such as the Heliodorus pillar at Besnagar, where he is called devadeva, “god of gods”. He was later identified with Kṛṣṇa and with Viṣṇu-Nārāyaṇa. The material record shows his worship centuries before the Purāṇic synthesis.
nodes.details:
In the material record Vāsudeva appears first as one of a pair with Saṅkarṣaṇa. On the Indian-standard drachms of the Greco-Bactrian king Agathocles found at Aï Khanoum (c. 190–180 BCE) he is usually identified as the figure holding a conch and a wheel. The Heliodorus pillar at Besnagar (late 2nd c. BCE) calls him devadeva and records a Garuḍa-standard set up by a Greek envoy who styles himself a bhāgavata. The Hāthībāḍā–Ghosuṇḍī inscriptions (2nd–1st c. BCE) and the Nāṇeghāṭ inscription of Nāganikā (1st c. BCE) invoke Saṅkarṣaṇa and Vāsudeva together.

At Mathurā, the Mora well inscription (c. 15 CE) records images of the five Vṛṣṇi heroes, and the Vasu doorjamb inscription (early 1st c. CE) records a gateway and railing at a shrine of Bhagavat Vāsudeva, both from the time of the satrap Śoḍāsa. Grammatical literature mentions Vāsudeva earlier: Pāṇini 4.3.98 teaches the formation of a word for a devotee of Vāsudeva and Arjuna, and Patañjali's Mahābhāṣya refers to the slaying of Kaṃsa.

This record keeps Vāsudeva as a separate id from the epic character Kṛṣṇa (char:krishna). The identification of the two, and of Vāsudeva with Viṣṇu-Nārāyaṇa, is a historical synthesis attested in the epic and Purāṇic texts. It is recorded as an IDENTIFIED_WITH assertion (owned by the epic agent), not as a merge.

dates.label: c. 190–180 BCE (Agathocles coins; identification argued)
dates.basis: coin issue dated by the reign of Agathocles; the deity identification is scholarly

dates.label: late 2nd century BCE (Heliodorus pillar)
dates.basis: regnal synchronism with the Indo-Greek king Antialkidas; Brāhmī palaeography

nodes.limits: Establishes that Vāsudeva was worshipped by the late 2nd century BCE in central and western India, and by Greek envoys. It does not establish the historicity of the Kṛṣṇa of the epic or Purāṇas, nor the date at which Vāsudeva was identified with Kṛṣṇa Devakīputra or with Viṣṇu.
openQuestions: When was Vāsudeva first explicitly identified with Viṣṇu-Nārāyaṇa in a dated inscription?
How did the Vṛṣṇi-hero cult at Mathurā relate to the bhāgavata devotion recorded at Besnagar and Nagari?

earliestText.label: c. mid-4th c. BCE or later (terminus post quem c. 350 BCE)

nodes.name: Saṅkarṣaṇa (deity of early inscriptions)
nodes.subtype: deity attested in inscriptions and coins
nodes.summary: Saṅkarṣaṇa is the deity invoked together with Vāsudeva in inscriptions of the 2nd–1st centuries BCE, and is usually named first. He is identified with Balarāma, Kṛṣṇa's elder brother, and later became the first emanation (vyūha) of Vāsudeva in Pāñcarātra theology.
nodes.details:
Saṅkarṣaṇa is invoked with Vāsudeva in the compound “Saṃkarṣaṇa-Vāsudeva” in the Hāthībāḍā–Ghosuṇḍī inscriptions of king Sarvatāta, who had a stone enclosure built for their worship. He appears again in the opening invocation of the Nāṇeghāṭ inscription of the Sātavāhana queen Nāganikā. On the Agathocles drachms from Aï Khanoum (c. 190–180 BCE), the figure holding a plough and a pestle or club is identified as Saṅkarṣaṇa-Balarāma. Scholars take him to be one of the five Vṛṣṇi heroes of the Mora well inscription. That identification rests on the later Purāṇic list of the five, not on the inscription itself.

The graph keeps the deity of the inscriptions apart from the epic character Balarāma (char:balarama). The two are joined by an IDENTIFIED_WITH assertion qualified by tradition.
nodes.limits: The inscriptions show a cult of Saṅkarṣaṇa paired with Vāsudeva before the Common Era. They do not show the narrative of Balarāma as told in the Harivaṃśa or the Purāṇas, nor that the pair's legends already existed in their later form.

nodes.name: Heliodorus pillar inscription, Besnagar
nodes.summary: Two Brāhmī inscriptions in Prakrit on a stone pillar at Besnagar (ancient Vidiśā) record that Heliodorus of Taxila set up a Garuḍa-standard (garuḍadhvaja) for Vāsudeva, “god of gods”. Heliodorus, son of Dion, calls himself a bhāgavata and was a Greek envoy of the Indo-Greek king Antialkidas to king Kāsīputra Bhāgabhadra. It is among the earliest dated pieces of evidence for Vāsudeva devotion.
nodes.details:
The main inscription (A) says that this Garuḍa-standard of Vāsudeva, the god of gods, was made by Heliodorus. He is described as a bhāgavata, the son of Dion, a man of Taxila, and a Greek ambassador who came from the great king Antialkidas to king Kāsīputra Bhāgabhadra, the Saviour, in his fourteenth regnal year. The second, shorter inscription (B) names three immortal steps (amuta-pādāni) which, when practised, lead to heaven: self-restraint (dama), generosity (cāga) and attentiveness (apramāda).

Alexander Cunningham noticed the pillar during his tours of the 1870s. Wikipedia gives both 1874–75 and 1877, so the year is inconsistent in the sources checked. The inscriptions were found only in 1909, after a team led by H. H. Lake cleaned away the red paint; John Marshall reported them. D. R. Bhandarkar excavated around the pillar in 1913–15, and M. D. Khare's excavation of 1963–65 found the foundations of an elliptical temple next to it.

Dating: the record dates itself only to Bhāgabhadra's 14th regnal year, so its absolute date depends on the reign of Antialkidas. Bopearachchi dates that reign c. 115–95 BCE and R. C. Senior c. 130–120 BCE. The often-quoted single year “113 BCE” is a convention and is not stated in the inscription. Whether Bhāgabhadra was a Śuṅga king or a local ruler is also disputed.

dates.label: c. 115–95 BCE
dates.basis: regnal synchronism: 14th year of Bhāgabhadra during the reign of Antialkidas

dates.label: c. 130–120 BCE
dates.basis: regnal synchronism with Antialkidas as dated by R. C. Senior

dates.label: “c. 113 BCE” (conventional figure)
dates.basis: conventional single year found in secondary literature; not stated in the inscription

location.label: Besnagar, Vidisha district, Madhya Pradesh, India (in situ)

attributes.findspot: Besnagar (ancient Vidiśā), in situ beside the remains of an elliptical temple
attributes.repository: in situ; the Garuḍa capital is lost (a fragment in the Gujari Mahal Museum, Gwalior may belong to it)
attributes.reading: A: “Devadevasa Vā[sude]vasa Garuḍadhvaje ayaṃ karito i[a] Heliodoreṇa bhāgavatena Diyasa putreṇa Takhkhasilākena Yonadatena agatena mahārājasa Aṃtalikitasa upa[ṃ]tā samkāsam-raño Kāsīput[r]asa [Bh]āgabhadrasa trātārasa vasena [chatu]daseṃna rājena vadhamānasa”; B: “Trini amuta-pādāni (i me) (su)anuthitāni neyamti sva(gam) dama cāga apramāda” (transliteration as adapted on Wikipedia from Rapson, Sukthankar, Salomon and Wallace)
attributes.datingMethod: regnal year of Bhāgabhadra + synchronism with Antialkidas; palaeography
attributes.discovered: pillar noticed by A. Cunningham (1870s; 1874–75 or 1877 per sources); inscriptions found 1909 after cleaning (H. H. Lake), reported by J. Marshall

nodes.limits: Establishes that by the late 2nd century BCE Vāsudeva was worshipped as devadeva at Vidiśā with a Garuḍa-standard, and that a Greek envoy could call himself a bhāgavata. It does not identify Vāsudeva with the epic Kṛṣṇa or with Viṣṇu, and it does not show that any epic event took place. The parallel between inscription B and a Mahābhārata verse is an interpretation (claim:heliodorus-mbh-parallel).
openQuestions: Which year (1874–75 or 1877) did Cunningham first record the pillar?
Was Bhāgabhadra a Śuṅga king (the Purāṇic Bhāgavata?) or a local ruler of Vidiśā?

nodes.name: Hāthībāḍā–Ghosuṇḍī inscriptions
nodes.summary: Three fragmentary Sanskrit inscriptions in Brāhmī script from Ghosuṇḍī and Hāthībāḍā near Nagari (ancient Madhyamikā), Rajasthan, dated to the 2nd–1st century BCE. They record that king Sarvatāta of the Gājāyana lineage, a devotee of Bhagavat and performer of an aśvamedha, built a stone enclosure for the worship of Saṅkarṣaṇa and Vāsudeva, called Nārāyaṇa-vāṭikā. They are among the earliest Sanskrit (as opposed to Prakrit) inscriptions.
nodes.details:
Three incomplete copies (fragments A, B, C) are known. One was in an ancient well at Ghosuṇḍī, one in a boundary wall between Ghosuṇḍī and Bassi, and one in the inner wall of the Hāthībāḍā enclosure near Nagari. The legible words include Gājāyana, Pārāśarīputra, Sarvatāta, aśvamedha-yājin, Saṃkarṣaṇa-Vāsudeva, pūjāśilā-prākāra (stone enclosure for worship) and Nārāyaṇa-vāṭikā.

D. R. Bhandarkar's edition (Epigraphia Indica 22) reads the record as the building of the enclosure called Nārāyaṇa-vāṭikā for Saṅkarṣaṇa and Vāsudeva. Harry Falk notes that the king names neither his father nor the title rāja. The record matters because it links the Vṛṣṇi pair with the name Nārāyaṇa, and because a royal patron combines Vedic royal ritual (the aśvamedha) with bhāgavata devotion.

location.label: Nagari (ancient Madhyamikā), near Chittorgarh, Rajasthan, India (findspots)

attributes.findspot: Ghosuṇḍī (c. 4.8 km SW of Chittorgarh) and Hāthībāḍā enclosure near Nagari (c. 13 km N of Chittorgarh)
attributes.reading: key words: Gājāyanena Pārāśarīputreṇa … Saṃkarṣaṇa-Vāsudevābhyāṃ … pūjāśilā-prākāro Nārāyaṇa-vāṭikā; Sarvatātena aśvamedha-yājinā (as given on Wikipedia, after Bhandarkar)
attributes.published: D. R. Bhandarkar, Epigraphia Indica XXII, pp. 198–205

image.credit: F. W. Thomas (published 1921, Epigraphia Indica XVI)

nodes.limits: Shows royal patronage of a joint cult of Saṅkarṣaṇa and Vāsudeva in Rajasthan before the Common Era, and an early link with the name Nārāyaṇa. It says nothing about the narrative life of Kṛṣṇa or Balarāma, and the fragmentary text leaves the exact form of the shrine uncertain.
openQuestions: Is 'Nārāyaṇa-vāṭikā' the name of the enclosure or evidence that Nārāyaṇa was already identified with the pair?

nodes.name: Nāṇeghāṭ inscription of Nāganikā
nodes.summary: A long Brāhmī cave inscription at the Nāṇeghāṭ pass (Maharashtra), commissioned by the Sātavāhana queen Nāganikā (Nāyanikā). It opens by invoking Dharma, Indra, Saṅkarṣaṇa and Vāsudeva, the lunar line and the four Lokapālas (Yama, Varuṇa, Kubera, Vāsava), and lists Vedic sacrifices, including two horse sacrifices, with the fees paid for them. Most scholars date it to the 1st century BCE.
nodes.details:
The inscription is cut on the walls of a rock-cut rest-house at the head of a trade route over the Western Ghats. It is attributed to queen Nāganikā (Nāyanikā), probably the widow of Sātakarṇi, acting as queen mother for her son. It records Vedic rites such as the agnyādheya, rājasūya, two aśvamedhas, the gavāmayana and various soma rituals, together with the cattle, coins and other fees given for them.

Documentation: William Sykes made an eye-copy in 1828 and published it in 1833/1837; Bhagvanlal Indraji gave a partial translation in 1878; Georg Bühler published the first complete edition in 1883. Dating views: D. C. Sircar puts it in the second half of the 1st century BCE, and Upinder Singh in the 1st century BCE. Some scholars prefer the 2nd century BCE, and Alcock places it after Kaṇha's Nasik inscription on palaeographic grounds.

dates.label: second half of the 1st century BCE

location.label: Naneghat pass, Pune district, Maharashtra, India (in situ)

attributes.findspot: rock-cut cave at the head of the Nāṇeghāṭ pass
attributes.reading: opening invocation (as summarised on Wikipedia): Dharma, Indra, Saṃkarṣaṇa and Vāsudeva, the descendants of the Moon, and the four Lokapālas Yama, Varuṇa, Kubera and Vāsava
attributes.discovered: copied by W. Sykes in 1828; complete edition by G. Bühler 1883

nodes.limits: Establishes that a Sātavāhana court in the Deccan combined Vedic śrauta sacrifice with invocation of Saṅkarṣaṇa and Vāsudeva in the 1st century BCE. It does not show a Vaiṣṇava theology of avatāras, and the deities are invoked alongside others, not as supreme.

nodes.name: Mora well inscription (Mathurā)
nodes.summary: A fragmentary Sanskrit inscription on a stone slab from the Mora well near Mathurā, from the time of the Mahākṣatrapa Śoḍāsa, son of Rājuvula (c. 15 CE). It records the installation of images (pratimā) of the five Vṛṣṇi heroes (pañcavīra), called bhagavat, in a stone shrine linked to a woman named Toṣā. It is the earliest epigraphic reference to cult images of the Vṛṣṇi heroes.
nodes.details:
Line 2 of the slab refers to the images (pratimā[ḥ]) of the holy five heroes (paṃcavīrāṇāṃ) of the Vṛṣṇis (vṛṣṇīnā[ṃ]), with the epithet bhagavatāṃ. The inscription names the Great Satrap Rājuvula. It is generally taken to date from the rule of his son Śoḍāsa, and Quintanilla gives c. 15 CE. The slab and a male torso, probably one of the five heroes, are in the Government Museum, Mathurā; the slab is identified as GMM Q.1.

The inscription does not name the five heroes. Scholars identify them as Saṅkarṣaṇa, Vāsudeva, Pradyumna, Sāmba and Aniruddha by comparison with a later Purāṇic list (Vāyu Purāṇa). That identification is an argument, not a reading. The Mora mound was excavated in 1911–12.

dates.label: c. 15 CE (time of Śoḍāsa)
dates.basis: names Mahākṣatrapa Rājuvula; satrapal chronology of Mathurā; palaeography

location.label: Mora village, c. 11 km from Mathura, Uttar Pradesh, India (findspot)

attributes.findspot: Mora well, Mora village near Mathurā
attributes.reading: line 2 (fragments): “… pratimā[ḥ] … paṃcavīrāṇāṃ … vṛṣṇīnā[ṃ] … bhagavatāṃ …” (as given on Wikipedia)

image.credit: Ms Sarah Welch (from Lüders & Janert 1961, p. 301)

nodes.limits: Establishes worship of images of five Vṛṣṇi heroes at Mathurā in the early 1st century CE. It does not name them; their identification with Saṅkarṣaṇa, Vāsudeva, Pradyumna, Sāmba and Aniruddha comes from later texts. It is not evidence for the historicity of the Yādava narratives.

nodes.name: Torso of a Vṛṣṇi hero from Mora
nodes.summary: A stone male torso of c. 15 CE found at Mora near Mathurā together with the Mora well inscription and a carved doorjamb. It is now in the Government Museum, Mathurā, and is probably one of the five Vṛṣṇi heroes whose images the inscription records. It is among the earliest surviving cult images associated with the Vāsudeva–Saṅkarṣaṇa group.
nodes.details: Wikipedia's caption describes it as a 'torso probably of one of the five Vrishni heroes, Mora, circa 15 CE, Mathura Museum'. The mound also produced two male torsos and the lower half of a female torso inscribed with the names Kaniṣka and Toṣā; their present location is not stated. Which hero the torso represents cannot be determined.

dates.label: c. 15 CE
dates.basis: association with the dated Mora well inscription; style

location.label: Findspot: Mora, near Mathura, Uttar Pradesh, India

attributes.findspot: Mora mound/well, near Mathurā

nodes.limits: Shows that the Vṛṣṇi heroes were worshipped as life-size anthropomorphic images in the early 1st century CE. The identity of the individual hero is unknown, and the torso is not evidence for the narratives about them.

nodes.name: Vasu doorjamb inscription (Mathurā)
nodes.summary: A twelve-line Sanskrit inscription in Brāhmī on the back of a red sandstone doorjamb found in an old well at Mathurā. It dates from the time of the Mahākṣatrapa Śoḍāsa (early 1st century CE) and records that a donor named Vasu set up a gateway (toraṇa) and railing (vedikā) at the great shrine of Bhagavat Vāsudeva. It is held in the Government Museum, Mathurā (GMM 13.367).
nodes.details:
The first five lines are too damaged to read. The last seven mention a toraṇa, a vedikā and a shrine (mahāsthāna) of Bhagavat Vāsudeva established in Śoḍāsa's time; the name Vāsudeva survives as “-devaḥ” in line 10. Readings differ. Chanda (1920) read catuḥśāla, a quadrangle; N. P. Chakravarti (Epigraphia Indica 24, 1942) thought that unlikely and suggested devakula or śaila; Quintanilla (2007) translates “a stone toraṇa and railing were erected by Vasu at the great temple of Vāsudeva”.

Dating: Salomon places the inscription in Śoḍāsa's time, early 1st century CE, and Quintanilla c. 15 CE. Joanna Williams suggested the carving of the jamb might be later (3rd century CE); Quintanilla argues that carving and inscription are both 1st century.

dates.label: 3rd century CE (carving of the jamb)
dates.view: J. Williams (carving later than the text)

attributes.findspot: an old well at Mathurā (red sandstone doorjamb)
attributes.reading: legible portion mentions toraṇa, vedikā and the shrine of bhagavat Vāsudeva in the time of Śoḍāsa; “-devaḥ” in line 10 (per Wikipedia)

nodes.limits: Establishes a shrine of Bhagavat Vāsudeva at Mathurā with stone gateway and railing in the early 1st century CE. It is not evidence for the Kṛṣṇa-janmabhūmi tradition at any specific modern site, nor for the historicity of Kṛṣṇa's birth at Mathurā.

nodes.name: Coins of Agathocles with Saṅkarṣaṇa and Vāsudeva
nodes.summary: Six Indian-standard silver drachms of the Greco-Bactrian king Agathocles (c. 190–180 BCE), found in 1970 at Aï Khanoum (Afghanistan), each show two male deities. One holds a plough and a pestle or club, the other a conch and a wheel. They are usually identified as Saṅkarṣaṇa-Balarāma and Vāsudeva-Kṛṣṇa, and are often called the earliest unambiguous images of the Vṛṣṇi heroes.
nodes.details:
On 3 October 1970 the French archaeological mission (DAFA) found a hoard in a small room of the palace administrative quarter at Aï Khanoum. It held 677 punch-marked coins and six silver drachms in the name of Agathocles. The drachms carry the deity with plough and pestle or club on the Greek-legend side and the deity with conch and wheel on the Brāhmī side; the Brāhmī legend is given as Rājane Agathukleyesa, “of king Agathocles”.

Evidence class: the coins themselves are class 4. That they show Saṅkarṣaṇa and Vāsudeva is a scholarly identification (class 5), based on the attributes and on the pairing in later Indian inscriptions. The coins show that the iconography of the pair already existed far from Mathurā in the early 2nd century BCE. Aï Khanoum was later looted, and the present whereabouts of the six drachms could not be verified.

dates.label: deposited before c. 145 BCE
dates.basis: Aï Khanoum abandoned c. 145 BCE after nomad capture

location.label: Findspot: Aï Khanoum, Takhar province, Afghanistan

attributes.findspot: Aï Khanoum, palace administrative quarter (hoard found 3 October 1970)
attributes.repository: unverified (excavated finds went to the National Museum of Afghanistan; whereabouts of these six coins not confirmed)
attributes.reading: Brāhmī legend given as “Rājane Agathukleyesa” (King Agathocles), per Wikipedia
attributes.discovered: 1970, DAFA excavations directed by Paul Bernard

nodes.limits: Shows that two deities with the attributes later associated with Saṅkarṣaṇa and Vāsudeva were depicted on royal coins c. 190–180 BCE. The identification is argued from attributes, and the coins carry no divine names. They do not show the Kṛṣṇa narrative, nor any connection with the Bhagavad Gītā.
openQuestions: Where are the six 1970 Aï Khanoum drachms now held, and did they survive the looting of the Kabul museum?

nodes.name: Megasthenes’ “Herakles” of the Sourasenoi as Kṛṣṇa
nodes.subtype: identification of a deity in a Greek ethnography
nodes.summary: Megasthenes (c. 300 BCE), as excerpted by Arrian, Diodorus and Strabo, reported that an Indian people called the Sourasenoi especially honoured “Herakles”. They had two great cities, Methora and Kleisobora, and the navigable river Iobares ran through their land. Many scholars identify this Herakles with (Hari-)Kṛṣṇa, the Sourasenoi with the Śūrasenas, Methora with Mathurā and the Iobares with the Yamunā. Others propose Indra, Śiva or Balarāma, or doubt that the Greek label maps onto a single Indian deity.
nodes.details:
The case for: the geography fits closely (Śūrasena country, Mathurā, the Yamunā). Grammatical and epigraphic evidence shows Vāsudeva devotion by the 2nd century BCE (Pāṇini 4.3.98; Heliodorus pillar; Agathocles coins). Edwin Bryant writes that there is little doubt the Sourasenoi are the Śūrasenas.

The case against, or for caution: Greek authors routinely mapped foreign gods onto Herakles or Dionysos by analogy. Megasthenes' Herakles is “earth-born”, is credited with founding cities and with a daughter, Pandaia, and carries Herakles' club and lion-skin. These are Greek traits, not specifically Kṛṣṇa's. Dahlquist (1962) argued for Indra. Puskás (cited on Wikipedia) notes there is no independent evidence of Kṛṣṇa worship as early as the 4th century BCE. The fragments survive only as later excerpts.
nodes.limits: Even if correct, the identification shows only that a Herakles-like deity was honoured in the Mathurā region c. 300 BCE as perceived by a Greek observer. It does not establish the content of Kṛṣṇa narratives at that date or the historicity of Kṛṣṇa.
openQuestions: Can the Kleisobora of the fragments be securely located?
Does 'Herakles' render Hari, Kṛṣṇa, Saṅkarṣaṇa-Balarāma, or a generic heroic god?

nodes.name: Chāndogya’s Kṛṣṇa Devakīputra as the epic Kṛṣṇa
nodes.summary: The Chāndogya Upaniṣad (CU 3.17.6) names a Kṛṣṇa Devakīputra, “son of Devakī”, as a pupil of Ghora Āṅgirasa who learns a teaching that allegorises the sacrifice. Some scholars take him to be the epic and Purāṇic Kṛṣṇa, son of Devakī, which would be the earliest textual reference to Kṛṣṇa. Others regard the shared name and matronymic as a coincidence, or the verse as an unrelated figure.
nodes.details:
For the identification: the name together with the matronymic Devakīputra is distinctive. Raychaudhuri (1920) and others built early Vaiṣṇava history on it, and some note parallels between Ghora's teaching and ideas in the Bhagavad Gītā. Max Müller allowed that the verse might be a source of later Kṛṣṇa lore. Archer argues the shared name in one verse cannot easily be dismissed.

Against: the Upaniṣadic passage gives no Vṛṣṇi, Yādava or epic context, and the name Kṛṣṇa was not rare. The later Śāṇḍilya Bhakti Sūtras, which cite other Upaniṣads, never use this verse (noted on Wikipedia). Bryant and Ekstrand allow that the Chāndogya figure may be a different person. The vedic agent's char:krishna-devakiputra is therefore kept apart from char:krishna.

dates.label: c. 7th–6th century BCE (Chāndogya, as commonly dated)
dates.basis: scholarly dating of the early prose Upaniṣads

nodes.limits: A single verse naming a pupil cannot by itself establish that the epic Kṛṣṇa tradition existed in the Upaniṣadic period; nor can the absence of context disprove it.
openQuestions: Is there any datable intermediate source linking Devakīputra with the Vṛṣṇis before the Mahābhārata?

nodes.name: Heliodorus inscription B echoes a Mahābhārata verse
nodes.subtype: textual parallel claimed for an inscription
nodes.summary: Inscription B on the Heliodorus pillar lists three immortal steps: self-restraint, generosity and attentiveness (dama, cāga, apramāda). Since Raychaudhuri, scholars have compared this triad with a verse in the Mahābhārata's Strīparvan (MBh book 11). Some treat it as evidence that the epic, or its ethical verse tradition, was known in Vidiśā in the late 2nd century BCE.
nodes.details: Wikipedia, citing Irwin and Raychaudhuri, says inscription B “recites a verse” from the Mahābhārata. The Krishna article gives the locator as Mahābhārata 11.7. This record does not supply a Critical-Edition verse number because none was verified. A shared triad of virtues may come from a common pool of gnomic verse rather than from the epic itself, so the parallel does not date the Mahābhārata.

dates.label: late 2nd century BCE (date of the inscription)

nodes.limits: At most this shows the triad dama–tyāga–apramāda circulated by the late 2nd century BCE. It does not show that the Mahābhārata existed in written or epic form at that time.
openQuestions: Which Critical Edition verse (MBh 11.7.x) is the closest parallel, and is the triad attested elsewhere (e.g. in Buddhist or Jain gnomic verse)?

nodes.name: “Paśupati” seal, Mohenjo-daro
nodes.summary: A steatite stamp seal (c. 3.56 × 3.53 cm) excavated at Mohenjo-daro in 1928–29. It shows a horned, seated figure, possibly three-faced, in a yoga-like posture, surrounded by an elephant, a tiger, a water buffalo and a rhinoceros, with two deer or ibexes below and seven Indus signs above. John Marshall called it a “proto-Śiva” as Paśupati, lord of animals. The identification has been widely disputed since the 1960s. The seal is now in the National Museum, New Delhi.
nodes.details:
Findspot: Block 1, southern portion of the DK-G area of Mohenjo-daro, at a depth of 3.9 m, during the 1928–29 season of the Archaeological Survey of India. Ernest Mackay, who directed the excavations, numbered it 420 in his report Further Excavations at Mohenjo-daro (1938). He assigned it to his Intermediate I period, now roughly 2350–2000 BCE. At Partition in 1947 it was allocated to India and is held in the National Museum, New Delhi.

The iconography is described neutrally as a horned headdress, bangles, a seated posture with heels together, surrounding animals, and an undeciphered inscription. Because the Indus script is not read, any identification of the figure is an interpretation (see claim:proto-shiva).

location.label: Findspot: Mohenjo-daro, Larkana district, Sindh, Pakistan (held in New Delhi)

attributes.findspot: Mohenjo-daro, DK-G area, Block 1, depth 3.9 m (1928–29)
attributes.accession: Mackay seal no. 420 (excavation number; museum accession not verified)
attributes.discovered: 1928–29 season, ASI (excavation directed by E. J. H. Mackay)

image.credit: Unknown Indus Valley Civilization seal-maker, Mohenjo-daro (image via F. W. Pritchett, Columbia University)

nodes.limits: Establishes that a horned, seated figure among animals was a motif of Mature Harappan glyptic art. Without a deciphered script it cannot establish the figure's name or role, or any continuity with the later Śiva of Vedic, epic or Purāṇic religion.
openQuestions: What is the National Museum's accession number for the seal?
Do the other Mohenjo-daro seated-figure seals (e.g. nos. 222, 235) share the same iconography?

nodes.name: The “proto-Śiva” interpretation of the Paśupati seal
nodes.subtype: identification of a prehistoric image with a later deity
nodes.summary: John Marshall (1928–29; Mohenjo-daro and the Indus Civilization, 1931) proposed that the seated horned figure on the Mohenjo-daro seal 420 is a prototype of Śiva as Paśupati (lord of animals) and Mahāyogin. His view was widely accepted for about two generations. Since the 1960s it has been contested on iconographic, methodological and chronological grounds. There is no scholarly consensus.
nodes.details:
Marshall's arguments: (1) the figure is three-faced, possibly with a fourth face behind, like later multi-faced Śiva; (2) the horned headdress resembles a trident; (3) the posture is yogic (Śiva as Mahāyogin); (4) the surrounding animals suggest Paśupati; (5) in 1931 he added a possible ithyphallic feature and the deer below the seat.

Critiques: Sullivan (1964) argued for a female figure, reading the “phallus” as the end of a girdle. Doris Srinivasan (1975–76; 1997) argued that the side “faces” are bovine ears and the figure a buffalo-man, not a proto-Śiva. Hiltebeitel (1978) read the horns as a buffalo's and linked the figure to Mahiṣa and to the goddess's vāhanas. Parpola compared Proto-Elamite seated bulls and linked the figure to an aquatic deity; Fairservis and Krishna Rao proposed other identifications (the latter Indra). Doniger and Samuel urge caution, and Samuel notes the interpretations “certainly cannot all be right”. A methodological objection is that the Indus script is undeciphered and that some 1,500 years separate the seal from the earliest clear Śaiva texts and images.
nodes.limits: The claim cannot at present be verified or falsified. Even if the figure were a deity of animals, that would not establish continuity of name, cult or theology with historical Śaivism.
openQuestions: Would a decipherment of the Indus script, or a bilingual, settle the figure's identity?

nodes.name: Gudimallam liṅga
nodes.summary: A stone liṅga about 1.5 m high in the Paraśurāmeśvara temple at Gudimallam, near Tirupati (Andhra Pradesh). It carries a standing two-armed figure in high relief, holding a ram or antelope and a water pot, with an axe on the shoulder, standing on a crouching dwarf or yakṣa. It is widely regarded as one of the earliest surviving liṅgas with a figural Śiva. Dates proposed range from the 3rd century BCE to the 3rd–4th century CE.
nodes.details:
The liṅga is carved from hard, dark brown local stone, with a seven-faceted shaft about a foot in diameter. It is still in worship and stands in a square stone enclosure with a modern golden frame. The temple building itself is later (Cōḻa and Vijayanagara periods) and has been protected by the ASI since 1954.

In 1973–74 the ASI under I. K. Sarma (Karthikeya Sharma) excavated around it. They found that the liṅga originally had a pedestal, along with Sātavāhana-period sherds, Black-and-Red Ware attributed to the 2nd–3rd century CE, and large bricks. Dating views: Harle and Blurton put it in the 2nd–1st century BCE, and Elgood at the end of the BCE period into the 1st century CE. P. Arundhati compares it with Bharhut, Karle and Nāṇeghāṭ sculpture and proposes an early Sātavāhana date. Doniger suggests the 3rd century BCE. Other authors propose the 2nd or 3rd–4th century CE.

dates.label: 2nd–4th century CE
dates.basis: stylistic; association with excavated Black-and-Red Ware of the 2nd–3rd century CE

location.label: Gudimallam, Tirupati district, Andhra Pradesh, India (in worship)

attributes.findspot: in situ in the sanctum of the Paraśurāmeśvara temple
attributes.dimensions: height c. 5 ft (1.5 m); shaft c. 1 ft diameter, seven-faceted
attributes.iconography: standing figure with ram/antelope, water pot and paraśu, on a dwarf/yakṣa
attributes.discovered: described by an early author named Rao on Wikipedia (probably T. A. Gopinatha Rao); ASI excavation 1973–74 under I. K. Sarma

nodes.limits: Shows that a liṅga with an anthropomorphic deity was made and worshipped in the south-eastern Deccan around the turn of the Common Era (date disputed). It does not show which myths were told about the deity, and identifying the figure as Śiva rests on later iconography.
openQuestions: Does the 1973–74 stratigraphy date the installation, or only later activity around the liṅga?

nodes.name: The Gudimallam liṅga dates to the 2nd–1st century BCE
nodes.summary: Several art historians (e.g. Harle) date the Gudimallam liṅga to the 2nd–1st century BCE on stylistic grounds. If correct, it is the earliest surviving figural liṅga in worship. Other scholars prefer dates in the early centuries CE, partly because of finds from the 1973–74 excavation.
nodes.limits: Whatever its date, the liṅga does not by itself date the textual liṅga myths (e.g. Liṅgodbhava) or Śaiva theology.
openQuestions: Could scientific dating (e.g. of associated organic material) refine the stylistic dates?

nodes.name: Oesho (OHÞO), deity of Kuṣāṇa coins
nodes.summary: Oesho (Bactrian ΟΗϷΟ) is the name of a deity on Kuṣāṇa coins from Kaniṣka I onward. On some issues he is shown with a bull, a trident and, from Huviṣka, several heads and four arms. Many numismatists identify him with Śiva. Others, notably Katsumi Tanabe and Helmut Humbach, read the name as the Iranian wind god Vāyu (Wēš), whose image took on Śaiva features.
nodes.details: The Bactrian legend OHÞO appears on gold and copper coins of Kaniṣka I, Huviṣka and Vāsudeva I, and later on coins of the later Kuṣāṇas. The figure's attributes include the trident, the vajra, a water pot, the bull, and on some coins multiple heads and arms. The graph does not merge Oesho with Śiva. Two IDENTIFIED_WITH assertions record the competing readings (deity:shiva; deity:vayu), and claim:oesho-shiva-identity holds the debate.
nodes.limits: The coins establish that a deity named Oesho with Śaiva-like attributes was part of the Kuṣāṇa royal pantheon. They do not establish whether Kuṣāṇa viewers understood him as Śiva, as Vāyu, or as both.

nodes.name: Oesho on Kuṣāṇa coins is Śiva
nodes.summary: The traditional numismatic view holds that the Kuṣāṇa coin deity Oesho is Śiva, as his trident, bull and multiple heads and arms suggest. The alternative view holds that Oesho is the Bactrian form of the Iranian wind god Vāyu (Wēš). On this view the Śaiva iconography was borrowed and full syncretism with Śiva came later, as seen in Sogdian Weshparkar.
nodes.details:
For: the iconography of trident, bull, ithyphallic figure on some Wima Kadphises coppers and multi-headed figures on Huviṣka's issues. Wima Kadphises' Kharoṣṭhī legend includes mahiśvarasa, read by many as “of the devotee of Maheśvara (Śiva)”, though others read it as a royal epithet. A Kharoṣṭhī inscription from Māṭ near Mathurā is reported to commemorate Wima as devoted to, and receiving his kingdom from, Śiva.

Against: the name ΟΗϷΟ is best explained as Bactrian for Vāyu (Avestan vaiiu), and the Rabatak inscription lists Iranian deities. Tanabe (1997) argues the coin deity is Vāyu and that Śaiva syncretism came later through Sogdian art. Humbach reads Weshparkar as Vayuš uparō kairyō.
nodes.limits: Resolving the identification would clarify Kuṣāṇa religious policy, but neither reading establishes the content of contemporary Śaiva texts.

nodes.name: Gold coins of Wima Kadphises with a deity and bull
nodes.subtype: coin type (gold double stater, stater, quarter stater; copper)
nodes.summary: Gold and copper coins of the Kuṣāṇa king Wima (Vima) Kadphises show on the reverse a deity holding a long trident, sometimes with a bull and on some coppers ithyphallic, together with the triratna or nandipada symbol. The Kharoṣṭhī legend calls the king mahiśvara, read by many as “devotee of Maheśvara”. The deity is usually identified with Śiva. Wima was also the first Kuṣāṇa ruler to issue gold coins.
nodes.details:
Obverse: the king, with Greek legend ΒΑΣΙΛΕΥΣ ΟΟΗΜΟ ΚΑΔΦΙΣΗΣ. Reverse: a deity with a long trident, sometimes with a bull. The Kharoṣṭhī legend as given on Wikipedia reads MAHARAJASA RAJADIRAJASA SARVALOGA ISVARASA MAHISVARASA VIMA KATHPHISASA TRADARA. The gold standard was about 8 g, in double staters, staters and quarter staters.

The core registry calls this the 'Oesho coin'. On Wima's own coins the deity is not labelled OHÞO; that label appears from Kaniṣka I onward (see art:kushan-oesho-coins). This entity is a coin type, not one specimen. Cleveland Museum of Art 1999.225 is a Wima gold coin with a Herakles reverse, a different type.

dates.label: c. 50–78 CE (older chronology)
dates.basis: pre-Rabatak chronology used in some museum records

attributes.reading: Kharoṣṭhī legend (per Wikipedia): MAHARAJASA RAJADIRAJASA SARVALOGA ISVARASA MAHISVARASA VIMA KATHPHISASA TRADARA

sources.locator: 1999.225 (Wima Kadphises gold coin, Hercules reverse — a different type)

nodes.limits: Establishes Śaiva-style iconography and probably Śaiva devotion in Kuṣāṇa royal imagery in the late 1st or early 2nd century CE. It does not show which Śaiva texts or sects existed, and the epithet mahiśvara is open to more than one reading.

nodes.name: Kuṣāṇa coins naming OHÞO (Oesho)
nodes.summary: Gold and copper coin types of Kaniṣka I, Huviṣka and Vāsudeva I bear the Bactrian legend ΟΗϷΟ (Oesho) beside a deity with a trident, vajra, water pot and sometimes a bull. Under Huviṣka the deity has three heads and four arms. The type is central to the debate over whether Oesho is Śiva or the Iranian Vāyu.
nodes.details: Captions on Wikipedia's Oesho article show Oesho with bull and trident on coins of Vāsudeva I, holding vajra and trident on coins of Huviṣka, and with a worshipper on a 3rd-century Bactrian issue. Kaniṣka's coins place Oesho in a mixed pantheon with Mao (moon), Miiro (sun), Nana, Oado (wind) and the Buddha. That makes a simple 'Hindu' reading of the series misleading.

dates.label: c. 127–230 CE (Kaniṣka I to Vāsudeva I)

nodes.limits: The series shows a named deity with Śaiva-like attributes in the Kuṣāṇa royal pantheon. The name points to an Iranian origin, so it cannot alone establish Śiva worship by the Kuṣāṇa court.

nodes.name: Varāha relief, Udayagiri Cave 5
nodes.summary: A monumental rock-cut relief in the shallow niche called Cave 5 at Udayagiri near Vidiśā. It shows Viṣṇu as the boar-headed Varāha lifting the Earth goddess, who clings to his tusk, out of the cosmic ocean, watched by rows of gods and sages. It dates from the reign of the Gupta king Candragupta II (c. 401–412 CE) and is among the most studied reliefs of the Gupta period.
nodes.details:
Varāha stands in a heroic posture with the goddess Earth (Bhūdevī or Pṛthvī) at his tusk. The surrounding registers include Brahmā, Śiva, the Ādityas, Agni, Vāyu, the Vasus and Rudras, ṛṣis, a nāga king, and the sages Nārada and Tumburu. The Udayagiri article identifies a kneeling figure below as probably Candragupta II, with his minister Vīrasena.

Dating: no inscription is cut on the panel. Its date rests on the dated Gupta inscriptions of the same hill, Cave 6 (Gupta year 82 = 401/402 CE) and Cave 8 (Vīrasena). Heinrich von Stietencron proposed 410–412 CE and linked the panel to Candragupta's assumption of the title Vikramāditya. Michael Willis (2009) reads the hill as a royal ritual landscape tied to the solstice.

dates.label: c. 401–415 CE (reign of Candragupta II)
dates.basis: association with Cave 6 inscription of Gupta year 82 and the Cave 8 inscription of Vīrasena

location.label: Udayagiri hills, near Vidisha, Madhya Pradesh, India (in situ)

attributes.findspot: Udayagiri Cave 5 (a niche on the east face of the hill)
attributes.iconography: Varāha (man-boar) lifting Bhūdevī; cosmic ocean with nāga; assembled gods and sages
attributes.datingMethod: association with dated Gupta inscriptions at the site
attributes.discovered: studied by A. Cunningham, reported in ASI Tour Reports vol. X (1880)

nodes.limits: Shows that the Varāha avatāra narrative was a major royal theme by c. 401–415 CE. It does not date the Purāṇic texts that narrate the story, and the reading of the panel as royal political allegory is interpretive.
openQuestions: Is the kneeling figure Candragupta II, a nāga, or a devotee?

nodes.name: Udayagiri Cave 6 inscription of the time of Candragupta II (year 82)
aliases: Udayagiri Cave Inscription of Chandragupta II, Year 82
nodes.summary: A short Sanskrit inscription at the entrance of Udayagiri Cave 6, dated year 82 (Gupta era, 401/402 CE), on the 11th day of the bright half of Āṣāḍha. It records the pious gift (deyadharma) of a Sanakānīka mahārāja, son of Viṣṇudāsa and grandson of Chagalaga, who calls himself a devotee of the feet of the paramabhaṭṭāraka mahārājādhirāja Candragupta. It is the earliest dated record of Candragupta II.
nodes.details: The edition on Dharmalekha (from the Siddham project) gives the date as “saṁvatsare 80 2” in Āṣāḍha, śukla 11, and the key word deyadharmmaḥ, “pious gift”. The donor's personal name or domain after “mahārāja” is lost. Fleet suggested “ḍha” and Sircar “Soḍhala”, but both are guesses. The first critical edition is Fleet 1888 (CII III, item 3).

location.label: Udayagiri hills, near Vidisha, Madhya Pradesh, India (in situ)

attributes.findspot: Udayagiri Cave 6
attributes.reading: “saṁvatsare 80 2 …” (year 82) … “deyadharmmaḥ” … Sanakānika mahārāja, son of mahārāja Viṣṇudāsa, grandson of mahārāja Chagalaga … pādānuddhyāta of Candragupta (per Dharmalekha)

nodes.limits: Dates Gupta-period activity at Udayagiri to 401/402 CE and shows a feudatory acknowledging Candragupta II. It records a gift but does not name the deity of Cave 6, and it does not date every sculpture on the hill.

nodes.name: Udayagiri Cave 8 inscription of Vīrasena
nodes.summary: A five-line Sanskrit verse inscription in Udayagiri Cave 8 (the Tawa cave). It records that Vīrasena of the Kautsa gotra, surnamed Śāba, a minister of Candragupta II, made the cave as a temple of Śambhu (Śiva) when he came to the place with the king. It is undated but falls within Candragupta II's reign.
nodes.details: The inscription shows Śaiva and Vaiṣṇava foundations side by side on a hill patronised by the Gupta court. The Varāha relief is Vaiṣṇava, and this record says the cave was made out of devotion to Śambhu.

location.label: Udayagiri hills, near Vidisha, Madhya Pradesh, India (in situ)

attributes.findspot: Udayagiri Cave 8 (Tawa cave)

nodes.limits: Establishes royal-ministerial Śaiva patronage in Candragupta II's reign. It does not describe Śaiva doctrine or ritual.

nodes.name: Iron pillar inscription of Candra (Delhi)
nodes.summary: A Sanskrit verse inscription on the wrought-iron pillar now in the Qutb complex, Mehrauli, Delhi. It records that a king named Candra, a devotee of Viṣṇu, set up a standard (dhvaja) of Viṣṇu on a hill called Viṣṇupada. By script and style it dates to the late 4th or early 5th century CE, and Candra is generally identified with Candragupta II.
nodes.details: The pillar is 7.21 m high, forge-welded wrought iron weighing over six tonnes. Its resistance to corrosion is attributed to a high phosphorus content. Where it first stood is disputed. Fleet (1898) suggested Mathurā. Dass and Balasubramaniam (2004), followed by Michael Willis, proposed Udayagiri. F. B. Flood (2009) argued it was brought from Vidiśā by Iltutmish. A later short inscription of Samvat 1109 is linked with the Tomara king Anaṅgapāla, and its reading is contested.

dates.label: late 4th – early 5th century CE
dates.basis: palaeography; poetic style; identification of Candra with Candragupta II

location.label: Qutb complex, Mehrauli, Delhi, India (present location; not original)

attributes.repository: in situ at Qutb complex (moved from an original site)

nodes.limits: Shows royal Vaiṣṇava devotion and the erection of a Viṣṇu-dhvaja c. 400 CE. It does not say where Viṣṇupada was, and the identification of Candra is argued, not stated.
openQuestions: Was the pillar's original site Udayagiri, Mathurā or elsewhere?

nodes.name: Colossal Varāha of Eran
nodes.summary: A free-standing red sandstone image of Varāha in full boar form, about 4.2 m long and 3.4 m high, standing in the open at Eran (ancient Airikiṇa). Small figures of gods and sages cover its body and the Earth goddess hangs from its tusk. An eight-line Sanskrit inscription on its chest is dated in the first regnal year of the Hūṇa king Toramāṇa. It records that Dhanyaviṣṇu, younger brother of the late Mātṛviṣṇu, had a stone temple built for Nārāyaṇa in the form of a boar.
nodes.details: The image stands among the ruins of a Gupta-period temple group at Eran, a site whose inscriptions run from Samudragupta to the Goparāja memorial pillar of 510 CE. Cunningham reported the site in ASI Reports vol. X (1880). The Wikipedia article on the inscription gives its date as after 510 and before 513 CE, following R. K. Mookerji. The Toramana article also gives the bound 'after 484/85 CE', which leaves a wider range open.

dates.label: c. 510–513 CE (first year of Toramāṇa)
dates.basis: regnal year of Toramāṇa in the chest inscription; historical reconstruction

dates.label: between c. 485 and 515 CE
dates.basis: after Budhagupta's Eran pillar (484/85) and before Toramāṇa's death (c. 515)

location.label: Eran, Sagar district, Madhya Pradesh, India (in situ)

attributes.findspot: Eran, in the open among Gupta temple ruins
attributes.dimensions: c. 4.22 m long × 3.40 m high × 1.56 m wide
attributes.datingMethod: inscription on the chest (regnal year 1 of Toramāṇa)

nodes.limits: Shows Varāha worship as Nārāyaṇa, and a local Vaiṣṇava family acknowledging a Hūṇa overlord, in central India c. 500 CE. It is evidence for cult and politics, not for the cosmogonic event depicted.

nodes.name: Eran boar inscription of Toramāṇa
nodes.summary: An eight-line Sanskrit inscription in Brāhmī on the chest of the colossal Varāha at Eran, dated the 10th day of Phālguna in the first year of the reign of the mahārājādhirāja Toramāṇa. It records that Dhanyaviṣṇu, younger brother of the deceased mahārāja Mātṛviṣṇu, built a stone temple of the boar-formed Nārāyaṇa at Airikiṇa (Eran).
nodes.details: The first three lines are in verse and the rest in prose. Fleet's and Hall's translations differ in wording but agree on the content. The inscription is a key document for the Hūṇa (Alchon) advance into central India. The Toramana article quotes its opening: “In year one of the reign of the King of Kings Sri-Toramana …”.

dates.label: first regnal year of Toramāṇa (c. 510–513 CE per Mookerji)

location.label: Eran, Sagar district, Madhya Pradesh, India (in situ)

attributes.findspot: chest of the Eran Varāha
attributes.reading: dated in the first year of mahārājādhirāja Śrī-Toramāṇa; Dhanyaviṣṇu builds a temple of Nārāyaṇa in boar form (summary per Wikipedia/Fleet)

nodes.limits: Dates the Varāha's dedication relative to Toramāṇa's reign only. The conversion to an absolute year is reconstructed, not stated.

nodes.name: Eran pillar inscription of the time of Budhagupta (Gupta year 165)
nodes.summary: A Sanskrit inscription on a monolithic pillar at Eran topped by a double Garuḍa with a wheel behind. It is dated Gupta year 165 (484/485 CE) in the reign of Budhagupta and records the erection of the pillar as a standard in honour of Janārdana (Viṣṇu).
nodes.details: According to Fleet's edition the pillar was raised by the brothers Mātṛviṣṇu and Dhanyaviṣṇu, the same family as the boar inscription. The Wikipedia article checked does not name them, so this detail is marked from recall. Together, the two records show one local family moving from Gupta to Hūṇa suzerainty within a generation.

location.label: Eran, Sagar district, Madhya Pradesh, India (in situ)

attributes.findspot: Eran, near the platform of the pillar

nodes.limits: Establishes a Viṣṇu-dhvaja dedicated under Budhagupta in 484/85 CE. It does not by itself date the adjacent temples.

nodes.name: Gajendramokṣa panel, Daśāvatāra temple, Deogarh
nodes.summary: A relief niche (about 3.25 × 5 ft) on the north wall of the Gupta-period Daśāvatāra temple at Deogarh. It shows the elephant Gajendra, held in a lotus pond by a nāga and makara, raising a lotus in his trunk as Viṣṇu arrives on Garuḍa to free him. It is one of the earliest monumental depictions of the Gajendramokṣa story.
nodes.details: The temple was found in jungle growth c. 1871 by Charles Strahan, visited by Cunningham in 1875, surveyed by P. C. Mukerji in 1899, and published by M. S. Vats (1952). The three great wall niches face north (Gajendramokṣa), east (Nara-Nārāyaṇa) and south (Anantaśayana).

nodes.summary: The east wall niche of the Daśāvatāra temple at Deogarh shows the sages Nara and Nārāyaṇa seated in penance with rosaries, with flying celestials above, a lion and a deer below, and four-headed Brahmā on a lotus.

nodes.name: Anantaśayana Viṣṇu panel, Daśāvatāra temple, Deogarh
nodes.summary: The south wall niche of the Daśāvatāra temple at Deogarh shows Viṣṇu reclining on the seven-hooded serpent Śeṣa (Ananta), with Lakṣmī at his feet and a small four-headed Brahmā above. In a register below stand five male figures and a woman, read as the Pāṇḍavas and Draupadī or as personified weapons (āyudhapuruṣas) confronting Madhu and Kaiṭabha.
nodes.details: The identification of the lower register is debated. Wikipedia's caption reads it as the Pāṇḍavas with Draupadī, and the Commons file title records the alternative reading as āyudhapuruṣas facing Madhu and Kaiṭabha. Brahmā is shown above, not rising from the navel as in later iconography.

dates.label: c. 425–525 CE

It does not date the textual versions of the story or show that the events happened. The reading of the lower register as the Pāṇḍavas is disputed.

nodes.name: Rāmāyaṇa and Kṛṣṇa plinth panels, Deogarh
nodes.summary: A series of relief panels from the plinth of the Daśāvatāra temple at Deogarh, many now in the National Museum, New Delhi.
