nodes.name: Caṅkam (Sangam) literature
nodes.summary: The earliest corpus of Tamil poetry — the Eight Anthologies (Eṭṭuttokai) and Ten Idylls (Pattuppāṭṭu) — together with the grammar Tolkāppiyam, composed roughly between the turn of the era and the 5th–6th century CE, with later layers such as the Paripāṭal and Tirumurukāṟṟuppaṭai.
nodes.limits: The corpus is largely secular (akam love and puṟam heroic poetry); religious references are scattered and later poems are more devotional.

nodes.name: Tirumurai
nodes.summary: The twelve-book canon of Tamil Śaiva devotional literature: Tēvāram (1–7), Māṇikkavācakar’s Tiruvācakam and Tirukkōvaiyār (8), Tiruvicaippā and Tiruppallāṇṭu (9), Tirumūlar’s Tirumantiram (10), a miscellany including the Tirumurukāṟṟuppaṭai (11) and Cēkkiḻār’s Periya Purāṇam (12).

dates.event: arrangement of books 1–11 (Nampi Āṇṭār Nampi) and addition of book 12
dates.label: c. late 10th – 12th c. CE
dates.basis: tradition of Nampi’s compilation; date of the Periya Purāṇam

nodes.name: Pāñcarātra Saṃhitās
nodes.summary: The scriptures of the Pāñcarātra tradition — traditionally 108, with over 200 known titles — including the Sāttvata, Pauṣkara and Jayākhya (“three gems”), the Ahirbudhnya, Pārameśvara, Īśvara and Lakṣmī Tantra.

dates.label: c. 7th–14th c. CE (disputed)
dates.basis: cross-citation and borrowing from Śaiva tantras

nodes.name: Śaiva Āgamas (Siddhānta tantras)
nodes.summary: The Sanskrit scriptures of the Śaiva Siddhānta, traditionally twenty-eight Āgamas with subsidiary Upāgamas, beginning with the Kāmika; the earliest surviving tantra of the wider Mantramārga is the Niśvāsatattvasaṃhitā.

dates.event: composition of the surviving Siddhānta scriptures
dates.label: c. 5th–12th c. CE

nodes.limits: The South Indian “28 Āgamas” in current temple use are in part later recastings; the early Siddhānta canon is reconstructed largely from Nepalese manuscripts.

nodes.name: Śākta Tantras
nodes.summary: Tantras centred on the Goddess and her retinue (yoginīs, Kālī, Tripurasundarī, Kubjikā), including the Brahmayāmala (Picumata) of the early Vidyāpīṭha, the Kaula texts and later Śrīvidyā literature.

dates.label: c. 7th–15th c. CE
dates.basis: manuscripts and citation by Kashmirian authors

nodes.name: Maṅgalkāvya
nodes.summary: Bengali narrative poems (c. 13th–18th c.) celebrating the power of local or Purāṇic deities — Manasā, Caṇḍī, Dharma Ṭhākur, Annadā — and the establishment of their worship among reluctant devotees.

nodes.name: Sthala-purāṇas (temple and place legends)
nodes.summary: Texts recounting the sacred history of a particular shrine or town — its deity’s manifestation, divine marriages, miracles and royal patrons — in Sanskrit (often as māhātmyas within Purāṇas) and in Tamil and other languages.
nodes.details: Shulman (1980) analyses the Tamil talapurāṇams as a genre with recurring motifs (the goddess’s marriage, the self-manifested liṅga, the local flood myth). Their claims are evidence of temple tradition (class 6), not of the dates of the temples’ structures.
nodes.limits: A sthala-purāṇa’s account of a temple’s foundation is not a date for the surviving building.

nodes.name: Tolkāppiyam
nodes.summary: The oldest extant Tamil grammar and poetics, in three books (phonology, morphology, “subject-matter” — poruḷ). Its Akattiṇaiyiyal assigns presiding deities to the landscapes: Māyōṉ to the forest-pasture (mullai), Cēyōṉ to the hills (kuṟiñci), Vēntaṉ to farmland (marutam) and Varuṇaṉ to the shore (neytal).
nodes.details: Sūtra 5 of the Akattiṇaiyiyal reads: “māyōṉ mēya kāṭuṟai ulakamum / cēyōṉ mēya maivarai ulakamum / vēntaṉ mēya tīmpuṉal ulakamum / varuṇaṉ mēya perumaṇal ulakamum / mullai kuṟiñci marutam neytal eṉac / colliya muṟaiyāṟ collavum paṭumē.” The commentator Nacciṉārkkiṉiyar glosses Māyōṉ as “the one of sea-dark colour” (kaṭalvaṇṇaṉ) and Cēyōṉ as “red Murukaṉ.”
nodes.limits: The sūtra names Māyōṉ and Cēyōṉ; their glosses as Viṣṇu/Kṛṣṇa and Murukaṉ come from medieval commentators and modern scholarship.

nodes.name: Paripāṭal
nodes.summary: A late Caṅkam anthology (fifth of the Eight Anthologies) of musical poems: of the 24 that survive complete, 7 are addressed to Tirumāl (Viṣṇu/Kṛṣṇa), 8 to Murukaṉ (Cevvēḷ) and 9 to the river Vaikai at Madurai.
nodes.details: The poems to Murukaṉ celebrate the Tiruparaṅkuṉṟam hill near Madurai and know the Skanda birth story; the Tirumāl poems are among the earliest Tamil Vaiṣṇava devotional verse.

dates.label: c. 3rd–6th c. CE
dates.view: Vaiyapuri Pillai & Takahashi (3rd–4th c.); Ramanujan (c. 6th c.)

nodes.name: Tirumurukāṟṟuppaṭai
nodes.summary: Nakkīrar’s poem “guiding [the devotee] to Murukaṉ,” the first of the Ten Idylls and also included in Tirumurai 11. It describes six places where Murukaṉ is present and blends Tamil and northern (Skanda) imagery.
nodes.details: The poem (317 lines in the critical edition) uses the old guide-poem form, in which a bard directs another to a generous patron, now redirected to the god. Later tradition maps its six sites onto the six temples of the āṟupaṭai vīṭu.

dates.label: late Caṅkam (c. 3rd–6th c. CE); some scholars later

nodes.name: Tiruppāvai
nodes.summary: Āṇṭāḷ’s thirty Tamil verses in the voice of cowherd girls who rise before dawn in the month of Mārkaḻi to wake one another and Kṛṣṇa for a vow (nōṉpu). It is part of the Divya Prabandham and recited daily in Śrīvaiṣṇava worship.
nodes.details: The verses address Kṛṣṇa as born in “northern Mathurā” and living among the cowherds, and invoke Nappiṉṉai, his Tamil cowherd consort. Its title, with that of Māṇikkavācakar’s Tiruvempāvai, survives in the Thai royal Brahman ceremony Triyampawai–Trippawai (McGovern 2017).

nodes.name: Nācciyār Tirumoḻi
nodes.summary: Āṇṭāḷ’s 143 Tamil verses of longing for union with Viṣṇu–Kṛṣṇa, including the celebrated dream of her wedding to him (vāraṇam āyiram), part of the Divya Prabandham.

nodes.name: Tiruvāymoḻi
nodes.summary: Nammāḻvār’s 1,102-verse Tamil poem to Viṣṇu, in a hundred decads; Śrīvaiṣṇavas call it the Tamil (Drāviḍa) Veda and it was the subject of the first Śrīvaiṣṇava commentary, Piḷḷāṉ’s Āṟāyirappaṭi.

attributes.commentaries: Piḷḷāṉ’s Āṟāyirappaṭi (12th c.) and later maṇipravāḷa commentaries

nodes.name: Tiruvācakam
nodes.summary: Māṇikkavācakar’s Tamil hymns to Śiva, forming (with his Tirukkōvaiyār) Tirumurai book 8; intensely personal poems of grace, longing and Śiva as dancer at Tillai (Chidambaram).

nodes.name: Tiruvempāvai
nodes.summary: Māṇikkavācakar’s twenty-verse pāvai poem within the Tiruvācakam, in which young women wake each other at dawn in Mārkaḻi to bathe and praise Śiva — a Śaiva counterpart of Āṇṭāḷ’s Tiruppāvai.

nodes.name: Tirumantiram
nodes.summary: Tirumūlar’s Tamil verse treatise on Śaiva doctrine, yoga and tantra (c. 3,000 verses), Tirumurai book 10, regarded as the earliest Tamil statement of Śaiva Siddhānta ideas; its date is much disputed.

nodes.name: Tiruviḷaiyāṭal Purāṇam
nodes.summary: The Tamil sthala-purāṇa of Madurai narrating the sixty-four “sacred sports” (tiruviḷaiyāṭal) of Śiva as Cuntarēcuvarar, including his marriage to the warrior-princess Taṭātakai (Mīnākṣī). The best-known version is by Parañcōti Muṉivar.
nodes.details: Episodes include Mīnākṣī’s birth with three breasts and her conquest of the world until she meets Śiva at Kailāsa, Viṣṇu giving her in marriage, and stories involving Māṇikkavācakar (jackals turned into horses) and the Pāṇḍya kings. An earlier Tamil version is attributed to Perumpaṟṟappuliyūr Nampi, and the cycle has a Sanskrit counterpart in the Hālāsya Māhātmya.

dates.label: the reigns of the early (legendary) Pāṇḍya kings

nodes.limits: Temple-tradition narrative (class 6); it does not date the Mīnākṣī temple’s structures.

nodes.name: Kanta Purāṇam
nodes.summary: Kacciyappa Civācāriyar’s Tamil Skanda Purāṇa, recounting Murukaṉ’s birth and his war against the asura Cūrapatmaṉ (Śūrapadma), traditionally first recited at the Kumarakōṭṭam shrine in Kanchipuram.

attributes.author: Kacciyappa Civācāriyar
attributes.model text: Śaṅkara-saṃhitā of the Sanskrit Skanda Purāṇa (per tradition)

nodes.name: Āndhra Mahābhāratamu
nodes.summary: The Telugu Mahābhārata of the “poet trinity” (kavitrayam): Nannaya began it under the Eastern Cāḷukya king Rājarāja Narēndra (11th c.), Tikkana wrote fifteen books from the Virāṭa onward (13th c.), and Errana completed the Araṇya book (14th c.).

dates.event: Nannaya’s portion (Ādi, Sabhā, part of Araṇya)
dates.label: c. 1054–1061 CE

sources.locator: V. Narayana Rao, ch. on Telugu

nodes.name: Raṅganātha Rāmāyaṇamu
nodes.summary: Telugu Rāmāyaṇa in dvipada couplets by Gona Budda Reddy (pen-name Raṅganātha), 13th–14th c. Its singable metre suited folk and puppet performance; it contains popular episodes absent from Vālmīki, such as the squirrel who helps build the bridge and Lakṣmaṇa drawing a protective line.

nodes.name: Āndhra Mahābhāgavatamu (Pōtana)
nodes.summary: Bammera Pōtana’s 15th-century Telugu rendering of the Bhāgavata Purāṇa, dedicated not to a king but to Rāma; much loved for its Gajendra-mokṣa and Kṛṣṇa narratives.

sources.locator: V. Narayana Rao, ch. on Telugu

nodes.name: Vikramārjuna Vijaya (Pampa Bhārata)
nodes.summary: The Kannada Mahābhārata in campū form by the Jain poet Pampa, completed c. 941 CE at the court of the Vēmulavāḍa Cāḷukya Arikēsari II; Pampa equates his patron with the hero Arjuna.
nodes.details: Pollock (2006) treats Pampa’s two works — the Jain Ādipurāṇa and this “worldly” (laukika) epic — as founding texts of cosmopolitan vernacular literature in Kannada. A Jain poet’s Mahābhārata, it is not a Jain purāṇa: it follows the Bhārata story while making Arjuna, rather than Yudhiṣṭhira, the crowned hero, an identification with the patron.

dates.label: c. 941 CE
dates.basis: internal dating of Pampa’s works (Ādipurāṇa 941; the epic shortly after, or c. 939–941)
dates.view: sources differ on the order of the two works

sources.locator: D. R. Nagaraj, ch. on Kannada

nodes.name: Karṇāṭa Bhārata Kathāmañjarī (Gadugina Bhārata)
nodes.summary: Kumāravyāsa’s Kannada Mahābhārata (first ten books) in bhāminī ṣaṭpadi six-line stanzas, completed c. 1430 under the Vijayanagara king Dēvarāya II; it remains a living recitation text (gamaka) in Karnataka.
nodes.details: Local legend says it was composed in the Vīranārāyaṇa temple at Gadag, where a pillar bears the poet’s name.

sources.locator: D. R. Nagaraj, ch. on Kannada

nodes.name: Vacanas of Basavaṇṇa
nodes.summary: The free-verse Kannada sayings (vacana) attributed to Basava, addressed to Kūḍalasaṅgamadēva, criticising temple ritual and caste and exalting the devotee’s body as Śiva’s temple.
nodes.limits: The vacanas were compiled long after Basava; individual attributions are uncertain.

nodes.name: Adhyātma Rāmāyaṇam Kiḷippāṭṭu
nodes.summary: Eḻuttacchaṉ’s 16th-century Malayalam rendering of the Sanskrit Adhyātma Rāmāyaṇa in the “parrot-song” form, in which a parrot recites the story; it is read aloud in Kerala households during the month of Karkkaṭakam.

nodes.name: Saptakāṇḍa Rāmāyaṇa (Assamese)
nodes.summary: Mādhava Kandali’s 14th-century Assamese rendering of Vālmīki, made for the Barāhī (Kachari) king Mahāmāṇikya — among the earliest renderings of a Sanskrit epic into a modern Indo-Aryan language. Its first and last books were lost and replaced in the 16th century by Mādhavadeva (Ādi) and Śaṅkaradeva (Uttara).
nodes.details: Kandali’s Rāma and Sītā are portrayed in human rather than divine terms, which later Vaiṣṇava readers considered unsuitable for devotional use — part of why Śaṅkaradeva and Mādhavadeva supplied new frame books.

nodes.name: Kīrtana Ghoṣā
nodes.summary: Śaṅkaradeva’s Assamese collection of devotional narrative songs, largely drawn from the Bhāgavata Purāṇa, the core scripture recited in the nāmghars and sattras of Ekaśaraṇa Vaiṣṇavism.

nodes.name: Śāraḷā Mahābhārata
nodes.summary: Śāraḷā Dāsa’s 15th-century Odia Mahābhārata, begun under the Gajapati Kapilendra Deva (r. 1435–1467). It follows the Bhārata outline but adds many episodes and Odia local colour, written in colloquial, unsanskritised Odia.

nodes.name: Vilaṅkā Rāmāyaṇa
nodes.summary: Śāraḷā Dāsa’s Odia narrative of a war against a thousand-headed Rāvaṇa of the land of Vilaṅkā, after the defeat of the ten-headed one — a theme shared with the Sanskrit Adbhuta Rāmāyaṇa’s Sahasra-Rāvaṇa.
openQuestions: Does Sītā (as goddess) or Rāma kill the thousand-headed Rāvaṇa in Śāraḷā’s text? Sources consulted say only “a battle between Rāma and the thousand-headed Rāvaṇa”.

nodes.name: Odia Bhāgabata
nodes.summary: Jagannātha Dāsa’s Odia rendering of the Bhāgavata Purāṇa (late 15th – early 16th c.), in a simple nine-syllable metre; it became the most widely read devotional book of Odisha and the basis of village Bhāgabata-ghara reading houses.

dates.label: late 15th – early 16th c. CE
dates.basis: Jagannātha Dāsa’s association with Caitanya’s time at Puri

nodes.name: Manasāmaṅgal
nodes.summary: Bengali Maṅgalkāvya narratives of the snake goddess Manasā, centred on the merchant Cā̃d Sadāgar’s refusal to worship her and the devotion of his daughter-in-law Behulā, who wins back her dead husband Lakhindar.
nodes.details: Many poets composed Manasāmaṅgals; among the earliest named are Bijay Gupta and Bipradās Pipilāi (late 15th c.).

nodes.name: Caitanya Caritāmṛta
nodes.summary: Kṛṣṇadāsa Kavirāja’s Bengali–Sanskrit biography and theology of Caitanya (early 17th c.), which the Gauḍīya tradition treats as definitive; it presents Caitanya as Kṛṣṇa who took on the emotion and complexion of Rādhā.

nodes.name: Eknāthī Bhāgavata
nodes.summary: Eknāth’s Marathi ovī commentary on the eleventh book of the Bhāgavata Purāṇa (the Uddhava-gītā), 16th c.

nodes.name: Tukārām Gāthā
nodes.summary: The collection of Marathi abhaṅgas attributed to Tukārām (traditionally c. 4,500), sung by Vārkarī pilgrims on the road to Pandharpur.
nodes.limits: Manuscripts are unsystematic collections; individual abhaṅgas cannot all be securely attributed.

nodes.name: Sūrsāgar
nodes.summary: The “Ocean of Sūr”: the corpus of Braj Bhāṣā songs attributed to Sūrdās, chiefly on Kṛṣṇa’s childhood and the love of Rādhā and the gopīs, arranged in later recensions in twelve books after the Bhāgavata. Most of the received corpus is later than Sūr; Hawley and Bryant reconstruct an early core from manuscripts.
nodes.details: The earliest dated manuscript containing poems in Sūr’s name is reported by Hawley as the Fatehpur manuscript of VS 1639 (1582 CE); it contains a few hundred poems, far fewer than the thousands of the later vulgate.

dates.label: 1582 CE (VS 1639)
dates.basis: manuscript colophon as reported by Hawley (not checked in this session)

nodes.limits: Attribution of individual songs to Sūrdās is mostly uncertain.

nodes.name: Hanumān Cālīsā
nodes.summary: Forty-verse Awadhi hymn to Hanumān, traditionally attributed to Tulsīdās and now the most widely recited Hindu devotional hymn in North India.
nodes.limits: The attribution to Tulsīdās is traditional; Lutgendorf (2007) notes it is not secure.

nodes.name: Vākhs of Lal Ded
nodes.summary: Kashmiri four-line mystical sayings (vākh) attributed to the 14th-century yoginī Lal Ded (Lallā), venerated by Hindus as Lalleśvarī and by Muslims as Lal ʿĀrifa; they survived orally and were first written down systematically in the 20th century.
nodes.limits: Recorded from oral tradition some six centuries after her lifetime; attributions are uncertain.

nodes.name: Gāhā Sattasaī
nodes.summary: An anthology of 700 Mahārāṣṭrī Prakrit love verses attributed to the Sātavāhana king Hāla; dated between the 1st and 7th centuries (before Bāṇa, 7th c.). One verse mentions Kṛṣṇa and Rādhā, the earliest known literary mention of her.

dates.label: c. 3rd–4th c. CE
dates.basis: language; cited by Bāṇa before 640 CE

dates.label: by King Hāla (1st c. CE in tradition)

nodes.limits: The verses circulated in recensions; a given verse may be later than the anthology’s core.

nodes.name: Adbhuta Rāmāyaṇa
nodes.summary: A Sanskrit Śākta-inflected Rāma narrative in 27 sargas framed as a secret telling by Vālmīki to Bharadvāja. Sītā is born to Mandodarī, and in the climax she takes the form of Mahākālī and destroys the thousand-headed Sahasra-Rāvaṇa after Rāma falls unconscious.
openQuestions: A secure date is lacking; scholarly study of the text has been minor.

nodes.name: Bhaṭṭikāvya (Rāvaṇavadha)
nodes.summary: Bhaṭṭi’s 6th–7th-century Sanskrit mahākāvya telling the Rāma story while illustrating the rules of Pāṇini’s grammar; it was the model for the first half of the Old Javanese Kakawin Rāmāyaṇa.

nodes.name: Uttarapurāṇa of Guṇabhadra
nodes.summary: The 9th-century Digambara Jain Sanskrit universal history completing Jinasena’s Ādipurāṇa; its Rāma section follows a different Jain line from Vimalasūri, making Sītā the daughter of Rāvaṇa and Mandodarī, abandoned at birth because of a prophecy.

nodes.name: Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra
nodes.summary: A Mahāyāna Buddhist sūtra (c. 4th–5th c.) whose frame story has the Buddha visiting Laṅkā at the invitation of its king Rāvaṇa, who questions him on the dharma.
nodes.limits: Its Rāvaṇa is a devout questioner; the sūtra does not narrate the Rāmāyaṇa story.

nodes.name: Hikayat Seri Rama (Malay)
nodes.summary: The Malay prose Rāma narrative, put into its present form between the 13th and 17th centuries, with Islamic framing in some versions (Dasaratha as a descendant of the prophet Adam). Its oldest manuscript, in the Bodleian Library, was acquired by Archbishop Laud by 1633.
nodes.details: Characters: Seri Rama, Siti Dewi (Sītā), Laksamana, Maharaja Wana (Rāvaṇa), Hanuman Kera Putih. A related shadow-play repertoire (Hikayat Maharaja Wana) was among the most important wayang kulit tellings of the Malay peninsula.

nodes.name: Yama Zatdaw (Burmese)
nodes.summary: The Burmese Rāma tradition (Yamayana), known in Bagan-period terracottas as the Dasaratha Jātaka and in literature from a 1527 pyo poem; it was reshaped in the Konbaung period by Thai court drama brought back after the conquest of Ayutthaya.
nodes.details: Names: Yama (Rāma), Me Thida (Sītā), Lakkhana, Dasagiri (Rāvaṇa). Often called Myanmar’s unofficial national epic.

nodes.name: Phra Lak Phra Lam (Lao)
nodes.summary: The Lao Rāma epic, framed as a jātaka: Phra Lam is a previous birth of the Buddha, and Rāvaṇa (Hapmanasouane) is his cousin, compared with Devadatta or Māra. Versions were recorded on palm leaf from the 15th to the early 19th century.
nodes.details: Nang Sida is the daughter of Thôtsakane (Rāvaṇa) and Nang Chanta in the Lao character lists — another telling where Sītā is Rāvaṇa’s daughter.

nodes.name: Jayākhya Saṃhitā
nodes.summary: One of the “three gems” of the Pāñcarātra canon, a ritual and theological saṃhitā edited in 1931; its date is disputed, from an early proposal of c. 5th c. to later scholarship placing it around the 8th–9th c.

nodes.name: Sāttvata Saṃhitā
nodes.summary: Among the oldest and most authoritative Pāñcarātra saṃhitās (one of the “three gems”), with a commentary by Alaśiṅga Bhaṭṭa; date disputed.

nodes.name: Ahirbudhnya Saṃhitā
nodes.summary: Pāñcarātra saṃhitā known for its doctrine of the Sudarśana (Viṣṇu’s discus) and its cosmology; the subject of Schrader’s pioneering 1916 study, which placed it early, a dating later scholars question.

nodes.name: Niśvāsatattvasaṃhitā
nodes.summary: The earliest surviving tantra of the Śaiva Mantramārga, in five books; its editors date the oldest layer (Mūlasūtra) to c. 450–550 CE. It preserves an early stage of Śaiva Siddhānta ritual and the transition from the Atimārga.

dates.label: c. 450–550 CE
dates.basis: internal evidence; relationship to Pāśupata and Purāṇic material

nodes.name: Brahmayāmala (Picumata)
nodes.summary: An early Vidyāpīṭha tantra of the Bhairava stream, centred on Kapālīśabhairava and the goddess Caṇḍā Kāpālinī with their yoginīs; studied by Hatley as a key source for early Śākta-Śaiva yoginī cults.

dates.label: c. 7th–9th c. CE
dates.basis: Nepalese palm-leaf manuscript evidence and internal evidence

nodes.name: Civañāṉapōtam (Śivajñānabodham)
nodes.summary: Meykaṇṭār’s 13th-century twelve-sūtra Tamil treatise that founded the Tamil Śaiva Siddhānta school; tradition calls it a rendering of twelve Sanskrit verses from the Raurava Āgama, a claim scholars treat cautiously.

nodes.name: Tantrāloka
nodes.summary: Abhinavagupta’s encyclopaedic Sanskrit exposition of Trika Śaiva ritual and doctrine (c. 1000 CE), in thirty-seven chapters, based above all on the Mālinīvijayottara Tantra.

nodes.name: Nāthamuni
nodes.summary: Śrīvaiṣṇava ācārya (9th–10th c.) of Vīranārāyaṇapuram (Kāṭṭumaṉṉārkōyil), credited with collecting and arranging the Nālāyira Divya Prabandham and setting it to music; grandfather of Yāmuna.

nodes.name: Nampi Āṇṭār Nampi
nodes.summary: Tamil Śaiva poet-compiler of Tirunāraiyūr (10th–11th c.) who arranged the Tēvāram and other hymns into the first eleven books of the Tirumurai; tradition links his work to Rājarāja I.

nodes.name: Māṇikkavācakar
nodes.summary: Tamil Śaiva poet-saint, author of the Tiruvācakam and Tirukkōvaiyār (Tirumurai 8); hagiography makes him a minister of a Pāṇḍya king who renounced office after meeting Śiva at Tirupperuntuṟai. Most scholars place him in the 9th century, though earlier dates are proposed.

nodes.name: Cēkkiḻār
nodes.summary: Tamil poet and minister at the court of the Cōḻa king Kulōttuṅka II (12th c.), author of the Periya Purāṇam.

nodes.name: Nakkīrar
nodes.summary: Tamil poet to whom the Tirumurukāṟṟuppaṭai is attributed; tradition (including the Tiruviḷaiyāṭal Purāṇam) makes him the president of the Madurai academy (caṅkam) who dared to challenge Śiva’s poem.

dates.label: late Caṅkam (c. 3rd–6th c. CE)
dates.basis: date of the poem; several poets of the name may be conflated

nodes.name: Iḷaṅkō Aṭikaḷ
nodes.summary: The “venerable prince-ascetic,” brother of the Cēra king Ceṅkuṭṭuvaṉ according to the prologue of the Cilappatikāram, to whom the epic is attributed; the attribution rests on a later prologue and is doubted.
nodes.limits: Historicity and authorship uncertain.

nodes.name: Periyāḻvār
nodes.summary: Āḻvār of Śrīvilliputtūr (8th–9th c.), author of the Periyāḻvār Tirumoḻi with its celebrated poems of Kṛṣṇa’s infancy and of the Tiruppallāṇṭu; foster-father of Āṇṭāḷ.

nodes.name: Nannaya
nodes.summary: Telugu poet (11th c.), “first poet” (ādikavi) of Telugu, who began the Āndhra Mahābhāratamu at the request of the Eastern Cāḷukya king Rājarāja Narēndra.

nodes.name: Tikkana
nodes.summary: Telugu poet and minister (13th c.) who rendered fifteen books (Virāṭa to Svargārohaṇa) of the Āndhra Mahābhāratamu.

nodes.name: Errana
nodes.summary: Telugu poet (14th c.) at the court of Prolaya Vēma Reḍḍi who completed the Araṇya book of the Āndhra Mahābhāratamu.

nodes.name: Gona Budda Reddy (Raṅganātha)
nodes.summary: Telugu poet (13th–14th c.), author under the pen-name Raṅganātha of the dvipada Raṅganātha Rāmāyaṇamu.

nodes.name: Bammera Pōtana
nodes.summary: Telugu poet (15th c.) of Bammera near Warangal, author of the Āndhra Mahābhāgavatamu, who according to tradition refused to dedicate his work to the king of Rācakoṇḍa and offered it to Rāma.

nodes.name: Pampa (Ādikavi Pampa)
nodes.summary: Jain Kannada poet (902–c. 955) at the Vēmulavāḍa Cāḷukya court of Arikēsari II, author of the Ādipurāṇa (941) and the Vikramārjuna Vijaya.

nodes.name: Kumāravyāsa
nodes.summary: Kannada poet (Nāraṇappa, early 15th c.) of Gadag, author of the Karṇāṭa Bhārata Kathāmañjarī, active under Dēvarāya II of Vijayanagara.

nodes.name: Tuñcattu Rāmānujaṉ Eḻuttacchaṉ
nodes.summary: Malayalam poet (16th c.), called the father of modern Malayalam literature, author of the Adhyātma Rāmāyaṇam Kiḷippāṭṭu and a Mahābhāratam Kiḷippāṭṭu.

dates.label: c. 1495–1575 CE (Ulloor); 16th–17th c. in other views

nodes.name: Mādhava Kandali
nodes.summary: Assamese poet (14th c.) who rendered Vālmīki’s Rāmāyaṇa into Assamese for the Barāhī king Mahāmāṇikya.

nodes.name: Śrīmanta Śaṅkaradeva
nodes.summary: Assamese saint, poet, dramatist and founder of Ekaśaraṇa Vaiṣṇavism (1449–1568), author of the Kīrtana Ghoṣā, the Aṅkīyā Nāṭ one-act plays and the Bargīt songs, and of the Uttara kāṇḍa of the Assamese Rāmāyaṇa.

nodes.name: Mādhavadeva
nodes.summary: Assamese poet and chief disciple of Śaṅkaradeva (16th c.), author of the Nām Ghoṣā and of the Ādi kāṇḍa of the Assamese Rāmāyaṇa.

nodes.name: Śāraḷā Dāsa
nodes.summary: Odia poet (15th c.) of the reign of the Gajapati Kapilendra Deva, author of the Odia Mahābhārata, the Vilaṅkā Rāmāyaṇa and the Caṇḍī Purāṇa; his name, “by the grace of Sāraḷā,” refers to his goddess.

nodes.name: Jagannātha Dāsa
nodes.summary: Odia poet (late 15th – 16th c.) of Puri, one of the Pañcasakhā, author of the Odia Bhāgabata and founder of the Atibaḍī tradition.

nodes.name: Eknāth
nodes.summary: Marathi poet-saint of Paiṭhaṇ (c. 1533–1599), author of the Eknāthī Bhāgavata and the Bhāvārtha Rāmāyaṇa, who produced a corrected text of the Jñāneśvarī in 1584.

nodes.name: Tukārām
nodes.summary: Marathi poet-saint of Dehū (1608 or 1598 – 1649/1650), a grocer by caste whose abhaṅgas to Viṭṭhala are central to the Vārkarī pilgrimage.

dates.label: 1598/1608 – 1649/1650 CE
dates.basis: competing reconstructions; death in 1650 widely accepted

nodes.name: Nāmdev
nodes.summary: Marathi poet-saint (traditionally 1270–1350), a tailor of Pandharpur, devotee of Viṭṭhala and contemporary of Jñāneśvar; songs attributed to him are also in the Sikh Ādi Granth.

nodes.name: Sūrdās
nodes.summary: Braj Bhāṣā poet-singer of the 16th century to whom the Sūrsāgar is attributed; hagiography makes him blind and a disciple of Vallabha, claims modern scholarship treats as later constructions.

nodes.name: Lal Ded (Lalleśvarī)
nodes.summary: Kashmiri yoginī-poet of the 14th century, revered by Hindus as Lalleśvarī and by Muslims as Lal ʿĀrifa, to whom the vākhs are attributed.

nodes.name: Narsinh Mehtā
nodes.summary: Gujarati poet-saint of Junagadh (c. 1414 – 1480s), honoured as the Ādi Kavi of Gujarati, devotee of Kṛṣṇa and author of the bhajan “Vaiṣṇava jana to.”

nodes.name: Kṛṣṇadāsa Kavirāja
nodes.summary: Gauḍīya poet-theologian of Vṛndāvana (16th–17th c.), author of the Caitanya Caritāmṛta.

nodes.name: Meykaṇṭār
nodes.summary: Tamil Śaiva theologian (13th c.) of Tiruveṇṇainallūr, author of the Civañāṉapōtam and founder of the Tamil Śaiva Siddhānta lineage.

nodes.name: Abhinavagupta
nodes.summary: Kashmirian Śaiva philosopher and aesthetician (fl. c. 975–1025), author of the Tantrāloka, of commentaries on Utpaladeva’s Pratyabhijñā and of the Abhinavabhāratī on the Nāṭyaśāstra.

nodes.name: Rama I (Phutthayotfa Chulalok)
nodes.summary: First king of the Chakri dynasty of Siam (r. 1782–1809), founder of Bangkok, under whom the canonical Ramakien was compiled (1797–1807), partly by the king himself.

nodes.name: Kulōttuṅka Cōḻa II
nodes.summary: Cōḻa king (r. 1133–1150) at whose court Cēkkiḻār composed the Periya Purāṇam; Śaiva tradition associates him with the expansion of the Chidambaram temple.

nodes.name: Lakṣmaṇasena
nodes.summary: King of the Sena dynasty of Bengal (r. c. 1178–1206), at whose court tradition places Jayadeva together with the poets Umāpatidhara, Śaraṇa, Govardhana and Dhoyī.

nodes.name: Arikēsari II
nodes.summary: Vēmulavāḍa Cāḷukya ruler (10th c.), a feudatory of the Rāṣṭrakūṭa Kṛṣṇa III, patron of Pampa, who equated him with Arjuna in the Vikramārjuna Vijaya.

nodes.name: Viṭṭhala (Viṭhobā) of Pandharpur
nodes.summary: The deity of Pandharpur in Maharashtra, standing with hands on hips upon a brick, worshipped by Vārkarīs as a form of Kṛṣṇa/Viṣṇu; scholars debate his origins (pastoral hero-stone, Jain, Śaiva and Vaiṣṇava elements).
nodes.details: The Puṇḍalīka legend explains the brick: Kṛṣṇa came to the devotee Puṇḍalīka, who, busy serving his parents, threw him a brick to stand on, and the god remains standing there. Dhere (2011) reads Viṭṭhala as an amalgam of pastoral hero-gods of the Dhangar herders absorbed into Kṛṣṇa devotion; Deleury suggested a hero-stone origin. A monument dated 1189 and a Hoysala inscription of 1237 are the earliest dated references noted in the literature.

dates.label: 1189 (monument) and 1237 CE (inscription)
dates.basis: inscriptions as reported in secondary literature

nodes.limits: Inscriptions attest worship at Pandharpur by the late 12th–13th c.; they do not settle the deity’s origins.

earliestMaterial.label: 15th–16th c. CE, with major expansion under Kṛṣṇadevarāya (1509–1529)

nodes.name: Māyōṉ (Tamil)
nodes.summary: The “dark one,” presiding deity of the mullai (forest-pasture) landscape in the Tolkāppiyam, and in Caṅkam poetry a dark cowherd god (also called Māl, Tirumāl) later identified with Viṣṇu and Kṛṣṇa. Kept distinct from deity:vishnu and joined by IDENTIFIED_WITH.
nodes.details: Hardy (1983) argues that the Tamil cowherd god of the mullai landscape, with his beloved Piññai and his dances with cowherd girls, contributed to the emotional (viraha) bhakti later expressed by the Āḻvārs and, through the Bhāgavata Purāṇa, to pan-Indian Kṛṣṇa devotion.
nodes.limits: The name Māyōṉ in the sūtra does not by itself establish a theology identical with Sanskrit Viṣṇu.

nodes.name: Nappiṉṉai (Piññai)
nodes.summary: The Tamil cowherd girl beloved of Kṛṣṇa (Māyavaṉ) in the Cilappatikāram’s round-dance of the cowherdesses and in the Āḻvārs’ hymns, where she is his consort; some scholars see her as a southern parallel or precursor of Rādhā, others identify her with Nīḷā Devī.
nodes.limits: Whether Piññai and Rādhā share an origin is a scholarly hypothesis; the texts keep them apart.

nodes.name: Vaḷḷi
nodes.summary: Murukaṉ’s Tamil consort, a hunter (kuṟava) girl of the hills whom the god woos in disguise; she stands beside Teyvāṉai (Devasenā), daughter of Indra, in Tamil tradition.

nodes.name: Suvannamaccha
nodes.summary: Mermaid princess, daughter of Thotsakan (Rāvaṇa), in Thai and other Southeast Asian Rāma tellings; sent to sabotage the causeway to Laṅkā, she falls in love with Hanumān and bears him a son, Macchanu.
nodes.limits: Absent from Vālmīki; a Southeast Asian figure.

nodes.name: Macchanu
nodes.summary: Son of Hanumān and the mermaid Suvannamaccha in the Ramakien, half monkey and half fish, who later meets and fights his father before they recognise each other.

nodes.name: Thotsakan
nodes.summary: The ten-faced king of Laṅkā in the Thai Ramakien — the counterpart of Rāvaṇa (the name renders Daśakaṇṭha) — who in this telling is the father of Sida, keeps his heart outside his body, and dies when Hanumān crushes it.
nodes.limits: Kept separate from char:ravana because the Ramakien gives him a different family and fate; identified with Rāvaṇa by an assertion.

nodes.name: Māyā-Sītā (the illusory Sītā)
nodes.summary: The illusory double or reflection of Sītā who, in the Kūrma Purāṇa, Adhyātma Rāmāyaṇa, Brahmavaivarta Purāṇa and Tulsīdās’s Rāmcaritmānas, is the one Rāvaṇa abducts while the real Sītā is kept safe in Agni.
nodes.details: In the Mānas Rāma says: “tumha pāvaka mahuṃ karahu nivāsā, jau lagi karauṃ nisācara nāsā” (“dwell in the fire until I destroy the night-rovers”) and Sītā leaves “nija pratibimba,” her own reflection, “of the same character, form and modesty”; not even Lakṣmaṇa knows. At the fire-ordeal the reflection and the worldly stain burn in the fire and Agni returns the true Śrī to Rāma. Doniger (1999) traces the motif’s development and its theological work: protecting Sītā’s purity and recasting the ordeal.
nodes.limits: A theological and narrative motif of particular texts; not present in Vālmīki’s Rāmāyaṇa.

nodes.name: Bhāmaṇḍala
nodes.summary: In Jain Rāma tellings (Vimalasūri’s Paumacariya and successors), Sītā’s twin brother, carried off at birth and raised as a vidyādhara prince, who falls in love with Sītā from her portrait and seeks her hand before learning that she is his twin sister.

earliestText.label: c. 1st–5th c. CE (not later than the 3rd c. in the commonest view)

nodes.name: Sahasra-Rāvaṇa (the thousand-headed Rāvaṇa)
nodes.summary: A thousand-headed elder brother or double of Rāvaṇa who, in the Adbhuta Rāmāyaṇa, is destroyed by Sītā in the form of Mahākālī after Rāma is struck down; a thousand-headed Rāvaṇa is also fought in Śāraḷā Dāsa’s Odia Vilaṅkā Rāmāyaṇa.

nodes.name: Kaṇṇaki
nodes.summary: Heroine of the Cilappatikāram, who proves her executed husband Kōvalaṉ innocent before the Pāṇḍya king, burns Madurai with her curse and is deified as the chaste goddess Pattiṉi, worshipped in Tamil Nadu, Kerala and Sri Lanka.

nodes.name: Pandharpur
nodes.summary: Town on the Bhīmā (Candrabhāgā) river in Maharashtra, seat of the Viṭṭhala temple and goal of the Vārkarī pilgrimages (vārī) of Āṣāḍha and Kārttika.

location.label: Pandharpur, Solapur district, Maharashtra, India

nodes.name: Śrīvilliputtūr
nodes.summary: Temple town in Virudhunagar district, Tamil Nadu, home of Periyāḻvār and Āṇṭāḷ according to tradition, with twin shrines of Āṇṭāḷ and Vaṭapatrasāyī (Raṅganātha).

location.label: Srivilliputhur, Virudhunagar district, Tamil Nadu, India

nodes.name: Nevāsā
nodes.summary: Town on the Pravarā near its confluence with the Godāvarī (Ahmednagar district, Maharashtra), identified by tradition as the place where the Jñāneśvarī was composed, home of the Mohinīrāja (Mahālayā) temple named in the colophon.

location.label: Nevasa, Ahmednagar district, Maharashtra, India

nodes.limits: The colophon names the Godāvarī bank and Śrī Mahālayā; the identification with Nevāsā is traditional.

nodes.name: Vārkarī
nodes.summary: The Marathi devotional tradition of Viṭṭhala of Pandharpur, carried by pilgrims (vārkarī) who walk to Pandharpur twice a year singing the abhaṅgas of Jñāneśvar, Nāmdev, Eknāth, Tukārām and other saints.

nodes.name: Ekaśaraṇa Dharma
nodes.summary: The Assamese Vaiṣṇava movement founded by Śaṅkaradeva (15th–16th c.): exclusive refuge in Kṛṣṇa through congregational singing and hearing of his name and deeds, organised in sattras and village nāmghars; Rādhā is not worshipped alongside Kṛṣṇa.

nodes.name: Puṣṭimārga
nodes.summary: The Kṛṣṇa tradition founded by Vallabha (16th c.), centred on Śrīnāthjī and the “eight seals” (aṣṭachāp) of poets, among whom it counts Sūrdās.

nodes.name: Rāmānandī
nodes.summary: The North Indian Vaiṣṇava ascetic order tracing itself to Rāmānanda, centred on Rāma and Sītā; it claims Tulsīdās and is traditionally associated with the Adhyātma Rāmāyaṇa.

nodes.name: Rāmlīlā
nodes.summary: North Indian staged performance of the Rāma story based on Tulsīdās’s Rāmcaritmānas, held around Dussehra over ten to twelve days or (at Ramnagar, Varanasi) a month; inscribed on UNESCO’s Representative List in 2008 (proclaimed 2005).
nodes.details: UNESCO names the Rāmlīlās of Ayodhyā, Ramnagar, Banaras, Vṛndāvan, Almora, Sattna and Madhubani as the most representative. Lutgendorf (1991) describes the Ramnagar Rāmlīlā patronised by the Mahārājā of Banaras as an environmental performance in which the audience moves with the action across the town.

nodes.name: Kūṭiyāṭṭam
nodes.summary: Sanskrit theatre of Kerala performed by Cākyār and Nampyār families in temple theatres (kūttampalam), with long elaborations of single acts of Sanskrit plays (including Rāma plays); inscribed on UNESCO’s Representative List in 2008 (proclaimed 2001).

nodes.name: Yakṣagāna
nodes.summary: Dance-drama of coastal Karnataka, led by a singer-narrator (bhāgavata), performing episodes (prasaṅga) from the Rāmāyaṇa, Mahābhārata and Bhāgavata; an inscription of 1556 at Kurugodu records land given to performers.

dates.label: 1556 CE
dates.basis: inscription as reported in secondary literature

nodes.name: Kathakaḷi
nodes.summary: Kerala dance-drama that crystallised in the 16th–17th centuries from Rāmanāṭṭam (attributed to the Kottarakkara Tampurāṉ) and Kṛṣṇanāṭṭam (of the Zamorin Mānavēdaṉ), performing Rāmāyaṇa, Mahābhārata and Bhāgavata stories.

nodes.name: Wayang
nodes.summary: Indonesian puppet and shadow theatre (wayang kulit and related forms) led by a dalang with gamelan, performing stories from the Mahābhārata and Rāmāyaṇa among others; inscribed on UNESCO’s Representative List in 2008 (proclaimed 2003).

nodes.name: Khon
nodes.summary: Thai masked dance-drama performing episodes of the Ramakien, historically a court art; inscribed on UNESCO’s Representative List in 2018 as “Khon, masked dance drama in Thailand.”

nodes.name: Royal Ballet of Cambodia
nodes.summary: Khmer classical court dance, whose repertoire includes Reamker episodes; inscribed on UNESCO’s Representative List in 2008 (proclaimed 2003).
nodes.limits: The UNESCO record itself does not name the Reamker; the repertoire link rests on secondary literature.

nodes.name: Triyampawai–Trippawai ceremony
nodes.summary: Thai royal Brahman new-year ceremony (December–January) whose name comes from two Tamil devotional poems — Māṇikkavācakar’s Tiruvempāvai and Āṇṭāḷ’s Tiruppāvai — and during which hymns from these collections are chanted; it was historically linked to the Giant Swing in Bangkok.
nodes.details: McGovern (2017) writes that “Trīyampawāi is a corruption of Māṇikkavācakar’s Tiruvempāvai, and Trīppawāi is likewise a corruption of Āṇḍāḷ’s Tiruppāvai,” and reports Tamil texts in Thai and Grantha scripts in the National Library, Bangkok, together with recordings of the hymns sung in the ceremony. The present court Brahmans speak no Indian language.
nodes.limits: Shows the circulation of Tamil hymn names and texts into Thai court ritual; it does not show when or by whom they were brought.

nodes.name: Cāḷukyas of Vēmulavāḍa
nodes.summary: A 9th–10th-century dynasty in northern Telangana, feudatories of the Rāṣṭrakūṭas, patrons of the Kannada poet Pampa under Arikēsari II.

nodes.name: Rattanakosin Kingdom (Chakri dynasty)
nodes.summary: The Siamese kingdom ruled from Bangkok by the Chakri dynasty from 1782, under whose first kings the Ramakien was compiled and the Wat Phra Kaew murals painted.

nodes.name: Sena dynasty of Bengal
nodes.summary: Dynasty ruling Bengal in the 11th–13th centuries, whose king Lakṣmaṇasena is traditionally Jayadeva’s patron.

nodes.name: The Prambanan Rāmāyaṇa reliefs illustrate the Kakawin Rāmāyaṇa
nodes.summary: The claim that the 9th-century Rāmāyaṇa reliefs on the Śiva and Brahmā temples at Prambanan follow the Old Javanese Kakawin. Since Stutterheim (1925) scholars have noted episodes that diverge from the Kakawin and suggest another, possibly oral, telling.
nodes.limits: Both the reliefs and the poem belong to the Medang period; contemporaneity does not establish that one illustrates the other.

nodes.name: Sūrdās was a disciple of Vallabha
nodes.summary: The Puṣṭimārga hagiographic claim (Caurāsī Vaiṣṇavan kī Vārtā) that Sūrdās was initiated by Vallabha and became one of the aṣṭachāp poets; Hawley argues the connection is a later sectarian construction.

nodes.name: Basava founded the Vīraśaiva / Liṅgāyata tradition
nodes.summary: The traditional claim that Basava founded the Liṅgāyata community; modern scholars using Kalacuri-period inscriptions and the vacana corpus often see him as a reformer and organiser of an existing Śaiva milieu.

nodes.name: The Dasaratha Jātaka preserves an older form of the Rāma story than Vālmīki
nodes.summary: Argued in the 19th century (notably by Albrecht Weber) because of the jātaka’s simpler plot and sibling-marriage motif; most later scholars regard it as a Buddhist reworking of a story already known in Rāmāyaṇa form, though its verses may be old.

nodes.name: Āgamas and Tantras
nodes.summary: The large body of post-Vedic scriptures (Āgama, Tantra, Saṃhitā) of the Śaiva, Vaiṣṇava Pāñcarātra and Śākta traditions, which regulate initiation, mantra, temple building, image worship, festivals and yoga.
nodes.details:
The corpus is not one canon but several: the Śaiva Mantramārga (Siddhānta and the non-dualist Bhairava/Kaula streams), the Vaiṣṇava Pāñcarātra Saṃhitās (traditionally 108), the Vaikhānasa texts, and Śākta Tantras. Sanderson (2009) describes the early medieval period as a “Śaiva Age” in which these ritual systems, and the royal and temple institutions that used them, spread across South and Southeast Asia.

The earliest surviving Śaiva tantra is generally taken to be the Niśvāsatattvasaṃhitā, whose oldest layer its editors place c. 450–550 CE. Most Pāñcarātra saṃhitās are later and their dates are disputed. In South Indian temple practice the Śaiva Āgamas (traditionally 28) and selected Pāñcarātra saṃhitās remain the ritual authorities.

dates.label: c. 5th–14th c. CE
dates.basis: manuscript dating, cross-citation and internal evidence

nodes.limits: A collection label: dates and authority differ sharply between sub-corpora; traditional claims of eternal or divine origin are recorded as tradition, not as dates.

nodes.name: Devotional (bhakti) literature
nodes.summary: Devotional poetry, song and hagiography addressed to Śiva, Viṣṇu/Kṛṣṇa/Rāma, the Goddess and other deities in Tamil, Kannada, Telugu, Marathi, Hindi dialects, Bengali, Assamese, Odia, Gujarati, Kashmiri and other languages, from the Tamil saints of c. 6th–9th c. onward.
nodes.details: Treated here as an umbrella for regionally distinct corpora with their own canons (Nālāyira Divya Prabandham, Tirumurai, Vārkarī abhaṅgas, Vīraśaiva vacanas, Sūrsāgar, the Assamese Kīrtana Ghoṣā…). The common label is a modern scholarly one; each tradition defines its own corpus and authority.

dates.event: composition (Tamil beginnings to early-modern North India)
dates.label: c. 6th–17th c. CE

nodes.limits: “Bhakti movement” as a single pan-Indian wave is a scholarly construct that some historians question; the dates are ranges for disparate corpora.

nodes.name: Regional and vernacular retellings
nodes.summary: Tellings of the Rāma and Bhārata narratives (and of Purāṇic material) in Indian languages, in later Sanskrit, and in Jain and Buddhist traditions. Each telling is recorded as a work with its own date, author and theology, not as a deviation from an original.
nodes.details: Ramanujan’s essay “Three Hundred Rāmāyaṇas” proposed speaking of many “tellings” sharing a pool of signifiers rather than of versions of a single Ur-text, a framing taken up in Richman (ed.) 1991. This collection follows that approach: RETELLS / DERIVED_FROM edges record documented literary dependence only, and differences are recorded in Comparison tables rather than as errors.
nodes.limits: Membership in this collection says nothing about relative “authenticity”; Jain and Buddhist tellings are included as members of the Rāma narrative tradition, not as Hindu texts.

nodes.name: Southeast Asian adaptations
nodes.summary: Rāma and other Indic narratives as written, carved, recited and performed in Java, Bali, Cambodia, Thailand, Laos, Myanmar and the Malay world, from the Old Javanese Kakawin Rāmāyaṇa (late 9th–early 10th c.) to the Thai Ramakien of Rama I (1797–1807).
nodes.details: These tellings are often Buddhist (Lao Phra Lak Phra Lam is framed as a jātaka), Islamic-framed (some Malay Hikayat Seri Rama versions) or court-ritual (Thai and Khmer royal drama). Characters are renamed and re-characterised: Rāvaṇa becomes Thotsakan (Thai) or Krong Reap (Khmer), Sītā is sometimes Rāvaṇa’s daughter, and Hanumān is an amorous hero who fathers a son with the mermaid Suvannamaccha.

dates.event: composition of the surviving literary tellings
dates.label: c. 856 – 1807 CE
dates.basis: Robson’s dating of the Kakawin; Rama I’s Ramakien

nodes.limits: Temple reliefs (Prambanan, Angkor Wat) attest the circulation of the story but do not by themselves show which telling the sculptors followed.

nodes.name: Kamba Rāmāyaṇam (Irāmāvatāram)
nodes.summary: The Tamil Rāma epic of the poet Kampaṉ, in six kāṇṭams of viruttam verse (c. 10,500 stanzas in the standard edition), dated variously between the 9th and 12th centuries. It is the most celebrated Tamil telling and is shaped by Tamil poetics and Śrīvaiṣṇava devotion.
nodes.details:
Kampaṉ names his patron, Caṭaiyappa Vaḷḷal of Tiruveṇṇainallūr, at intervals in the poem. The standard text is the edition prepared by a committee of the Kamban Kazhagam (1976) which set aside many interpolated verses; the seventh book (Uttara kāṇṭam) is attributed to Oṭṭakkūttar, not Kampaṉ.

Among the episodes that distinguish the telling: Rāma and Sītā glimpse each other in Mithilā before the breaking of the bow; in the Āraṇya kāṇṭam Rāvaṇa does not touch Sītā but lifts her away with the earth on which her hermitage stands; and Rāvaṇa is given tragic grandeur. Temple tradition holds that the poem was first publicly recited (araṅkēṟṟam) at the Raṅganātha temple, Srirangam.

dates.label: Śaka 807 (≈ 885 CE), per an anonymous traditional verse
dates.basis: traditional verse giving a Śaka year; widely doubted

dates.label: 12th c. CE
dates.basis: references to Rāmānuja’s era, patron identification, language

dates.label: 9th c. CE
dates.view: minority view of some Tamil scholars

openQuestions: Which external evidence (inscription, datable citation) gives the firmest terminus ante quem for Kampaṉ?

nodes.name: Rāmcaritmānas
nodes.summary: Tulsīdās’s Awadhi Rāma epic in seven kāṇḍs of caupāī–dohā verse, begun at Ayodhyā in Saṃvat 1631 (1574 CE) according to the poem itself. It is the dominant Rāma text of North India and the basis of the Rāmlīlā.
nodes.details:
The poem is framed as a set of nested dialogues: Śiva to Pārvatī, the crow-sage Kākabhuśuṇḍi to Garuḍa, and Yājñavalkya to Bharadvāja. Its theology presents Rāma as the supreme Brahman who takes on a human līlā; following the Adhyātma Rāmāyaṇa, it has Sītā enter the fire before the abduction and leave her reflection (pratibimba) to be carried off, and the fire-ordeal burns the reflection (Laṅkākāṇḍa chand before dohā 109).

The text states its own starting date: “saṃbata soraha sai ekatīsā … naumī bhauma bāra madhu māsā, avadhapurīṃ yaha carita prakāsā” — the year 1631, on the ninth, a Tuesday, in the month Madhu (Caitra), at Ayodhyā. This is Rāmanavamī, Rāma’s birthday.

dates.label: 1574 CE (Saṃvat 1631, Caitra śukla 9)
dates.basis: date stated in the poem itself (Bālakāṇḍa)

sources.quote: संबत सोरह सै एकतीसा। करउँ कथा हरि पद धरि सीसा ॥ नौमी भौम बार मधु मासा। अवधपुरीं यह चरित प्रकासा ॥

dates.label: c. 1576–77 CE (traditional: 2 years 7 months after starting)

attributes.metre: caupāī with dohā, soraṭhā and chand
attributes.author: Tulsīdās

nodes.limits: The internal date fixes when composition began, not when the text reached its received form; the oldest manuscripts and their dates were not checked in this session.

nodes.name: Kṛttivāsī Rāmāyaṇa
nodes.summary: The Bengali Rāma narrative (Śrīrām Pā̃cālī) attributed to Kṛttibās Ojhā, composed probably in the 15th century in the pā̃cālī form for recitation and singing, and the most widely read Rāmāyaṇa in Bengal.
nodes.details: The received text has been heavily reworked by singers and editors; it was first printed at the Serampore Mission Press (1803). It keeps Vālmīki’s overall plot while adding localised episodes — popularly, Rāma’s out-of-season worship of Durgā (akāla-bodhana) before the final battle, and the devotion of Rāvaṇa’s side characters such as Taraṇīsen — which are central to its Bengali reception.

dates.label: 15th c. CE (if the popular identification of the poet is correct)
dates.basis: autobiographical verses in some manuscripts; identification of the Gauḍa king named

nodes.limits: The printed vulgate reflects centuries of performance; episodes popularly ascribed to Kṛttibās may be later accretions.

nodes.name: Adhyātma Rāmāyaṇa
nodes.summary: A Sanskrit Rāma narrative in seven kāṇḍas presented as a Śiva–Pārvatī dialogue within the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa, re-reading the story through Advaita Vedānta: Rāma is the supreme Brahman and events are his līlā. Dated to roughly the 13th–15th c.
nodes.details: The work is c. 65 chapters (about 4,500 verses). Its best-known innovation is the māyā-Sītā: Rāma, knowing what is to come, asks Sītā to enter the fire and leave an illusory double, who is the one Rāvaṇa carries off; at the fire-ordeal the double vanishes and Agni restores the real Sītā. The text deeply influenced Tulsīdās’s Rāmcaritmānas and was rendered into Malayalam by Eḻuttacchaṉ. Tradition also links it to Rāmānanda.

dates.label: c. 13th–15th c. CE
dates.basis: doctrinal content, citations, relation to Rāmānandī circles

dates.label: part of the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa, by Vyāsa (traditional)

openQuestions: Exact sarga locators for the māyā-Sītā episode in a named edition (recalled as Araṇyakāṇḍa 7).

nodes.name: Tēvāram
nodes.summary: The Tamil Śaiva hymns (patikams) of Campantar, Appar and Cuntarar (7th–8th c.), forming the first seven books of the Tirumurai; about 796 hymns survive. The hymns praise Śiva at named temples, which tradition counts as the 275 Pāṭal Peṟṟa Talams.
nodes.details: Books 1–3 are Campantar’s (c. 383–384 hymns), 4–6 Appar’s (c. 313), 7 Cuntarar’s (c. 100). According to the Tirumuṟai Kaṇṭa Purāṇam tradition, the Cōḻa king Rājarāja I sought the hymns and Nampi Āṇṭār Nampi found palm-leaf manuscripts, partly eaten by white ants, in a sealed chamber of the Chidambaram temple; Nampi then arranged them by musical mode (paṇ). The hymns are still sung by hereditary ōtuvār singers in Tamil Śaiva temples.

dates.label: c. 7th–8th c. CE
dates.basis: synchronisms with Pallava and Pāṇḍya kings named in hagiography; internal evidence

dates.label: late 10th–11th c. CE
dates.basis: tradition linking the recovery to Rājarāja I (r. 985–1014)

nodes.limits: The recovery story is a later traditional account; it does not by itself date the compilation.

nodes.name: Nālāyira Divya Prabandham
nodes.summary: The “Four Thousand Sacred Compositions”: Tamil hymns of the twelve Āḻvārs (c. 6th–9th c.) praising Viṣṇu at named shrines, compiled by Nāthamuni in the 9th–10th century. Śrīvaiṣṇavas regard it as a Tamil Veda and recite it in temple worship.
nodes.details: The collection includes Āṇṭāḷ’s Tiruppāvai and Nācciyār Tirumoḻi and Nammāḻvār’s Tiruvāymoḻi (1,102 verses). The shrines praised in the hymns are counted by tradition as the 108 Divya Deśams. Śrīvaiṣṇava hagiography holds that Nāthamuni recovered the hymns after reciting Madhurakavi’s Kaṇṇinuṇ Ciṟuttāmpu at Kurukūr until Nammāḻvār appeared to him.

dates.label: c. 6th–9th c. CE
dates.basis: internal references, relation to Pallava-period Tamil

nodes.name: Periya Purāṇam
nodes.summary: Cēkkiḻār’s 12th-century Tamil hagiography of the sixty-three Śaiva saints (Nāyaṉmār), composed at the Cōḻa court of Kulōttuṅka II and placed as the twelfth and last book of the Tirumurai.
nodes.details: It expands the list of devotees in Cuntarar’s Tiruttoṇṭattokai and Nampi Āṇṭār Nampi’s Tiruttoṇṭar Tiruvantāti into full narratives. Tradition holds that Kulōttuṅka II asked his minister Cēkkiḻār to write it to wean him from the Jain epic Cīvaka Cintāmaṇi, and that it was first recited at Chidambaram.

dates.label: 12th c. CE (reign of Kulōttuṅka II, 1133–1150)
dates.basis: regnal synchronism from tradition and internal references

nodes.limits: A hagiography composed four to five centuries after most of its subjects; it is evidence for 12th-century Śaiva memory, not a contemporary record of the saints.

nodes.name: Gītagovinda
nodes.summary: Jayadeva’s 12th-century Sanskrit lyrical poem in twelve cantos (24 songs, aṣṭapadī) on the love, separation and reunion of Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa. It is the first major Sanskrit work centred on Rādhā and is sung nightly in the Jagannātha temple, Puri.
nodes.details: The opening hymn on the ten avatāras (daśāvatāra) includes Balarāma and the Buddha. The poem was taken up as ritual song (sevā) in the Puri temple and as a foundational text in Gauḍīya and other Kṛṣṇa traditions, and inspired a large painting tradition. Jayadeva’s birthplace “Kindubilva” is claimed for Kenduli (Birbhum, Bengal), Kenduli Sasan (Odisha) and a village in Mithilā.

dates.label: 12th c. CE (late)
dates.basis: tradition of Jayadeva at the court of Lakṣmaṇasena; manuscript and commentary history

nodes.name: Jñāneśvarī
nodes.summary: Jñānadeva’s Marathi ovī commentary (Bhāvārthadīpikā) on the Bhagavad Gītā in eighteen chapters, completed in Śaka 1212 (1290 CE) according to its colophon. It is the foundational scripture of the Vārkarī tradition and among the earliest major works of Marathi literature.
nodes.details: The colophon places the work “on the bank of the Godāvarī” in the ancient pañcakrośa kṣetra where Śrī Mahālayā dwells — traditionally identified with Nevāsā — during the reign of Śrī Rāmacandra “of the Yadu line” (the Yādava king Rāmacandra), written by Jñānadeva, disciple of Nivṛttinātha, with Saccidānanda Bābā as scribe. An appended verse records that Eknāth produced a corrected text in Śaka 1506 (1584 CE) because variant readings had crept in.

dates.label: Śaka 1212 (1290 CE)
dates.basis: colophon with regnal reference to the Yādava king Rāmacandra

nodes.name: Kakawin Rāmāyaṇa (Old Javanese)
nodes.summary: The Old Javanese Rāmāyaṇa in kakawin (Indic-metre court poetry), the longest kakawin of the Hindu-Buddhist period, composed in Central Java c. 856–930 CE. Its first half closely follows the Sanskrit Bhaṭṭikāvya rather than Vālmīki.
nodes.details: The poem is anonymous in the manuscripts; Balinese tradition names a poet Yogīśvara. It belongs to the period of the Medang (Mataram) kingdom, which also built the Prambanan temple compound with its Rāmāyaṇa reliefs; whether the reliefs follow this poem or another telling has been debated since Stutterheim (1925). The text survives in Balinese manuscripts and is still recited in Bali.

dates.label: c. 856 – c. 930 CE
dates.basis: linguistic and historical evidence; links with Medang court culture

nodes.name: Ramakien (Thai)

scripts.text: รามเกียรติ์

nodes.summary: The Thai national Rāma epic. Earlier Ayutthaya-period versions were largely lost in 1767; the canonical recension was compiled under King Rama I (Phutthayotfa Chulalok) in 1797–1807, partly written by the king, and a shorter version for dance-drama was made under Rama II.
nodes.details: Phra Ram is an incarnation of Phra Narai (Nārāyaṇa) and Nang Sida of Lakshmi; Thotsakan (Rāvaṇa) is Sida’s father in this telling, who sets her adrift because of an ill omen, after which she is raised by King Chanok (Janaka). Hanuman is a brilliant, amorous white monkey who fathers Macchanu with the mermaid Suvannamaccha. The Ramakien is painted in the galleries of Wat Phra Kaew, Bangkok, and performed in khon masked drama.

dates.event: compilation of the Rama I recension
dates.label: 1797–1807 CE
dates.basis: court records of Rama I’s reign

dates.label: Ayutthaya period, before 1767
dates.basis: fragmentary survivals after the sack of Ayutthaya

nodes.name: Reamker (Khmer)

scripts.text: រាមកេរ្តិ៍

nodes.summary: The Khmer Rāma epic (Rāmakerti, “Glory of Rāma”), whose surviving text dates from the 16th–17th c. (first part) and later centuries. It recasts the story in Theravāda Buddhist terms and is a mainstay of Cambodian court dance and Lkhon Khol masked theatre.
nodes.details: Characters: Preah Ream (Rāma), Neang Seda (Sītā), Preah Leak (Lakṣmaṇa), Krong Reap (Rāvaṇa), Hanuman. The surviving first part does not narrate Rāvaṇa’s death; the second part includes Seda’s second exile and her descent into the earth. The encounter of Hanuman and the mermaid Sovann Maccha is a favourite episode. Rāma narratives were carved at Angkor (e.g. Angkor Wat, 12th c.) centuries before the surviving Reamker text.

dates.event: composition of the surviving first part
dates.label: 16th–17th c. CE

nodes.limits: Angkorian reliefs show the Rāma story was known in the Khmer world; they are not evidence for the Reamker text, which is later.

nodes.name: Paumacariya of Vimalasūri (Jain)
nodes.summary: The earliest Jain telling of the Rāma story, in Mahārāṣṭrī Prakrit, by Vimalasūri. Its own colophon dates it 530 (variant 520) years after Mahāvīra’s nirvāṇa; scholars disagree on how to convert this and many place the work between the 1st and 5th centuries CE.
nodes.details: Rāma is “Pauma” (Padma). The work rationalises the story for Jain readers: rākṣasas and vānaras are human vidyādhara clans (the monkey is a banner emblem), Rāvaṇa is a learned Jain devotee who is not literally ten-headed, and in keeping with the Jain pattern of Baladeva, Vāsudeva and Prativāsudeva it is Lakṣmaṇa, not Rāma, who kills Rāvaṇa. Rāma ends as a Jain monk and attains liberation; Rāvaṇa is to become a future tīrthaṅkara. The frame has King Śreṇika asking Gautama how the popular tellings — monkeys defeating rākṣasas, Kumbhakarṇa sleeping six months — can be true, so the work presents itself as a corrective telling.

dates.label: 530 (var. 520) years after Mahāvīra’s nirvāṇa
dates.basis: praśasti at the end of the text

dates.event: composition (colophon read on the traditional Vīra era)
dates.label: c. 4 CE

dates.event: composition (colophon read on Jacobi’s nirvāṇa date)
dates.label: c. 53–63 CE
dates.basis: colophon converted with Jacobi’s later Vīra-nirvāṇa

dates.label: c. 1st–5th c. CE (not later than the 3rd c. in the commonest view)
dates.basis: language, metre, content; terminus ante quem the Kuvalayamālā of 778 CE

nodes.limits: A Jain work: it belongs to the Rāma narrative tradition but is not a Hindu scripture, and its corrective framing is a Jain literary strategy, not evidence about an “original” Rāmāyaṇa.

nodes.name: Dasaratha Jātaka (Buddhist)
nodes.summary: Jātaka no. 461 of the Pali canon’s Jātaka collection: a birth-story in which Rāma-paṇḍita, the Bodhisatta, his brother Lakkhaṇa and their sister Sītā, children of King Dasaratha of Bārāṇasī, live twelve years in the Himalaya. There is no abduction and no Rāvaṇa.
nodes.details:
Dasaratha sends his children away to protect them from a second queen who wants the throne for her son Bharata; he dies in the ninth year, but Rāma-paṇḍita keeps to his father’s twelve-year term and sends his sandals to rule in his place. On their return Sītā is made queen consort and Rāma reigns sixteen thousand years. In the closing identification the Buddha says that Suddhodana was Dasaratha, the mother of Rāhula was Sītā, Ānanda was Bharata, and “I myself was Rāmapaṇḍita.”

The verse (gāthā) portion is older than the prose commentary in which the narrative is told; whether the story preserves an older form of the Rāma legend than Vālmīki’s (Weber’s view) or is a Buddhist reworking (the more common view) is disputed.
nodes.limits: A Buddhist text; it is part of the Rāma narrative tradition but not a Hindu text. Its relative age vis-à-vis Vālmīki is unresolved.

nodes.name: Cilappatikāram
nodes.summary: The Tamil epic of Kaṇṇaki and Kōvalaṉ attributed to Iḷaṅkō Aṭikaḷ, in three books set in the Cōḻa, Pāṇḍya and Cēra capitals, probably composed around the 5th–6th century. It contains early Tamil depictions of Kṛṣṇa, Murukaṉ and Koṟṟavai worship.
nodes.details: Kōvalaṉ is executed in Madurai on a false charge of stealing the queen’s anklet; Kaṇṇaki proves his innocence, curses and burns the city, and is deified as the goddess Pattiṉi. The epic’s set-piece songs include the hunters’ song to Koṟṟavai, the cowherdesses’ round-dance (āycciyar kuravai) in which girls enact Kṛṣṇa, Balarāma and Piññai, and the hill-people’s dance for Murukaṉ (kuṉṟakkuravai). The attribution to the Cēra prince-ascetic Iḷaṅkō rests on a later prologue; the author is often thought to have been Jain, but the poem honours Vedic, Vaiṣṇava, Śaiva and Jain religion alike.

nodes.name: Rādhā
nodes.summary: The cowherd beloved of Kṛṣṇa. She is not named in the Bhāgavata Purāṇa; the earliest datable literary mentions are scattered Prakrit and Sanskrit verses (Gāhā Sattasaī, 9th-c. poetics), she becomes the heroine of Jayadeva’s Gītagovinda (12th c.), and the supreme goddess of the Brahmavaivarta Purāṇa and Gauḍīya theology.
nodes.details:
Her development is a clear case of a figure growing across texts. (1) A single Gāhā Sattasaī verse addresses Kṛṣṇa about Rādhā (date of the anthology disputed, before 640 CE); (2) 9th–10th-c. poetics (Ānandavardhana’s Dhvanyāloka, Bhaṭṭa Nārāyaṇa’s Veṇīsaṃhāra) cite verses about her; (3) the Bhāgavata’s rāsa narrative has Kṛṣṇa vanish with one unnamed favoured gopī, whom later commentators identify as Rādhā; (4) the Gītagovinda makes her love the poem’s subject; (5) the Brahmavaivarta Purāṇa (extant version c. 15th–16th c., Bengal) makes her Kṛṣṇa’s eternal śakti in Goloka; (6) Gauḍīya theologians call her Kṛṣṇa’s hlādinī-śakti and regard Caitanya as Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa in one body.

The Tamil cowherd beloved Piññai (Nappiṉṉai) of the Cilappatikāram and the Āḻvārs is a separate figure; some scholars see her as a southern parallel or precursor (Hardy 1983).

dates.label: before 640 CE (anthology dated 1st–7th c.; disputed)
dates.basis: date of the anthology; Bāṇa cites it in the 7th c.

dates.event: supreme goddess in the extant Brahmavaivarta Purāṇa
dates.label: c. 15th–16th c. CE

openQuestions: Verse number of the Gāhā Sattasaī Rādhā verse in a named edition (often cited as 1.89 in Weber’s numbering — unverified).

nodes.name: Murukaṉ (Tamil)
nodes.summary: The Tamil god of the hills, Cēyōṉ (“the red one”) of the Tolkāppiyam, praised in the Paripāṭal and Tirumurukāṟṟuppaṭai. From the late Caṅkam period he converges with the northern Skanda-Kārttikeya; the two are kept as separate ids here, joined by an IDENTIFIED_WITH assertion.
nodes.details:
The Tolkāppiyam assigns Cēyōṉ to the kuṟiñci (hill) landscape alongside Māyōṉ (forest-pasture), Vēntaṉ (riverine farmland) and Varuṇaṉ (seashore) — the medieval commentator Nacciṉārkkiṉiyar glosses Cēyōṉ as “red Murukaṉ.” Early poetry knows him as Vēlaṉ, the spear-bearer, worshipped in possession dances (veṟiyāṭṭu). By the Tirumurukāṟṟuppaṭai and the Paripāṭal (c. 3rd–6th c.) he has the six faces and twelve arms, the Kṛttikā birth and the war against Cūr (Śūrapadma) of northern Skanda mythology. His Tamil consort Vaḷḷi, a hunter girl, stands beside Teyvāṉai (Devasenā), Indra’s daughter.

The Tirumurukāṟṟuppaṭai names six places of the god; later tradition identifies these with six temples, the āṟupaṭai vīṭu (Tiruparaṅkuṉṟam, Tiruccentūr, Paḻaṉi, Cuvāmimalai, Tiruttaṇi, Paḻamutircōlai). The identification of the poem’s sites with these six shrines is itself a traditional reading.

dates.event: convergence with Skanda evident in Tamil poetry
dates.label: c. 3rd–6th c. CE
dates.basis: Skanda motifs in Paripāṭal and Tirumurukāṟṟuppaṭai

nodes.limits: Tamil Murukaṉ and Sanskrit Skanda are distinct in origin; their identification is historical convergence plus theological identification, not a single original deity.

nodes.name: Pāñcarātra
nodes.summary: The Vaiṣṇava ritual and theological tradition of the Pāñcarātra Saṃhitās, centred on Vāsudeva-Nārāyaṇa and the doctrine of four emanations (vyūha: Vāsudeva, Saṅkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna, Aniruddha). It governs worship in many South Indian Vaiṣṇava temples, including Srirangam.
nodes.details: The name appears already in the Nārāyaṇīya section of the Mahābhārata’s Śāntiparvan. Tradition counts 108 saṃhitās, though more than 200 titles are known; the Sāttvata, Pauṣkara and Jayākhya are called the “three gems.” Rāmānuja and Yāmuna defended the Vedic validity of Pāñcarātra against critics. Temple practice: according to the tradition, Srirangam follows the Pārameśvara Saṃhitā, Melkote the Īśvara Saṃhitā and the Varadarāja temple at Kanchipuram the Jayākhya.

dates.label: c. 7th–10th c. CE (disputed)
dates.basis: textual borrowing from Śaiva tantras, citations

nodes.name: Śaiva Siddhānta
nodes.summary: The dualist, Veda-congruent school of the Śaiva Mantramārga, based on the Siddhānta Āgamas (traditionally 28), systematised by Kashmirian exegetes (Sadyojyoti, Bhaṭṭa Nārāyaṇakaṇṭha, Bhaṭṭa Rāmakaṇṭha) and later by Aghoraśiva at Chidambaram. In Tamil it fused with the Tirumurai hymns through Meykaṇṭār’s Civañāṉapōtam (13th c.).
nodes.details: Sanderson (2009) traces the rise of the Siddhānta and its ritual (initiation, daily worship, temple consecration) as the institutional backbone of early medieval Śaivism across India, Cambodia and Java. The Tamil Śaiva Siddhānta of the Meykaṇṭār lineage claims the Tirumurai poets as its saints; the relation between this Tamil school and the older pan-Indian Sanskrit Siddhānta is a subject of scholarship.

dates.label: c. 450–550 CE
dates.basis: editors’ dating of the Niśvāsa Mūlasūtra

nodes.name: Śrīvaiṣṇava
nodes.summary: The South Indian Vaiṣṇava tradition that joins the Tamil hymns of the Āḻvārs (as a “Tamil Veda”) with Sanskrit Vedānta (Viśiṣṭādvaita) and Pāñcarātra temple ritual, centred on Viṣṇu with Śrī (Lakṣmī). Its ācāryas include Nāthamuni, Yāmuna, Rāmānuja and Vedānta Deśika.
nodes.details: The tradition calls its dual heritage ubhaya-vedānta (Sanskrit and Tamil Vedas). Its great temples are Srirangam, Tirumala–Tirupati, Kanchipuram and Melkote; the Divya Prabandham is recited in their liturgy. From the 14th c. it divided into the Vaṭakalai and Teṉkalai schools.

nodes.name: Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇava
nodes.summary: The Bengal Vaiṣṇava tradition stemming from Caitanya (1486–1534), centred on the love of Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa, with a theology elaborated by the Gosvāmīs of Vṛndāvana and a hagiographic canon including Kṛṣṇadāsa Kavirāja’s Caitanya Caritāmṛta.
nodes.details: The Bhāgavata Purāṇa is its principal scripture; Jayadeva’s Gītagovinda and Bengali songs of Caṇḍīdās and Vidyāpati were loved by Caitanya. The Gosvāmīs (Rūpa, Sanātana, Jīva and others) systematised a theology of devotional rasa and of Rādhā as Kṛṣṇa’s hlādinī-śakti. Caitanya is regarded by followers as Kṛṣṇa, and as Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa combined.

dates.label: early 16th – early 17th c. CE
dates.basis: Caitanya’s life; dates of Gosvāmī works and the Caitanya Caritāmṛta

nodes.name: Vīraśaiva / Liṅgāyata
nodes.summary: The Kannada-speaking Śaiva tradition associated with Basava (12th c.) and the vacana poets (Allama Prabhu, Akka Mahādēvi and others), marked by wearing the personal iṣṭaliṅga, devotion to Śiva alone, and — in the vacanas — criticism of caste, temple ritual and Brahmanical sacrifice.
nodes.details: Whether Basava founded the tradition or reshaped an existing one is debated (Michael 1992). The relation between the names “Vīraśaiva” and “Liṅgāyata” is also contested in modern Karnataka; both are recorded as aliases without taking sides. The vacanas were written down long after Basava’s time.

dates.event: formative period (Basava and the vacanakāras at Kalyāṇa)
dates.label: 12th c. CE

nodes.name: Kashmir Śaivism (Trika)
nodes.summary: The non-dualist Śaiva traditions of Kashmir — Trika, Krama, Spanda and the Pratyabhijñā philosophy of Somānanda and Utpaladeva — culminating in Abhinavagupta (c. 975–1025) and Kṣemarāja.
nodes.details: Sanderson stresses that “Kashmir Śaivism” is a modern umbrella for several Kashmirian Śaiva systems, including Kashmirian Śaiva Siddhānta, which was dualist. The fourteenth-century Kashmiri poet Lal Ded (Lallā) is associated by later tradition with Trika thought.

dates.label: c. 9th–11th c. CE
dates.basis: dated works of Utpaladeva and Abhinavagupta

nodes.name: Jain tradition
nodes.summary: The Jain religion, here recorded chiefly as the source of its own Rāma and Kṛṣṇa tellings (Vimalasūri’s Paumacariya, Raviṣeṇa’s Padmapurāṇa, Svayambhū’s Paumacariu, Guṇabhadra’s Uttarapurāṇa, Hemacandra) and of Jain poets in Kannada and Tamil such as Pampa.
nodes.details: In Jain universal history Rāma, Lakṣmaṇa and Rāvaṇa are the eighth Baladeva, Vāsudeva and Prativāsudeva among the sixty-three “illustrious persons” (śalākāpuruṣa); Kṛṣṇa is likewise a Vāsudeva. Jain tellings therefore differ systematically from Hindu ones (e.g. Lakṣmaṇa kills Rāvaṇa). Tagging a work trad:jain records its tradition; it does not make it a deviant Hindu text.

nodes.name: Buddhist tradition
nodes.summary: The Buddhist religion, here recorded as the source of the Dasaratha Jātaka, of the Mahāyāna Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra’s frame story with Rāvaṇa, and of the Theravāda-framed Rāma tellings of mainland Southeast Asia (Lao Phra Lak Phra Lam as a jātaka; Khmer Reamker; Thai Ramakien).
nodes.details: In these tellings Rāma is often a bodhisatta, a previous birth of the Buddha, and Rāvaṇa may be compared with Devadatta or Māra. They are part of the Rāma narrative tradition, not Hindu texts.

nodes.name: Kampaṉ (Kambar)
nodes.summary: Tamil poet, author of the Irāmāvatāram (Kamba Rāmāyaṇam), patronised by Caṭaiyappa Vaḷḷal of Tiruveṇṇainallūr. His date is disputed between the 9th and the 12th century, with most modern scholars favouring the 12th.
nodes.details: Tradition places his birth at Tiruvaḻuntūr in the Cōḻa country and has him honoured by a Cōḻa king with the title Kavicakravarti. Temple tradition holds that his epic was first recited at Srirangam. Other works attributed to him include poems in praise of Nammāḻvār (Caṭakōpar Antāti) and of the plough (Ēr Eḻupatu); these attributions are traditional.

nodes.name: Tulsīdās
nodes.summary: Awadhi and Braj poet (d. 1623), author of the Rāmcaritmānas (begun 1574), the Vinaya Patrikā, Kavitāvalī and other Rāma-devotional works; he lived in Ayodhyā and above all in Kāśī (Vārāṇasī).
nodes.details: Hagiography (e.g. Priyādās’s commentary on Nābhādās’s Bhaktamāl) tells of his marriage, renunciation and visions of Hanumān; the Hanumān Cālīsā is attributed to him by tradition, an attribution some scholars question. He is claimed by the Rāmānandī order.

dates.label: 1574 (Mānas begun) – 1623 CE (death)
dates.basis: internal date of the Mānas; death year in tradition widely accepted

dates.label: Saṃvat 1554 (1497 CE) per some hagiographies; c. 1532 in common scholarly estimates

nodes.name: Kṛttibās Ojhā
nodes.summary: Bengali poet to whom the Śrīrām Pā̃cālī (Kṛttivāsī Rāmāyaṇa) is attributed; tradition places him at Phuliyā on the Bhāgīrathī and in the 15th century, though the identification of the king he mentions is disputed.

nodes.name: Jayadeva
nodes.summary: Sanskrit poet of the late 12th century, author of the Gītagovinda; tradition makes him a poet at the court of Lakṣmaṇasena of Bengal, and both Bengal and Odisha claim his birthplace “Kindubilva.” Two hymns attributed to him are in the Sikh Ādi Granth.
nodes.details: Odia tradition links him to Puri and to his wife Padmāvatī, a temple dancer; early commentators and modern scholars do not support the Padmāvatī story. Sixteenth-century texts call him a native of Utkala.

dates.label: late 12th c. CE
dates.basis: court of Lakṣmaṇasena (r. c. 1178–1206) per tradition

nodes.name: Jñāneśvar
nodes.summary: Marathi poet-saint (traditionally 1275–1296), disciple of his elder brother Nivṛttinātha, author of the Jñāneśvarī (1290) and the Amṛtānubhava, and revered as a founder of the Vārkarī tradition of Viṭṭhala devotion.
nodes.details: In the colophon he calls himself “Jñānadeva, son (disciple) of Śrī Nivṛttinātha, born of the line of Maheśa” (i.e. in Nivṛtti’s Nātha lineage). Tradition holds that he entered living samādhi at Āḷandī in 1296.

dates.label: 1275–1296 CE (traditional)
dates.basis: hagiography; colophon date 1290 falls within it

nodes.name: Āṇṭāḷ
nodes.summary: The only woman among the twelve Āḻvārs, foster-daughter of Periyāḻvār at Śrīvilliputtūr, author of the Tiruppāvai (30 verses) and Nācciyār Tirumoḻi (143 verses in the standard count); she is usually dated to the 8th–9th century.
nodes.details: Hagiography tells that Periyāḻvār found her as an infant under a tulasī plant in the temple garden, that she wore the garland meant for the god before it was offered (hence “she who gave the garland she had worn”), and that she was united with Raṅganātha at Srirangam. The Tiruppāvai is sung during the month of Mārkaḻi; its name survives, with that of Māṇikkavācakar’s Tiruvempāvai, in the Thai royal Brahman ceremony Triyampawai–Trippawai.

dates.label: c. 8th–9th c. CE
dates.basis: relation to Periyāḻvār and Pāṇḍya synchronisms

nodes.name: Nammāḻvār
nodes.summary: The foremost Āḻvār (Caṭakōpaṉ, Māṟaṉ) of Kurukūr (Āḻvārtirunagari) in the far south of Tamil Nadu, author of the Tiruvāymoḻi (1,102 verses) and three shorter works; scholars date him to the 8th–9th century.
nodes.details: His works: Tiruvāymoḻi (1,102 verses), Tiruviruttam (100), Tiruvāciriyam (7) and Periya Tiruvantāti (87). Śrīvaiṣṇavas regard the four as Tamil counterparts of the four Vedas. Hagiography says he sat in silent meditation in a tamarind tree until his disciple Madhurakavi came to him.

nodes.name: Appar (Tirunāvukkaracar)
nodes.summary: Tamil Śaiva poet-saint of the 7th century, author of Tirumurai books 4–6. The Periya Purāṇam tells that he was first a Jain monk named Dharmasena, returned to Śaivism, and brought the Pallava king Mahendravarman I back to Śiva.

dates.label: 7th c. CE
dates.basis: synchronism with Mahendravarman I in hagiography

nodes.name: Campantar (Tiruñāṉacampantar)
nodes.summary: Tamil Śaiva child-poet of Cīrkāḻi (7th c.), author of Tirumurai books 1–3 — the largest share of the Tēvāram. The Periya Purāṇam narrates his contest with Jain monks at Madurai and the return of the Pāṇḍya king to Śaivism.

dates.label: 7th c. CE
dates.basis: synchronism with Appar and Pāṇḍya Neṭumāṟaṉ in hagiography

nodes.limits: The Madurai contest is a hagiographic narrative (12th c.); it is evidence of later Śaiva–Jain polemic, not a contemporary record.

nodes.name: Cuntarar
nodes.summary: Tamil Śaiva poet-saint of the 8th century (Cuntaramūrtti), author of Tirumurai book 7; his Tiruttoṇṭattokai lists the devotees whom the Periya Purāṇam later expanded into the sixty-three Nāyaṉmār. Tradition calls him the “friend of Śiva” and links him to Tiruvārūr.

dates.label: 8th – early 9th c. CE
dates.basis: internal references to earlier saints and to Pallava-period kings

nodes.name: Rāmānuja
nodes.summary: Śrīvaiṣṇava ācārya and Vedāntin of Śrīperumbudūr, chief exponent of Viśiṣṭādvaita and author of the Śrībhāṣya; he reorganised worship at Srirangam and, during a sojourn in the Hoysala country, at Melkote. Traditional dates are 1017–1137; many scholars prefer 1077–1157.

nodes.name: Caitanya
nodes.summary: Bengali Vaiṣṇava saint (1486–1534), born at Navadvīpa, who spent his last two decades at Puri; the Gauḍīya tradition regards him as Kṛṣṇa, and as Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa in one body. The eight-verse Śikṣāṣṭaka is the only work accepted as his.

dates.label: 1486–1534 CE
dates.basis: hagiographies and regnal synchronisms (Pratāparudra of Odisha)

nodes.name: Basava
nodes.summary: Kannada Śaiva poet and minister at the Kalacuri court of Bijjala II at Kalyāṇa (12th c.), whose vacanas, addressed to Kūḍalasaṅgamadēva, are central to the Vīraśaiva / Liṅgāyata tradition.
nodes.details: The vacanas attributed to him reject caste distinctions, temple worship and sacrifice in favour of devotion and the personal liṅga; tradition credits him with the Anubhava Maṇṭapa assembly of devotees. The vacana collections were compiled long after his death, so individual attributions are uncertain.

dates.label: mid-12th c. CE (minister of Bijjala II)

nodes.name: Vimalasūri
nodes.summary: Jain (Śvetāmbara) monk-poet, author of the Prakrit Paumacariya, the earliest surviving Jain Rāma narrative. His date depends on the disputed reading of his colophon (530 years after Mahāvīra) and is placed by scholars anywhere from the 1st to the 5th century CE.

nodes.name: Bṛhadīśvara temple, Thanjavur
nodes.summary: Granite Śiva temple built by the Cōḻa king Rājarāja I at his capital Thanjavur and consecrated in 1010 CE; its c. 60 m vimāna was the tallest of its age and the walls carry a large corpus of Rājarāja’s own Tamil inscriptions.
nodes.details:
The temple, called Rājarājeśvaram in its inscriptions, was built between c. 1003 and 1010 CE. Its inscriptions record that on the 275th day of Rājarāja I’s 25th regnal year (1010 CE) the king presented the gold-plated finial (kalaśa) for the vimāna, and they list endowments, temple staff and the bronzes the king and his family gave.

The circumambulatory passage around the sanctum preserves Cōḻa-period wall paintings (partly over-painted in the Nāyaka period). Later Nāyaka and Marāṭhā rulers of Thanjavur added subsidiary shrines and halls within the enclosure. The temple remains in worship.

dates.label: c. 1003–1010 CE
dates.basis: regnal synchronism from the temple’s own inscriptions

dates.label: 1010 CE (25th regnal year of Rājarāja I)
dates.basis: dated inscription: gift of the gold-plated finial on the 275th day of the king’s 25th regnal year

dates.label: 16th–19th c. Nāyaka and Marāṭhā additions
dates.basis: style and later inscriptions of the Thanjavur Nāyakas and Marāṭhās

location.label: Thanjavur, Tamil Nadu, India

attributes.unesco: Great Living Chola Temples — inscribed 1987 (as Brihadisvara Temple, Thanjavur), extended 2004; UNESCO list no. 250
attributes.protection: World Heritage property managed by the Archaeological Survey of India

image.credit: Original: Rainer Halama Derivative work: UnpetitproleX (Wikimedia Commons)

nodes.limits: The fabric and inscriptions securely date Rājarāja I’s construction and the 1010 CE consecration and document the temple’s staffing and endowments; they do not show how old Śiva worship at Thanjavur was before the Cōḻa foundation, and the Cōḻa paintings survive only in part beneath later layers.

nodes.name: Bṛhadīśvara temple, Gangaikondacholapuram
nodes.summary: Śiva temple at the new capital founded by Rājendra I after his northern campaign to the Gaṅgā (c. 1025); its vimāna has a gently concave profile, unlike Thanjavur’s straight-sided pyramid. Part of the Great Living Chola Temples World Heritage property.
nodes.details: Rājendra I (r. 1014–1044) took the title Gaṅgaikoṇḍa (“who took the Gaṅgā”) after his army reached the Gaṅgā and established the city of Gaṅgaikoṇḍacōḻapuram as Cōḻa capital around 1025; it remained the capital for about two and a half centuries. The temple is usually dated to c. 1035, i.e. within his reign. Famous sculptures include Śiva garlanding the devotee Caṇḍeśa.

dates.label: c. 1025–1044 CE (often given as c. 1035)
dates.basis: regnal synchronism with Rājendra I and his founding of the capital

location.label: Gangaikondacholapuram, Ariyalur district, Tamil Nadu, India

attributes.unesco: Great Living Chola Temples — added in the 2004 extension; UNESCO list no. 250

nodes.name: Airāvateśvara temple, Darasuram
nodes.summary: Twelfth-century Śiva temple near Kumbakonam built under the Cōḻa king Rājarāja II; its maṇḍapa is designed as a stone chariot and its reliefs include narrative friezes of the 63 Nāyaṉmār saints.
nodes.details: The temple takes its name from the tradition that Indra’s white elephant Airāvata worshipped Śiva here. It is attributed to Rājarāja II (r. c. 1146–1173). Small labelled panels illustrate episodes from the lives of the Śaiva saints later collected in the Periya Purāṇam.

dates.label: Airāvata, Indra’s elephant, worshipped Śiva here (sthala tradition)
dates.basis: temple tradition (sthala-purāṇa / local narrative); not a historical date
