nodes.summary: Ninth-century Hindu temple compound in Central Java with towering shrines to Śiva, Brahmā and Viṣṇu; it is identified with the Śiva temple whose inauguration on 12 November 856 is recorded in the Śivagṛha inscription, and its balustrade reliefs tell the Rāmāyaṇa and the Kṛṣṇa story.
nodes.details: Construction was probably begun by Rakai Pikatan of Medang (a painted name “pikatan” was found on a finial of the Śiva temple) and inaugurated by his successor Lokapāla. The Śivagṛha inscription (856), edited by de Casparis, describes a Śiva temple compound and a river diversion that closely match Prambanan. The Rāmāyaṇa reliefs run on the Śiva and Brahmā temples, the Kṛṣṇāyana on the Viṣṇu temple. Prambanan Temple Compounds were inscribed as a World Heritage property in 1991.

dates.label: Legend of Rara Jonggrang, the princess turned to stone (Javanese folk tradition)
dates.basis: temple tradition (sthala-purāṇa / local narrative); not a historical date

dates.label: 12 November 856 CE (Śivagṛha inscription)
dates.basis: dated inscription identified with the compound

dates.label: c. 850 CE (begun under Rakai Pikatan)
dates.basis: painted name on finial and inscription

location.label: Prambanan, Sleman Regency, Yogyakarta / Central Java, Indonesia

attributes.unesco: Prambanan Temple Compounds — inscribed 1991; UNESCO list no. 642

nodes.limits: The identification of the Śivagṛha inscription with Prambanan is a strong scholarly argument (class 5), not an inscription found on the temple. The reliefs show a Javanese Rāmāyaṇa tradition, not the events themselves.

nodes.name: Arjuna temple group, Dieng Plateau
nodes.summary: Small Śaiva stone temples on the volcanic Dieng Plateau of Central Java (mid-7th to late 8th c.), among the oldest standing stone structures in Java; their Mahābhārata names (Arjuna, Semar, Srikandi, Puntadewa) were given much later by local people.
nodes.details: Dates for the Dieng temples range from the mid-7th to the end of the 8th century; an inscription of 809 CE is often cited for the site (not verified here).

location.label: Dieng Plateau, Banjarnegara Regency, Central Java, Indonesia

nodes.limits: The Pāṇḍava names are modern and do not indicate original dedications or any link with the Mahābhārata.

nodes.name: Angkor Wat
nodes.summary: State temple of the Khmer king Sūryavarman II (r. 1113–c. 1150), built as a temple-mountain to Viṣṇu at Yaśodharapura (Angkor); its galleries carry vast bas-reliefs of the churning of the ocean, the Kurukṣetra battle and the war in Laṅkā. From the late 13th century it became a Theravāda Buddhist monastery.
nodes.details: The temple faces west, unusually, which has been linked to Viṣṇu and to a funerary function. The western gallery shows the Battle of Laṅkā (northern half) and the Kurukṣetra war (southern half); the eastern gallery shows the Churning of the Ocean of Milk (Samudra-manthana), with 92 asuras and 88 devas pulling the serpent Vāsuki; the northern gallery shows Kṛṣṇa’s victory over Bāṇa; another gallery shows Sūryavarman II himself in procession. Angkor was inscribed as a World Heritage property in 1992. Astronomical alignments proposed by Stencel et al. (1976) and Mannikka (1996) remain debated.

dates.label: c. 1113–1150 CE (reign of Sūryavarman II)
dates.basis: regnal synchronism; labelled relief of the king

dates.label: conversion to Theravāda Buddhist use from the late 13th c.

location.label: Angkor, Siem Reap Province, Cambodia

attributes.unesco: Angkor — inscribed 1992; UNESCO list no. 668
attributes.principalDeity: Viṣṇu (original); Buddhist worship since the late 13th c.

nodes.limits: The reliefs are a 12th-century Khmer reading of Sanskrit epic and Purāṇic narratives; they attest the reception of those texts, not the historicity of the events.

nodes.name: Banteay Srei
nodes.summary: Small, exquisitely carved red-sandstone Śiva temple near Angkor consecrated on 22 April 967 CE, unusual in having been built not by a king but by the court official Yajñavarāha; its pediments include Rāvaṇa shaking Mount Kailāsa.
nodes.details: Yajñavarāha (and Viṣṇukumāra) served as counsellors to Rājendravarman II and tutor to Jayavarman V. The temple’s Khmer name means “citadel of women”, a modern name; its original name was Tribhuvanamaheśvara. Part of the Angkor World Heritage property.

location.label: near Angkor, Siem Reap Province, Cambodia

attributes.unesco: part of Angkor (1992; no. 668)

nodes.limits: Securely dated; the Rāvaṇa pediment attests the Rāvaṇānugraha narrative in 10th-c. Cambodia.

nodes.name: Preah Vihear temple
nodes.summary: Khmer Śiva temple stretched along a north–south axis on a cliff of the Dângrêk escarpment, built mainly in the 11th–12th centuries under Sūryavarman I and Sūryavarman II; the International Court of Justice ruled in 1962 that it lies in Cambodia, and it was inscribed as a World Heritage property in 2008.
nodes.details: The temple was dedicated to Śiva as Śikhareśvara (“Lord of the peak”). The 2008 inscription was followed by armed clashes on the border; the ICJ’s 2013 interpretation judgment concerned the surrounding promontory.

location.label: Choam Khsant District, Preah Vihear Province, Cambodia

attributes.unesco: Temple of Preah Vihear — inscribed 2008; UNESCO list no. 1224

nodes.limits: The UNESCO list number (1224) is from recall and should be checked on whc.unesco.org (blocked to automated fetching in this session).

nodes.name: Vat Phou
nodes.summary: Khmer-period Śiva sanctuary at the foot of Mount Phou Kao (Liṅgaparvata, named for its liṅga-shaped summit) in southern Laos, with structures from the 5th to the 13th century; now a Theravāda Buddhist site and a World Heritage property (2001).
nodes.details: The sanctuary was associated with the early city of Śreṣṭhapura on the Mekong. Most standing buildings date from the 11th–12th centuries. The World Heritage property is the Vat Phou and Associated Ancient Settlements within the Champasak Cultural Landscape.

location.label: Champasak Province, Laos

attributes.unesco: Vat Phou and Associated Ancient Settlements within the Champasak Cultural Landscape — inscribed 2001; UNESCO list no. 481

nodes.limits: UNESCO number (481) from recall. The liṅga-mountain is a natural feature venerated as Śiva.

nodes.name: Mỹ Sơn sanctuary
nodes.summary: Valley of Cham brick temple-towers in central Vietnam, the principal religious centre of the kings of Champa from the 4th to the 13th century, dedicated chiefly to Śiva as Bhadreśvara; inscribed as a World Heritage property in 1999.
nodes.details: The first sanctuary is associated with the 4th-century king Bhadravarman. Many towers were destroyed by US bombing in a single week during the Vietnam War. The valley lies in former Quảng Nam province, which was merged into Đà Nẵng city in Vietnam’s 2025 administrative reorganisation.

location.label: Thu Bồn commune, Đà Nẵng (formerly Quảng Nam province), Vietnam

attributes.unesco: My Son Sanctuary — inscribed 1999; UNESCO list no. 949

nodes.limits: UNESCO number (949) from recall; coordinates are for the valley at minute precision.

nodes.name: Pura Besakih
nodes.summary: The “mother temple” of Balinese Hinduism, a complex of more than twenty temples terraced on the slopes of Mount Agung; in use as a Hindu sanctuary at least since the 14th century.
nodes.details: The principal Pura Penataran Agung is dedicated to Śiva, with associated temples for Brahmā and Viṣṇu. Wikipedia states it was used as a Hindu place of worship from 1284. The complex survived the 1963 eruption of Mount Agung.

dates.label: in Hindu use from the late 13th–14th c. CE

location.label: Besakih, Karangasem Regency, Bali, Indonesia

nodes.limits: The terraced sanctuary may be older; the buildings themselves are frequently renewed.

nodes.name: Batu Caves temple
nodes.summary: Murukaṉ shrine in limestone caves north of Kuala Lumpur, completed in 1891 and the focus since 1892 of one of the largest Thaipūsam festivals outside India; a very tall gilded statue of Murukaṉ was unveiled beside the steps in January 2006.
nodes.details: The Tamil trader K. Thamboosamy Pillai promoted the caves as a place of Hindu worship, reportedly inspired by the resemblance of the cave mouth to Murukaṉ’s vel (spear). Its festival reflects the Tamil diaspora in Malaysia.

location.label: Gombak, Selangor, Malaysia

nodes.limits: A diaspora foundation of the colonial period; it shows the reach of Murukaṉ worship, not an ancient sanctuary.

nodes.name: Naṭarāja (Śiva as lord of dance)
nodes.summary: Śiva as the king of dancers, above all in the South Indian ānanda-tāṇḍava form standardised in Cōḻa bronzes: four-armed, dancing within a ring of flames on the dwarf Apasmāra, worshipped above all at Chidambaram.
nodes.details:
Dancing forms of Śiva appear in Deccan cave sculpture from the 6th century (e.g. the many-armed dancer of Bādāmi Cave 1 and the Elephanta panel). The canonical Tamil ānanda-tāṇḍava type, with the drum (ḍamaru), fire, the abhaya gesture and the raised leg, was fixed in bronze under the Cōḻas by the 10th century. Śaiva Siddhānta theology reads the dance as Śiva’s five acts (pañcakṛtya): creation, preservation, destruction, concealment and grace.

In the Chidambaram tradition Naṭarāja dances in the golden hall before the sages Patañjali and Vyāghrapāda. The form is a Tamil and wider South Asian theological elaboration of Śiva; this dataset treats it as FORM_OF Śiva, qualified by tradition, not as a separate god.

dates.label: 6th c. CE (Deccan cave temples)
dates.basis: dated and stylistically dated cave reliefs (Bādāmi Cave 1, Elephanta)

dates.label: by the 10th c. CE (Cōḻa bronzes)
dates.basis: dated bronzes and inscriptions recording gifts of images

nodes.limits: Images and texts establish the history of the iconographic form and its theology; they say nothing about the antiquity of the idea of Śiva’s dance beyond the dated evidence.

nodes.name: Jagannātha
nodes.summary: “Lord of the world”, the deity of Puri worshipped in a stylised wooden image with large round eyes and stump arms, together with Balabhadra and Subhadrā; Vaiṣṇavas regard him as Viṣṇu/Kṛṣṇa, while scholars debate the cult’s tribal, Vaiṣṇava, Buddhist and Jain antecedents.
nodes.details:
The images are renewed in the Navakalevara rite (most recently 1996 and 2015), when the “life substance” is transferred to new figures carved from specially chosen nīm trees, and the Daitā priests — said to descend from the Śabara chief Viśvāvasu of the temple legend — have a central role. The Indradyumna legend itself tells that the deity was first worshipped by a Śabara as Nīlamādhava.

Eschmann, Kulke and Tripathi (1978) argued that Jagannātha developed from a tribal wooden deity progressively “Hinduised” and made into an imperial Vaiṣṇava cult by the Eastern Gaṅga kings, who styled themselves the god’s deputies; nineteenth-century writers proposed Buddhist origins (relic, triratna), which most modern scholars reject. For the Gauḍīya tradition, Caitanya’s ecstatic devotion at Puri identified Jagannātha with Kṛṣṇa.
nodes.limits: The temple, rituals and inscriptions document the cult from the 12th century; its earlier origins are reconstructed and contested.
openQuestions: Which pre-12th-century references to Puruṣottama/Puri refer to the same cult?

earliestMaterial.label: begun under Anantavarman Coḍagaṅga, early–mid 12th c.; completion given as 1161 in Wikipedia’s infobox

nodes.name: The tribal (Śabara) origin hypothesis for Jagannātha
nodes.summary: The scholarly hypothesis that Jagannātha began as a wooden deity of tribal (Śabara) communities of Odisha and was progressively integrated into Brahmanical Vaiṣṇavism and royal cult, culminating under the Eastern Gaṅgas.
nodes.details: Argued in Eschmann, Kulke and Tripathi (eds.) 1978. Supporting points: the aniconic wooden images and their periodic renewal, the role of the Daitā (non-brāhmaṇa) servitors, and the temple’s own Śabara legend. Competing views: Buddhist-origin theories of the 19th century; a continuous Vaiṣṇava (Puruṣottama) cult; Jain readings. The claim concerns history, not the theology of the tradition, which regards Jagannātha as Viṣṇu/Kṛṣṇa.

nodes.name: The claim that the Muṇḍeśvarī temple dates to 108 CE
nodes.summary: The claim, displayed by the ASI and the Bihar State Religious Trust Board, that the Muṇḍeśvarī temple was built in 108 CE and is the oldest functioning Hindu temple in the world.
nodes.details: The claim reads the year 30 of an inscription of Mahārāja Udayasena as Śaka 30. Palaeography indicates a post-Gupta script (Neuss: c. 570–590 CE), and a Harṣa-era reading gives 636 CE; architectural historians date the surviving sculpture to the 6th–7th century and have suggested that the octagonal shrine itself is a later reconstruction.

nodes.name: Veṅkaṭeśvara
nodes.summary: Viṣṇu as Lord of the Vēṅkaṭa hill, worshipped at Tirumala in a standing four-armed image; one of the most widely worshipped forms of Viṣṇu in South India and the diaspora.
nodes.details: The hill is praised by the Āḻvārs, and the temple’s epigraphy runs from the 10th century. The Veṅkaṭācala-māhātmya tells how Viṣṇu came to the hill as Śrīnivāsa and married Padmāvatī, borrowing from Kubera for the wedding — a debt devotees help repay through offerings. Older sectarian polemics debated whether the image was originally Vaiṣṇava, Śaiva, Śākta or Murukaṉ; the Śrīvaiṣṇava tradition credits Rāmānuja with settling its Vaiṣṇava identity.
nodes.limits: Hymns and inscriptions date the cult’s history; the descent narrative is the tradition’s own.

earliestMaterial.label: 966 CE gift of a silver image by the Pallava queen Sāmavai (earliest dated gift commonly cited)

nodes.name: Mīnākṣī
nodes.summary: The “fish-eyed” goddess of Madurai, who in the temple’s myth is born as a three-breasted Pāṇḍya princess, conquers the world and marries Śiva as Sundareśvara; she is identified with Pārvatī.
nodes.details: The myth is told in the Tiruviḷaiyāṭaṟpurāṇam and enacted at the Cittirai festival. Fuller (1984) documents the priests and ritual of her temple.
nodes.limits: A regional goddess integrated into Śaiva theology; the Pāṇḍya-princess story is temple mythology.

earliestMaterial.label: 14th c. CE restoration after Sultanate-period destruction

nodes.name: Raṅganātha
nodes.summary: Viṣṇu reclining on the serpent Ādiśeṣa, “lord of the stage (raṅga)”, worshipped above all at Srirangam on the Kāvēri.
nodes.limits: A temple-specific form; theological identity with Viṣṇu is recorded as FORM_OF.

nodes.name: Yamunā
nodes.summary: The river Yamunā personified as a goddess, daughter of Sūrya and sister of Yama, worshipped at her Himalayan source at Yamunotri and along the river, notably at Mathurā and Vṛndāvana.
nodes.limits: Thin record created to anchor the Yamunotri temple.

earliestMaterial.label: 19th c. CE (Mahārāja Pratāp Śāh of Tehri Garhwal per Wikipedia), rebuilt since

nodes.name: Hampi
nodes.summary: Ruined capital of the Vijayanagara empire on the Tuṅgabhadrā in Karnataka, a pilgrimage centre of Virūpākṣa–Pampā and, in local tradition, the Kiṣkindhā of the Rāmāyaṇa; the Group of Monuments at Hampi was inscribed on the World Heritage List in 1986.
nodes.details: The city flourished from the mid-14th century until it was sacked in 1565 after the battle of Tāḷikōṭa. Local tradition identifies its rocky landscape with Kiṣkindhā, the monkey kingdom: Ṛṣyamūka, Mataṅga hill and the Añjanādri hill (claimed as Hanumān’s birthplace, a claim also made for Añjanerī near Nashik and Tirumala’s Añjanādri) lie around the river. The World Heritage property was on the List in Danger from 1999 to 2006.

location.label: Hampi, Vijayanagara district, Karnataka, India

attributes.unesco: Group of Monuments at Hampi — inscribed 1986; UNESCO list no. 241 (List in Danger 1999–2006)

nodes.limits: Archaeology documents the Vijayanagara city and its temples; the identification with Kiṣkindhā is tradition and does not locate the epic geography.

nodes.name: Adam’s Bridge (Rāma Setu)
nodes.summary: Chain of limestone shoals and sandbanks, about 48 km long, between Pamban (Rameswaram) Island in India and Mannar Island in Sri Lanka; Hindu tradition identifies it with the causeway built by Rāma’s army to reach Laṅkā.
nodes.details: Geologists regard the shoals as a natural formation of sand and coral-derived limestone shaped by sea-level change and longshore currents; claims that it is a man-made structure are treated separately (claim:rama-setu-built). The name “Adam’s Bridge” derives from Islamic tradition. The identification with Rāma’s setu is ancient in the pilgrimage tradition of Rameswaram–Dhanushkodi, but the critical text of the Rāmāyaṇa does not locate the setu by modern geography, and this dataset keeps the epic’s Laṅkā distinct from Sri Lanka.

location.label: Palk Strait between Pamban Island (India) and Mannar Island (Sri Lanka)

nodes.limits: The physical feature is natural by current geological consensus; its sanctity is a matter of tradition and says nothing about the historicity of the setu-bandha episode.

nodes.name: Rameswaram (Pamban island)
nodes.summary: Island in the Gulf of Mannar off Tamil Nadu, linked to the mainland by the Pamban bridges, home of the Rāmanāthasvāmī temple and of Dhanushkodi at its south-eastern tip, where pilgrimage tradition places the start of Rāma’s bridge.
nodes.details: Dhanushkodi was destroyed by the 1964 cyclone. The island’s pilgrimage circuit includes bathing at Agnitīrtham and the 22 wells in the temple.

location.label: Ramanathapuram district, Tamil Nadu, India

nodes.limits: Island geography and pilgrimage practice; the Rāmāyaṇa associations are tradition.

nodes.name: Rājarāja I
nodes.summary: Cōḻa king (r. 985–1014) whose conquests made the Cōḻas the leading power of South India; builder of the Bṛhadīśvara temple at Thanjavur.

nodes.summary: Tuḷuva emperor of Vijayanagara (r. 1509–1529), a major patron of temples including Tirumala, Hampi’s Virūpākṣa and Viṭṭhala temples and Srikalahasti.

nodes.name: Rāṇī Rāsmaṇi
nodes.summary: Kolkata zamindar and philanthropist (1793–1861) who founded the Dakṣiṇeśvar Kālī temple, consecrated in 1855.

nodes.summary: King of Travancore (r. 1729–1758) who rebuilt the Padmanābhasvāmī temple and in 1750 dedicated his kingdom to Padmanābha.

nodes.summary: Queen of the Bundela state of Orchha (Tikamgarh) who built the Jānakī Mandir at Janakpur, completed in 1910.

nodes.name: Bāḷājī Bājīrāv (Nānāsāheb Peshwa)
nodes.summary: Peshwa of the Marāṭhā state (r. 1740–1761) who built the present Tryambakeśvara temple.
nodes.limits: Regnal dates are approximate and follow standard chronologies; this record exists to anchor temple patronage.

nodes.name: Pāṇḍya dynasty
nodes.summary: Tamil dynasty centred on Madurai, attested from the early historic period and powerful again in the 7th–10th and 13th centuries; patrons of rock-cut and structural temples in southern Tamil Nadu.

dates.label: c. 3rd c. BCE – 14th c. CE (with interruptions)

nodes.name: Nāyakas of Madurai
nodes.summary: Telugu-speaking governors of Vijayanagara who became independent rulers of Madurai (c. 1529–1736) and rebuilt the Mīnākṣī temple on a monumental scale.

nodes.name: Hoysaḷa dynasty
nodes.summary: Karnataka dynasty (c. 10th–14th c.) whose capitals Belur and Dvārasamudra (Halebidu) gave their name to the ornate Hoysaḷa temple style.

nodes.name: Kākatīya dynasty
nodes.summary: Telugu dynasty ruling from Warangal (c. 1163–1323), patrons of the Rāmappa and Thousand Pillar temples.

nodes.name: Caulukya (Solaṅkī) dynasty of Gujarat
nodes.summary: Dynasty ruling Gujarat from Aṇahilapāṭaka (c. 940–1244), patrons of the Māru-Gurjara temple style including Modhera and the medieval Somanātha.

nodes.name: Paramāra dynasty
nodes.summary: Dynasty of Mālava (c. 9th–14th c.) ruling from Dhārā, best known for King Bhoja.

nodes.name: Kārkoṭa dynasty
nodes.summary: Dynasty of Kashmir (c. 625–855) whose greatest king, Lalitāditya, is credited with the Mārtaṇḍa temple.

nodes.name: Koch kingdom
nodes.summary: Kingdom in western Assam and northern Bengal founded by Viśva Siṃha in the early 16th century; it rebuilt the Kāmākhyā temple in 1565.

nodes.name: Somavaṃśī dynasty of Odisha
nodes.summary: Dynasty of Dakṣiṇa Kosala and Odisha (c. 9th–12th c.) credited with early Bhubaneswar temples including the Mukteśvara and Liṅgarāja.

nodes.name: Holkar state of Indore
nodes.summary: Marāṭhā ruling house of Indore (18th c. – 1948), best known for Ahilyābāī Holkar’s temple patronage.

nodes.name: Malla dynasty of Nepal
nodes.summary: Rulers of the Kathmandu Valley (c. 1200–1769) under whom much of the valley’s surviving temple architecture was built or rebuilt.

nodes.name: Champa
nodes.summary: Cham kingdoms of central and southern Vietnam (c. 2nd–17th c.) whose royal sanctuary at Mỹ Sơn was dedicated to Śiva Bhadreśvara.

nodes.name: Kingdom of Travancore
nodes.summary: Kerala kingdom (1729–1949) whose rulers styled themselves servants of Padmanābha (Padmanābhadāsa).

nodes.name: Śilāhāra dynasty (northern Konkan)
nodes.summary: Dynasty of the northern Konkan (c. 800–1265) during whose rule the Ambarnath Śiva temple was built.

nodes.name: Pāṇḍuvaṃśīs of Dakṣiṇa Kosala
nodes.summary: Dynasty ruling from Śrīpura (Sirpur) in Chhattisgarh in the 6th–7th centuries, patrons of the brick Lakṣmaṇa temple.

nodes.name: Divya Deśams (the 108)
nodes.summary: The 108 abodes of Viṣṇu sung by the twelve Āḻvār poet-saints in the Nālāyira Divya Prabandham; 105 are in India, one in Nepal (Muktinath/Sāḷagrāmam), and two (Tiruppāṟkaṭal, the milk ocean, and Paramapadam) are beyond the earth.
nodes.details: The list is central to Śrīvaiṣṇava pilgrimage and theology. Srirangam is counted first. Most are in Tamil Nadu and Kerala; northern members include Badrinath, Ayodhyā, Naimiṣāraṇya, Mathurā and Dvārakā.
nodes.limits: A network is a traditional list; membership claims are religious tradition (class 6) and lists differ by text and region. Inclusion in a list does not date a temple.

nodes.name: Pāṭal Peṟṟa Talaṅkaḷ (the 276 Tēvāram shrines)
nodes.summary: The 276 Śiva temples praised in the Tēvāram hymns of the three Nāyaṉmār Appar, Campantar (Sambandar) and Cuntarar (Sundarar), 7th–9th c.; most are in the Kāvēri delta, with a few in Sri Lanka, northern India and the Himalaya.
nodes.details: Being “sung” in the Tēvāram is a defining mark of antiquity and sanctity in Tamil Śaiva tradition. The Sri Lankan members are Kōṇēsvaram (Trincomalee) and Kētīsvaram (Mannar); northern members include Kedarnath and Mount Kailāsa. Temples founded after the hymns (such as Thanjavur’s Bṛhadīśvara) are not on the list.
nodes.limits: A network is a traditional list; membership claims are religious tradition (class 6) and lists differ by text and region. Inclusion in a list does not date a temple.

nodes.name: Char Dham (the four dhāmas)
nodes.summary: Four pilgrimage “abodes” at the corners of India — Badrinath (north), Dwarka (west), Puri (east) and Rameswaram (south) — associated in tradition with Ādi Śaṅkara.
nodes.details: Three are Vaiṣṇava and Rameswaram Śaiva. The scheme is often aligned with the four maṭhas attributed to Śaṅkara (Jyotirmaṭh near Badrinath, Dvārakā, Govardhana at Puri and Śṛṅgeri — the last not at Rameswaram), a link that is traditional. Not to be confused with the Chota Char Dham of Uttarakhand.
nodes.limits: A network is a traditional list; membership claims are religious tradition (class 6) and lists differ by text and region. Inclusion in a list does not date a temple.

nodes.name: Chota Char Dham (Uttarakhand)
nodes.summary: Circuit of four Himalayan shrines in Garhwal — Yamunotri, Gangotri, Kedarnath and Badrinath — that became a mass pilgrimage after road access in the second half of the 20th century.
nodes.details: The circuit is traditionally made west to east, from Yamunotri to Badrinath. Seasonal opening runs roughly from April/May to October/November.
nodes.limits: A network is a traditional list; membership claims are religious tradition (class 6) and lists differ by text and region. Inclusion in a list does not date a temple.

nodes.name: Pañca Bhūta Sthalas (five element liṅgas)
nodes.summary: Five South Indian Śiva temples each identified with one of the five elements: earth (Kanchipuram Ekāmbareśvara), water (Tiruvanaikaval Jambukeśvara), fire (Tiruvannamalai Aruṇācaleśvara), air (Srikalahasti) and space/ether (Chidambaram).
nodes.details: Four are in Tamil Nadu and one (Srikalahasti) in Andhra Pradesh. Some versions give Tiruvarur rather than Kanchipuram as the earth shrine (recall; not verified).
nodes.limits: A network is a traditional list; membership claims are religious tradition (class 6) and lists differ by text and region. Inclusion in a list does not date a temple.

nodes.name: Āṟupaṭai Vīṭu (six abodes of Murukaṉ)
nodes.summary: Six Tamil Nadu shrines of Murukaṉ — Tirupparankundram, Tiruchendur, Palani, Swamimalai, Tiruttani and Pazhamudircholai — traditionally identified with the places named in Nakkīrar’s Tirumurukāṟṟuppaṭai, a guide-poem of the Pattuppāṭṭu.
nodes.details: The poem’s fifth “abode” is a general reference to Murukaṉ dancing on every hill (kuṉṟutōṟāṭal), conventionally assigned to Tiruttani, and the identification of the sixth with the modern Pazhamudircholai shrine is also traditional. Clothey (1978) analyses the network and its history.
nodes.limits: A network is a traditional list; membership claims are religious tradition (class 6) and lists differ by text and region. Inclusion in a list does not date a temple.

nodes.name: Rival identifications of jyotirliṅga sites
nodes.summary: The question of which modern temple corresponds to several of the twelve jyotirliṅgas named in the Śiva Purāṇa list, where the text gives only a region or an ambiguous name: Vaidyanātha, Nāgeśa, Bhīmaśaṅkara and Oṃkāra/Amaleśvara.
nodes.details: Vaidyanātha (“at the cremation ground”, citābhūmi): Deoghar (Jharkhand) is most widely accepted; Parli (Maharashtra) and Baijnath (Himachal Pradesh) are rival claimants. Nāgeśa (“in the Dārukā forest”): Nāgeśvara near Dwarka, Aundha Nāganātha (Maharashtra) and Jageshwar (Uttarakhand) all claim it. Bhīmaśaṅkara (“in Ḍākinī”): the Pune-district temple is most visited, but sites in Assam (near Guwahati) and Odisha are also claimed. Oṃkāra: the jyotirliṅga is shared in tradition between Oṃkāreśvara on Māndhātā island and Amaleśvara (Mamaleśvara) on the south bank. These are competing traditions; none can be settled by archaeology, since the list is a textual and devotional construct.

nodes.name: Vedic Saṃhitās
nodes.summary: The four mantra collections — Ṛgveda, Sāmaveda, Yajurveda (Śukla and Kṛṣṇa) and Atharvaveda — that form the base of the Vedic canon and were transmitted orally by recitation schools (śākhās).
nodes.details:
Each Saṃhitā belongs to one or more schools (śākhās) that also transmitted a Brāhmaṇa, and often an Āraṇyaka and Upaniṣad; in the traditional wide sense “Veda” covers this whole sequence Saṃhitā → Brāhmaṇa → Āraṇyaka → Upaniṣad. Scholars (e.g. Witzel) distinguish a Ṛgvedic period, a Mantra period (Atharvaveda, Sāmaveda, Yajurveda mantras), a period of Yajurveda Saṃhitā prose, the Brāhmaṇa period, and the late Vedic Upaniṣads and Sūtras.

Transmission was oral and remains so in living recitation lineages. UNESCO recognised the “Tradition of Vedic chanting” (India): proclaimed in 2003 and inscribed on the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in 2008; UNESCO notes that only thirteen of over a thousand recitation branches survive. Written manuscripts are late (second millennium CE).

dates.label: 2003 (UNESCO proclamation)

dates.event: inscription on the UNESCO Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity
dates.label: 2008 (inscribed, 3.COM)

attributes.transmission: oral recitation (śākhā lineages); manuscripts second millennium CE

nodes.name: Brāhmaṇas
nodes.summary: Prose texts attached to each Vedic school that explain the meaning, origin and correct performance of the śrauta rites, often through myths (ākhyāna) and identifications (bandhu).
nodes.details: Examples: Aitareya and Kauṣītaki (Ṛgveda); Pañcaviṃśa/Tāṇḍya and Jaiminīya (Sāmaveda); Taittirīya and Śatapatha (Yajurveda); Gopatha (Atharvaveda). Several first narrate stories later retold in the epics and Purāṇas: the flood of Manu (ŚB 1.8.1), the dwarf Viṣṇu winning the earth (ŚB 1.2.5), Purūravas and Urvaśī (ŚB 11.5.1), Śunaḥśepa (AB 7.13–18). Witzel places the main Brāhmaṇa period roughly in the early first millennium BCE, before the Upaniṣads.

nodes.name: Āraṇyakas
nodes.summary: Late Vedic texts, studied apart from the village, that treat esoteric or dangerous rites (e.g. the Pravargya) and contain or shade into the oldest Upaniṣads.
nodes.details: The Aitareya Āraṇyaka contains the Aitareya Upaniṣad (AĀ 2.4–6); the Kauṣītaki (Śāṅkhāyana) Āraṇyaka contains the Kauṣītaki Upaniṣad; the Taittirīya Āraṇyaka contains the Taittirīya Upaniṣad (TĀ 7–9) and the Mahānārāyaṇa Upaniṣad (TĀ 10); the Bṛhadāraṇyaka (“great Āraṇyaka”) forms the last part of the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa. These embeddings are the textual basis for the layered sequence Saṃhitā → Brāhmaṇa → Āraṇyaka → Upaniṣad.

sources.locator: Introduction (the Upaniṣads within the Vedic corpus)

nodes.name: Upaniṣads
nodes.summary: Texts at the end of the Vedic corpus (hence “Vedānta”) that discuss the self (ātman), brahman, death and rebirth, and liberation; the principal (“early”) Upaniṣads number about thirteen.
nodes.details:
Olivelle’s relative chronology: the prose Bṛhadāraṇyaka and Chāndogya are the oldest and pre-Buddhist (c. 7th–6th c. BCE, give or take a century); Taittirīya, Aitareya and Kauṣītaki follow (c. 6th–5th c. BCE); the verse Upaniṣads — Kena (the earliest of them), Kaṭha, Īśā, Śvetāśvatara, Muṇḍaka — belong to the last few centuries BCE; Praśna and Māṇḍūkya cannot be much older than the beginning of the common era. Olivelle warns that dating closer than a few centuries is unstable. Hundreds of later works also call themselves Upaniṣads.

The Upaniṣads, the Bhagavad Gītā and the Brahma Sūtra form the “triple foundation” (prasthānatrayī) on which Vedānta schools, including Advaita, write commentaries.

dates.label: c. 7th c. BCE – turn of the common era (principal Upaniṣads, as a group)
dates.basis: linguistic, stylistic and internal evidence; relative chronology of the Upaniṣads

nodes.name: Vedāṅgas
nodes.summary: The six “limbs of the Veda” — phonetics (śikṣā), ritual (kalpa), grammar (vyākaraṇa), etymology (nirukta), metre (chandas) and astronomy/calendar (jyotiṣa) — developed to preserve, understand and apply the Vedic texts.
nodes.details: The six are listed together in Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 1.1.5, which classes the four Vedas and these six disciplines as the “lower knowledge” (aparā vidyā). Representative works: the Prātiśākhyas and Śikṣās (phonetics), the Kalpa Sūtras (ritual), Pāṇini’s Aṣṭādhyāyī (grammar), Yāska’s Nirukta (etymology), Piṅgala’s Chandaḥsūtra (metre) and the Vedāṅga Jyotiṣa.

sources.quote: tatrāparā ṛgvedo yajurvedaḥ sāmavedo ’tharvavedaḥ śikṣā kalpo vyākaraṇaṃ niruktaṃ chando jyotiṣam iti

nodes.name: Kalpa Sūtras
nodes.summary: Aphoristic manuals of each Vedic school that codify the solemn (śrauta) rites, domestic (gṛhya) rites, rules of conduct (dharma) and altar geometry (śulba).
nodes.details: Well-known sets belong to Āpastamba, Baudhāyana and Hiraṇyakeśin (Taittirīya school), Āśvalāyana and Śāṅkhāyana (Ṛgveda), Kātyāyana (Śukla Yajurveda) and others. The Śrauta Sūtras are the operative manuals of living śrauta performances; the Dharma Sūtras precede the metrical Dharmaśāstras such as the Manusmṛti (`text:manusmriti`). Dating is debated; the older Sūtras are usually placed in the last centuries BCE.

sources.locator: vol. I (Dharmasūtras) and vol. II (śrauta and gṛhya rites)

nodes.name: Rigveda
nodes.summary: The oldest Vedic collection: 1,028 hymns in ten books (maṇḍalas) addressed chiefly to Indra, Agni and Soma, composed by hereditary poet families and transmitted orally with exceptional fidelity.
nodes.details:
Structure (checked against Aufrecht’s text on GRETIL): ten maṇḍalas of 191, 43, 62, 58, 87, 75, 104, 103 (incl. the eleven Vālakhilya hymns 8.49–59), 114 and 191 hymns — 1,028 in all, 10,552 verses. The “family books” 2–7 are each attributed to one poet clan (Gṛtsamada, Viśvāmitra, Vāmadeva, Atri, Bharadvāja, Vasiṣṭha) and form the oldest layer; maṇḍala 9 gathers all hymns to Soma Pavamāna; maṇḍalas 1 and 10 (191 hymns each) are later collections, maṇḍala 10 containing the late cosmogonic hymns (10.90, 10.121, 10.129) and dialogue hymns (10.10, 10.95, 10.108).

Only the Śākala recension survives complete; Śākalya’s word-by-word padapāṭha and the more complex recitation patterns (krama, jaṭā, ghana) protected the text in oral transmission, which UNESCO recognised (2003/2008). The oldest surviving manuscripts are of the 11th century CE (Nepal, per Witzel); the BORI collection in Pune (`ms:rigveda-bori`, owned by the material agent) was placed on UNESCO’s Memory of the World Register in 2007. Sāyaṇa’s 14th-century commentary is the standard traditional exegesis.

dates.label: c. 1500–1200 BCE (core)
dates.basis: linguistic, geographical and internal evidence; relative stratigraphy of the maṇḍalas

dates.label: c. 1500–1000 BCE
dates.basis: consensus range; Jamison and Brereton stress the date remains contested
dates.view: general scholarly range (e.g. Flood; Jamison & Brereton)

dates.event: collection and codification of the Saṃhitā
dates.label: c. 1200–1000 BCE (early Kuru realm)
dates.basis: association of the collection with the early Kuru polity

dates.label: c. 1040 CE (oldest surviving manuscripts, Nepal)
dates.basis: manuscript dating as reported by Witzel

nodes.limits: The hymns attest religious poetry and ritual of the Ṛgvedic poets; they are not a narrative history, and absolute dates are inferred, not documented.
openQuestions: Absolute chronology (proposals range from c. 1900 to c. 1000 BCE).
Whether the Bāṣkala recension survives in any independent form.

nodes.name: Samaveda
nodes.summary: The Veda of chants (sāman): verses, almost all drawn from the Ṛgveda, arranged for singing by the udgātṛ priests in the soma rites, with separate song-books (gāna) recording the melodies.
nodes.details: Three recensions are known: Kauthuma, Rāṇāyanīya and Jaiminīya. Its Brāhmaṇas include the Pañcaviṃśa (Tāṇḍya) and Jaiminīya; the Chāndogya Upaniṣad belongs to the Kauthuma school and the Kena Upaniṣad to the Jaiminīya (Jaiminīya Upaniṣad Brāhmaṇa). It is commonly stated that all but about 75 of its verses occur in the Ṛgveda (recall; check against an edition).

dates.label: c. 1200–1000 BCE (Mantra period)
dates.basis: relative stratigraphy of Vedic language and texts (Mantra period after the Ṛgveda)

nodes.name: Yajurveda
nodes.summary: The Veda of sacrificial formulas (yajus) recited by the adhvaryu priest who performs the manual acts of the rite; it exists in a “Black” (Kṛṣṇa) branch mixing mantra and explanatory prose and a “White” (Śukla) branch with mantras alone.
nodes.details: Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda Saṃhitās: Taittirīya, Maitrāyaṇī, Kāṭhaka and Kapiṣṭhala-Kaṭha. Śukla Yajurveda: the Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā in Mādhyandina and Kāṇva recensions, with the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa. Upaniṣads of the branch include the Bṛhadāraṇyaka and Īśā (Śukla) and the Taittirīya, Kaṭha and Śvetāśvatara (Kṛṣṇa).

dates.label: c. 1200–800 BCE (Mantra and Saṃhitā-prose periods; approximate)

nodes.name: Śukla Yajurveda (Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā)
nodes.summary: The “White” Yajurveda, the Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā in forty chapters (Mādhyandina and Kāṇva recensions), whose mantras are separated from the explanatory prose collected in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa.
nodes.details: Tradition, already in Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 6.5.3, attributes these “white formulas” to Yājñavalkya Vājasaneya. Notable chapters: VS 16 (the Śatarudriya, parallel to TS 4.5), VS 31 (a version of the Puruṣa hymn) and VS 40 (= the Īśā Upaniṣad). Witzel associates the school with the eastern, Videha region in the late Vedic period.

dates.label: c. 1000–700 BCE (approximate; later than the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda Saṃhitās)

sources.edition: Kāṇva recension (GRETIL; checked against Limaye & Vadekar 1958)

nodes.name: Taittirīya Saṃhitā (Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda)
nodes.summary: The principal Saṃhitā of the Black Yajurveda, in seven books (kāṇḍas) mixing ritual formulas with Brāhmaṇa-style prose explanation; it contains the Śatarudrīya litany to Rudra (TS 4.5).
nodes.details: The Taittirīya school, with its Brāhmaṇa, Āraṇyaka (incl. the Taittirīya Upaniṣad) and the Āpastamba, Baudhāyana and Hiraṇyakeśin Sūtras, is the most widely transmitted Yajurveda school in South India. TS 4.5 (eleven anuvākas, “namas te rudra manyave …”) and 4.7 (Camaka) are recited as the Śrī Rudram–Camakam in Śaiva worship.

sources.edition: TITUS, on the basis of Weber 1871–72
sources.quote: námas te rudra manyáva utó ta íṣave námaḥ

nodes.name: Atharvaveda
nodes.summary: The fourth Veda, a collection of hymns and spells for healing, protection, prosperity, love, kingship and domestic life, alongside speculative cosmological hymns; preserved in the Śaunaka and Paippalāda recensions.
nodes.details: The Śaunaka Saṃhitā has twenty books (about 730 hymns); books 19–20 are later supplements, book 20 consisting largely of Ṛgvedic hymns to Indra plus the Kuntāpa hymns (which praise a king Parikṣit). The Paippalāda recension survives in Kashmiri and Orissan manuscript traditions. Upaniṣads of this Veda include the Muṇḍaka, Praśna and Māṇḍūkya; its Brāhmaṇa is the Gopatha.

dates.label: c. 1200–1000 BCE (Mantra period; books 19–20 later)
dates.basis: relative stratigraphy of Vedic language and texts (Mantra period after the Ṛgveda)

nodes.name: Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa
nodes.summary: The Brāhmaṇa of the White Yajurveda, the largest and most systematic Brāhmaṇa (“of a hundred paths”), and a source of many narratives later retold in the epics and Purāṇas.
nodes.details: Mādhyandina recension: 14 kāṇḍas (100 adhyāyas); a Kāṇva recension also exists. Books 1–5 often cite Yājñavalkya, books 6–10 (the fire-altar) Śāṇḍilya; book 14 ends with the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad. Passages checked on GRETIL for this dataset include: the flood of Manu (1.8.1), the dwarf Viṣṇu who wins the earth for the gods (1.2.5), “yajño vai viṣṇuḥ” (1.1.2.13), Videgha Māthava and the eastward course of Agni Vaiśvānara (1.4.1.10–17), Rudra left behind by the gods (1.7.3.1), the eight names of the new-born Kumāra/Rudra (6.1.3.7–18), Purūravas and Urvaśī (11.5.1), Janaka’s sacrifice (11.6.3), the aśvamedha kings Janamejaya Pārikṣita and Bharata Dauḥṣanti, son of Śakuntalā (13.5.4), Puruṣa Nārāyaṇa’s five-night sacrifice (13.6.1.1) and the beheading of Viṣṇu (14.1.1).

dates.label: c. 8th–6th c. BCE (late Brāhmaṇa period; approximate)
dates.basis: relative stratigraphy; geography of the eastern (Kosala–Videha) Vedic schools

nodes.name: Aitareya Brāhmaṇa
nodes.summary: A Ṛgvedic Brāhmaṇa for the hotṛ priest in forty adhyāyas (eight pañcikās), best known for the royal consecration (rājasūya) material and the story of Śunaḥśepa (AB 7.13–18).
nodes.details: The Śunaḥśepa narrative (pañcikā 7, khaṇḍas 13–18 = adhyāya 33) is recited to the consecrated king in the rājasūya. Keith regarded books 1–5 as older than books 6–8. Sāyaṇa commented on it; Keith translated it (HOS 25, 1920).

sources.edition: TITUS, on the basis of Aufrecht 1879

nodes.name: Taittirīya Āraṇyaka
nodes.summary: The Āraṇyaka of the Taittirīya school in ten prapāṭhakas; books 7–9 are the Taittirīya Upaniṣad and book 10 the Mahānārāyaṇa Upaniṣad.
nodes.details: Includes material on the Pravargya and on the creation and cosmology; its embedded Upaniṣads show the gradual transition from Āraṇyaka to Upaniṣad.

nodes.name: Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad
nodes.summary: The largest and, with the Chāndogya, the oldest Upaniṣad, forming the end of the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa; it presents Yājñavalkya’s teachings at Janaka’s court, his dialogues with Maitreyī and Gārgī, and the earliest explicit doctrine of karma and rebirth.
nodes.details: Six adhyāyas in Kāṇva and Mādhyandina recensions: the Madhu-kāṇḍa (1–2), the Yājñavalkya-kāṇḍa (3–4) and supplements (5–6), each section closing with teacher lineages (vaṃśa). Key passages verified on GRETIL: 1.4 (the self alone in the beginning; “ahaṃ brahmāsmi” 1.4.10), 2.3.6 (“neti neti”), 2.4 and 4.5 (Maitreyī), 3.1–9 (the contest at Janaka’s sacrifice, incl. Gārgī 3.6 and 3.8), 3.2.13 and 4.4.5–6 (karma), 6.2 (Pravāhaṇa Jaivali’s doctrine of the two paths), 6.3.7 (Uddālaka Āruṇi teaches Yājñavalkya) and 6.5.3 (the “white” formulas of Yājñavalkya Vājasaneya). Śaṅkara’s commentary on it is accepted as authentic.

dates.label: c. 7th–6th c. BCE (pre-Buddhist; “give or take a century”)
dates.basis: linguistic, stylistic and internal evidence; relative chronology of the Upaniṣads

dates.label: parts possibly still being composed c. 4th–2nd c. BCE
dates.basis: relative chronology with grammarians and early Buddhist sources

sources.edition: Kāṇva recension (GRETIL; checked against Limaye & Vadekar 1958)

nodes.name: Chāndogya Upaniṣad
nodes.summary: An early prose Upaniṣad of the Kauthuma Sāmaveda school, in eight prapāṭhakas, containing Uddālaka Āruṇi’s instruction of Śvetaketu (“tat tvam asi”), the “five fires” doctrine of rebirth, and the only Vedic mention of a Kṛṣṇa son of Devakī (3.17.6).
nodes.details: Verified passages: 1.1.1 (meditation on Om as the udgītha), 3.14.1 (“sarvaṃ khalv idaṃ brahma”, Śāṇḍilya), 3.17.6 (Ghora Āṅgirasa teaches Kṛṣṇa Devakīputra), 4.4 (Satyakāma Jābāla), 5.3–10 (Pravāhaṇa Jaivali and the five fires; rebirth according to conduct 5.10.7), 6.1–16 (Uddālaka and Śvetaketu; “tat tvam asi” nine times from 6.8.7), 7.1.1 (Nārada approaches Sanatkumāra), 8.7–12 (Indra and Virocana as pupils of Prajāpati).

dates.label: c. 7th–6th c. BCE (pre-Buddhist; “give or take a century”)
dates.basis: linguistic, stylistic and internal evidence; relative chronology of the Upaniṣads

nodes.name: Taittirīya Upaniṣad
nodes.summary: Books 7–9 of the Taittirīya Āraṇyaka, in three vallīs (Śikṣā, Brahmānanda, Bhṛgu), known for the five sheaths of the self and Varuṇa’s instruction of his son Bhṛgu on brahman.
nodes.details: TU 3.1.1 (verified): Bhṛgu Vāruṇi approaches his father Varuṇa asking to be taught brahman and is told “that from which these beings are born, by which they live, into which they pass — seek to know that; that is brahman.” Śaṅkara’s commentary on TU is accepted as authentic.

dates.label: c. 6th–5th c. BCE (probably pre-Buddhist)
dates.basis: linguistic, stylistic and internal evidence; relative chronology of the Upaniṣads

sources.quote: bhṛgurvai vāruṇiḥ / varuṇaṃ pitaramupasasāra / adhīhi bhagavo brahmeti

nodes.name: Aitareya Upaniṣad
nodes.summary: A short Ṛgvedic Upaniṣad (Aitareya Āraṇyaka 2.4–6) describing creation by the self (“ātmā vā idam eka evāgra āsīt”) and ending with the equation “prajñānaṃ brahma” (3.3).

dates.label: c. 6th–5th c. BCE (probably pre-Buddhist)
dates.basis: linguistic, stylistic and internal evidence; relative chronology of the Upaniṣads

nodes.name: Kauṣītaki Upaniṣad
nodes.summary: A Ṛgvedic Upaniṣad in four chapters, part of the Kauṣītaki (Śāṅkhāyana) Āraṇyaka, in which kṣatriya teachers instruct brahmins: Citra Gāṅgyāyani teaches Āruṇi, Indra teaches Pratardana, and Ajātaśatru teaches Bālāki.
nodes.details: Its fourth chapter parallels Bṛhadāraṇyaka 2.1 (the dialogue of Ajātaśatru of Kāśī and Bālāki Gārgya). Locators here are from recall (Olivelle 1998) and should be checked against an edition.

dates.label: c. 6th–5th c. BCE (probably pre-Buddhist)
dates.basis: linguistic, stylistic and internal evidence; relative chronology of the Upaniṣads

sources.locator: text and translation of the Kauṣītaki Upaniṣad

nodes.name: Kena Upaniṣad
nodes.summary: A short Upaniṣad of the Jaiminīya Sāmaveda school: two verse sections on the unknowable brahman, followed by the prose parable in which Agni, Vāyu and Indra fail to recognise a mysterious being until Umā Haimavatī reveals that it is brahman.
nodes.details: Four khaṇḍas (checked in the Sanskrit Documents e-text): 1–2 in verse, 3–4 in prose. It forms part of the Jaiminīya Upaniṣad Brāhmaṇa (traditionally JUB 4.18–21; recall). Olivelle regards it as the oldest of the verse Upaniṣads.

dates.label: last few centuries BCE (Olivelle’s group of verse Upaniṣads; numeric range approximate)
dates.basis: relative chronology (verse Upaniṣads later than the prose BU/CU); numbers approximate Olivelle’s “last few centuries BCE”

nodes.name: Kaṭha Upaniṣad
nodes.summary: A verse Upaniṣad in six vallīs framed by the story of the boy Naciketas, who receives three boons from Yama, the third being the teaching about what happens after death and the imperishable self.
nodes.details: The frame narrative develops a story told in the Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa (3.11.8; recall). Verses verified on GRETIL (Olivelle numbering): 1.1 (Vājaśravasa’s gift and his son Naciketas), 1.11 (the father called “Auddālaki Āruṇi”), 2.15 (Om), 2.18–19 (the self is not born and does not die; “if the killer thinks he kills …” — closely paralleled in Bhagavad Gītā 2.19–20), 3.7 (the word saṃsāra), 3.9 (“that highest step of Viṣṇu”) and 6.14 (the mortal becomes immortal).

dates.label: last few centuries BCE (Olivelle’s group of verse Upaniṣads; numeric range approximate)
dates.basis: relative chronology (verse Upaniṣads later than the prose BU/CU); numbers approximate Olivelle’s “last few centuries BCE”

nodes.name: Īśā Upaniṣad
nodes.summary: A brief verse Upaniṣad forming the final chapter (40) of the Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, opening “īśā vāsyam idaṃ sarvaṃ” — all this is to be dwelt in by the Lord.

dates.label: last few centuries BCE (Olivelle’s group of verse Upaniṣads; numeric range approximate)
dates.basis: relative chronology (verse Upaniṣads later than the prose BU/CU); numbers approximate Olivelle’s “last few centuries BCE”

sources.quote: īśā vāsyam idaṃ sarvaṃ yat kiñca jagatyāṃ jagat

nodes.name: Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad
nodes.summary: A verse Upaniṣad of the Atharvaveda in three muṇḍakas that distinguishes the “lower” knowledge (the four Vedas and six Vedāṅgas) from the “higher” knowledge of the imperishable, taught by Aṅgiras to Śaunaka.
nodes.details: Opens with a transmission line: Brahmā → Atharvan → Aṅgir → Satyavāha Bhāradvāja → Aṅgiras, whom the householder Śaunaka approaches (1.1.1–3). 3.1.1 reuses RV 1.164.20 (“two birds, companions …”), and 3.1.6 contains “satyam eva jayate”, the motto of the Republic of India.

dates.label: last few centuries BCE (Olivelle’s group of verse Upaniṣads; numeric range approximate)
dates.basis: relative chronology (verse Upaniṣads later than the prose BU/CU); numbers approximate Olivelle’s “last few centuries BCE”

nodes.name: Praśna Upaniṣad
nodes.summary: A prose Upaniṣad of the Atharvaveda in which six students — among them Sukeśā Bhāradvāja, Satyakāma Śaibya and Kausalya Āśvalāyana — put six questions to the sage Pippalāda.
nodes.details: Note: its Satyakāma Śaibya (1.1) is a different figure from Satyakāma Jābāla of the Chāndogya.

dates.label: around the beginning of the common era

nodes.name: Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad
nodes.summary: The shortest principal Upaniṣad (twelve verses), which identifies the syllable Om with all that is, past, present and future, and the self (ātman) with brahman, analysed into four states (waking, dream, deep sleep and the “fourth”).
nodes.details: Verse 2: “sarvaṃ hy etad brahmāyam ātmā brahma” (verified). Gauḍapāda’s Māṇḍūkya Kārikā is the earliest surviving systematic Advaita treatise; the authenticity of the commentary on it ascribed to Śaṅkara is questioned.

dates.label: around the beginning of the common era

nodes.name: Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad
nodes.summary: A theistic verse Upaniṣad in six chapters that proclaims one Rudra, called Śiva and Maheśvara, as creator and lord, using Sāṃkhya and Yoga vocabulary; it is the earliest text to make Rudra–Śiva the supreme god and closes with the word bhakti.
nodes.details: Verified verses: 3.2 (“eko hi rudro na dvitīyāya tasthe”), 3.4, 3.5–6 (reusing Śatarudriya mantras), 3.11 (“sarvagataḥ śivaḥ”), 3.15 (= RV 10.90.2), 3.16 (paralleled in Bhagavad Gītā 13.13), 4.10 (māyā and the māyin Maheśvara), 4.21–22 (4.22 = RV 1.114.8), 5.2 (the seer Kapila), 6.16 (saṃsāra and mokṣa), 6.21 (the sage Śvetāśvatara) and 6.23 (supreme bhakti to god and teacher).

dates.label: last few centuries BCE (Olivelle’s group of verse Upaniṣads; numeric range approximate)
dates.basis: relative chronology (verse Upaniṣads later than the prose BU/CU); numbers approximate Olivelle’s “last few centuries BCE”

nodes.name: Aṣṭādhyāyī of Pāṇini
nodes.summary: Pāṇini’s grammar of Sanskrit in nearly 4,000 sūtras arranged in eight chapters, describing both the spoken language of his time and Vedic usage; it is an external, datable witness to names and cults of its period, including Vāsudeva and Arjuna (4.3.98).
nodes.details: Sūtra 4.3.98 “vāsudeva-arjunābhyāṃ vun” (verified) forms derivatives meaning “one whose bhakti is Vāsudeva / Arjuna” under the heading 4.3.95 “bhaktiḥ”; it is widely cited as the earliest reference to devotion to Vāsudeva. Pāṇini also cites earlier grammarians (e.g. Śākalya, 1.1.16).

dates.label: c. 5th – mid-4th c. BCE (not later than the early-to-mid 4th c. BCE)
c. mid-4th c. BCE or later (terminus post quem c. 350 BCE)
dates.basis: history of writing and numismatic arguments (von Hinüber, Falk), accepted by Bronkhorst

nodes.name: Mahābhāṣya of Patañjali
nodes.summary: Patañjali’s “Great Commentary” on Pāṇini and Kātyāyana’s vārttikas (c. mid-2nd c. BCE), whose example sentences incidentally attest the Kṛṣṇa–Kaṃsa story, its performance by actors (śobhikas), devotees of Vāsudeva, and contemporary events.
nodes.details: Verified in Kielhorn’s text (GRETIL): on P. 3.1.26 — “kaṃsavadham ācaṣṭe kaṃsaṃ ghātayati, balibandham ācaṣṭe baliṃ bandhayati”; śobhikas “before one’s eyes have Kaṃsa killed and Bali bound”; paintings show the blows; those who present the story (granthikas) are seen divided into “kaṃsabhaktāḥ” and “vāsudevabhaktāḥ” (Kielhorn II 34.14–36.21). On 3.2.111 — “jaghāna kaṃsaṃ kila vāsudevaḥ” and “aruṇad yavanaḥ sāketam / madhyamikām”. On 3.2.123 — “iha puṣyamitraṃ yājayāmaḥ”. On 2.2.24 — “saṅkarṣaṇadvitīyasya balaṃ kṛṣṇasya vardhatām”. On 2.2.34 — music “prāsāde dhanapati-rāma-keśavānām”. On 5.3.99 — images (arcā) set up by the Mauryas for gain. The GRETIL file lacks the commentary on adhyāya 4, so Patañjali’s remark on 4.3.98 was not checked.

dates.label: c. mid-2nd c. BCE
dates.basis: internal references to Puṣyamitra’s sacrifice and Yavana sieges of Sāketa and Madhyamikā

dates.label: late Maurya period (321–185 BCE)
dates.basis: alternative reading of the internal evidence

nodes.limits: Grammatical examples show that the Kṛṣṇa–Kaṃsa and Bali stories were known and performed in the 2nd c. BCE; they do not date the events narrated.

nodes.name: Nirukta of Yāska
nodes.summary: Yāska’s explanatory commentary on the Nighaṇṭu word-lists, the oldest surviving work of Vedic exegesis, which records rival schools of interpretation — the etymologists (nairuktas) and the “historians” (aitihāsikas).
nodes.details: Verified examples: 2.16 — “What is Vṛtra? A cloud, say the nairuktas; an asura, son of Tvaṣṭṛ, say the aitihāsikas”; 7.5 — the nairuktas hold there are only three deities: Agni (earth), Vāyu or Indra (mid-region) and Sūrya (sky); 12.1 — competing identifications of the Aśvins; 12.10 — the itihāsa of Saraṇyū, Yama and Yamī and the birth of the Aśvins and Manu.

dates.label: c. 6th–5th c. BCE (generally placed before Pāṇini)

nodes.name: Indra
nodes.summary: The most frequently praised god of the Ṛgveda (about 250 hymns, roughly a quarter), the soma-drinking warrior who wields the vajra and slays Vṛtra to release the waters; in the Upaniṣads, epics and Purāṇas he remains king of the gods but loses supremacy and is often humbled.
nodes.details:
Ṛgvedic profile: slayer of Vṛtra (RV 1.32), breaker of the Vala cave with the Aṅgirases, patron of the Bharata king Sudās in the Battle of the Ten Kings (RV 7.18, 7.33), sender of Saramā (RV 10.108). RV 10.86 refrains “viśvasmād indra uttaraḥ” (Indra above all). Yāska (Nirukta 7.5) records the view that Vāyu or Indra is the single god of the middle region.

Shift of prominence: in the Kena Upaniṣad (3–4) Indra cannot grasp the mysterious being and learns from Umā Haimavatī that it is brahman, though he is then called foremost of the gods for coming nearest; in the Chāndogya (8.7–12) he is a patient pupil of Prajāpati for 101 years. In epic and Purāṇic narrative he is the ruler of svarga and the guardian of the east, repeatedly threatened, cursed or displaced (e.g. the guilt of killing Vṛtra; the Govardhana episode of the Bhāgavata, where Kṛṣṇa turns the cowherds from Indra’s worship). Hymn counts are approximate (Macdonell 1897; Jamison & Brereton 2014) and depend on how shared hymns are counted.

nodes.name: Agni
nodes.summary: The sacrificial fire as god — messenger between gods and humans, divine hotṛ and purohita — praised in about 200 Ṛgvedic hymns, including the first (RV 1.1); central to all Vedic ritual and still present in every Hindu rite.
nodes.details: The family books 2–7 open with Agni hymns, as does the whole Ṛgveda (“agnim īḻe purohitaṃ”, RV 1.1.1). The Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa (1.4.1.10–17) narrates Agni Vaiśvānara burning eastward from the Sarasvatī to the Sadānīrā with Videgha Māthava. In the Kena (3.3–6) Agni Jātavedas cannot burn a straw before brahman. Later he becomes guardian of the south-east and a secondary figure in sectarian theology while remaining indispensable in ritual. Hymn counts are approximate (Macdonell 1897; Jamison & Brereton 2014) and depend on how shared hymns are counted.

sources.quote: agnim īḻe purohitaṁ yajñasya devam ṛtvijam

nodes.name: Soma
nodes.summary: The pressed ritual drink and its god, praised in about 120 Ṛgvedic hymns, including all 114 hymns of maṇḍala 9 to Soma Pavamāna (“self-purifying”); in later tradition Soma is identified with the Moon and becomes ancestor of the Lunar dynasty.
nodes.details: The identity of the original soma plant is unknown and debated. The identification of Soma with the Moon is already Vedic (late Saṃhitā and Brāhmaṇa texts) and becomes standard; Purāṇic genealogies trace the Candravaṃśa (`lin:chandravamsha`) from Soma through Budha and Purūravas. Hymn counts are approximate (Macdonell 1897; Jamison & Brereton 2014) and depend on how shared hymns are counted.

attributes.approx. RV hymns: ≈120 (all 114 of maṇḍala 9 plus a few elsewhere)

sources.locator: RV 9.1–9.114 (114 hymns counted in the e-text)

openQuestions: Botanical identity of soma (ephedra, a mushroom and other candidates are argued).

nodes.name: Varuṇa
nodes.summary: The sovereign Āditya of the Ṛgveda who guards cosmic and moral order (ṛta), sees all and binds wrongdoers with his fetters; praised alone in about a dozen hymns and often with Mitra. Later he declines to lord of the waters and guardian of the west.
nodes.details: Varuṇa is the deity of the Vasiṣṭha hymns of contrition (RV 7.86–89) and the god who releases the bound Śunaḥśepa (RV 1.24.12–13); in the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa he grants Hariścandra a son and then claims him. RV 7.33.11 makes Vasiṣṭha a son of Mitra and Varuṇa (maitrāvaruṇa). In Taittirīya Upaniṣad 3.1 he teaches his son Bhṛgu about brahman. With RV 2.27.1 he is one of the Ādityas, sons of Aditi. In the epics and Purāṇas his ethical sovereignty fades and he becomes ruler of the ocean and the waters. Hymn counts are approximate (Macdonell 1897; Jamison & Brereton 2014) and depend on how shared hymns are counted.

nodes.name: Mitra
nodes.summary: An Āditya personifying alliance and contract, almost always paired with Varuṇa; only one Ṛgvedic hymn (RV 3.59) is addressed to him alone. He is cognate with Iranian Mithra.
nodes.details: With Varuṇa he is named father of Vasiṣṭha and (by tradition) Agastya (RV 7.33.10–13). Mitra, Varuṇa, Indra and the Nāsatyas (Aśvins) are invoked as divine witnesses in a Mitanni treaty of the 14th c. BCE — an important external attestation that belongs to the material agent’s domain (no entity yet). Hymn counts are approximate (Macdonell 1897; Jamison & Brereton 2014) and depend on how shared hymns are counted.

nodes.name: Sūrya
nodes.summary: The Sun as god, praised in about ten Ṛgvedic hymns (e.g. RV 1.50, 1.115); closely related solar deities include Savitṛ, addressed in the Gāyatrī (RV 3.62.10). Sūrya later becomes the focus of Saura worship and of great temples such as Konark.
nodes.details: Note on identity: in the Ṛgveda Savitṛ (“impeller”) and Sūrya are distinct names with overlapping functions; the registry lists Savitṛ under Sūrya as “related”, and the Gāyatrī (to Savitṛ) is linked here with that caution. RV 5.40.6–9 tells how Atri found the Sun hidden by the darkness of Svarbhānu. Hymn counts are approximate (Macdonell 1897; Jamison & Brereton 2014) and depend on how shared hymns are counted.

nodes.name: Uṣas
nodes.summary: The goddess Dawn, daughter of heaven, celebrated in about twenty of the most admired Ṛgvedic hymns (e.g. RV 1.113); she has little independent cult in later Hinduism.
nodes.details: In the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa (7.16) the bound Śunaḥśepa is finally released while praising Uṣas. Hymn counts are approximate (Macdonell 1897; Jamison & Brereton 2014) and depend on how shared hymns are counted.

sources.edition: TITUS, on the basis of Aufrecht 1879

nodes.name: Rudra
nodes.summary: A fierce Ṛgvedic archer-god of storms, disease and healing, addressed in only about three hymns (RV 1.114, 2.33, 7.46), who through the Yajurvedic Śatarudrīya and the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad becomes the supreme god Śiva.
nodes.details: Ṛgveda: RV 2.33 asks him to spare and heal; he is “lord of this world” (īśāna, 2.33.9) and father of the Maruts. Brāhmaṇas: the gods leave him behind when they go to heaven by sacrifice (ŚB 1.7.3.1, “Vāstavya”); the new-born Kumāra receives eight names — Rudra, Sarva (Śarva), Paśupati, Ugra, Aśani, Bhava, Mahān Deva, Īśāna — as forms of Agni (ŚB 6.1.3.7–18). Taittirīya Saṃhitā 4.5 (Śatarudrīya) pays homage to him in hundreds of forms and includes “namaḥ śivāya ca śivatarāya ca” (4.5.8.1). The Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad (3–4) proclaims the one Rudra, called śiva and maheśvara, as creator and lord of all. Śaiva traditions identify Rudra with Śiva; historians describe a gradual convergence of Rudra with other, non-Vedic elements (Kramrisch; Chakravarti). Hymn counts are approximate (Macdonell 1897; Jamison & Brereton 2014) and depend on how shared hymns are counted.

sources.quote: īśānād asya bhuvanasya bhūrer na vā u yoṣad rudrād asuryam

sources.edition: TITUS, on the basis of Weber 1871–72

sources.quote: eko hi rudro na dvitīyāya tasthe

nodes.name: Prajāpati
nodes.summary: “Lord of creatures”, named as creator in the last verse of RV 10.121 and the central creator-god of the Brāhmaṇas, whose dismembered body is restored in the fire-altar ritual; his role passes to Brahmā in the epics and Purāṇas.
nodes.details: RV 10.121 repeatedly asks “to which god (kasmai devāya) shall we offer?”; its final verse answers “Prajāpati”, and the Brāhmaṇas make “Ka” (“Who?”) a name of Prajāpati. In the Chāndogya Upaniṣad (8.7–12) Prajāpati teaches Indra and Virocana about the self. The epics often call Brahmā “Prajāpati”, and Purāṇic cosmogony assigns him Prajāpati’s functions.

sources.quote: prajāpate na tvad etāny anyo viśvā jātāni pari tā babhūva

nodes.name: Yama
nodes.summary: Son of Vivasvat and, in the Ṛgveda, the first mortal who found the path to the world of the fathers and rules there (RV 10.14); he is the teacher of Naciketas in the Kaṭha Upaniṣad and later the god of death and judge of the dead (Dharmarāja).
nodes.details: Ṛgveda: three or so hymns (e.g. RV 10.14, 10.135) and the dialogue with his twin sister Yamī (RV 10.10); his two four-eyed dogs are “Sārameya”, sons of Saramā (RV 10.14.10). Yāska (Nirukta 12.10) records the itihāsa of Saraṇyū bearing the twins Yama and Yamī to Vivasvat. In the Mahābhārata Yama appears in the Sāvitrī story, and Dharma, the divine father of Yudhiṣṭhira, is often identified with him (the epic agent’s domain).

sources.quote: vaivasvataṁ saṁgamanaṁ janānāṁ yamaṁ rājānaṁ haviṣā duvasya

nodes.name: Vāyu
nodes.summary: The Wind, first to drink the soma, often paired with Indra (Indra–Vāyu); praised in a few Ṛgvedic hymns (e.g. RV 1.134–135, 7.90) and, as Vāta, in RV 10.168. Later he is the father of Hanumān and Bhīma.
nodes.details: In the Kena (3.7–10) Vāyu Mātariśvan cannot lift a straw before brahman. Yāska (Nirukta 7.5) gives “Vāyu or Indra” as the god of the middle region. Hymn counts are approximate (Macdonell 1897; Jamison & Brereton 2014) and depend on how shared hymns are counted.

attributes.approx. RV hymns: a few (alone and with Indra); Vāta in RV 10.168, 10.186

nodes.name: Aśvins
nodes.summary: Twin horsemen gods of the dawn, healers and rescuers who appear in more than fifty Ṛgvedic hymns (e.g. RV 1.116–120); in the Mahābhārata they are the fathers of Nakula and Sahadeva.
nodes.details: Yāska (Nirukta 12.1) lists competing identifications — heaven and earth, day and night, sun and moon, or (according to the aitihāsikas) two virtuous kings — and (12.10) the story of their birth from Saraṇyū in horse form. As Nāsatyas they are also named in the 14th-c. BCE Mitanni treaty. Hymn counts are approximate (Macdonell 1897; Jamison & Brereton 2014) and depend on how shared hymns are counted.

nodes.name: Aditi
nodes.summary: “Boundlessness”, mother of the Ādityas (Mitra, Varuṇa and others), who has no Ṛgvedic hymn of her own but is praised as all things (RV 1.89.10); later the wife of Kaśyapa, mother of the gods and of Vāmana.
nodes.details: RV 10.72 (verses 4–5, 8–9) has Dakṣa born from Aditi and Aditi from Dakṣa, and Aditi’s eight sons of whom she cast away Mārtāṇḍa; RV 2.27.1 names Mitra, Aryaman, Bhaga, Varuṇa, Dakṣa and Aṃśa as Ādityas. In Purāṇic narrative (e.g. the Bhāgavata) she bears Vāmana, who recovers the worlds from Bali.

sources.quote: aditir dyaur aditir antarikṣam aditir mātā sa pitā sa putraḥ

nodes.name: Sarasvatī
nodes.summary: In the Ṛgveda both a mighty river and its goddess, praised in three hymns (RV 6.61, 7.95, 7.96); identified with Vāc (speech) in the Brāhmaṇas, she becomes the goddess of learning, music and speech and consort of Brahmā.
nodes.details: The river (`place:sarasvati-river`, owned by the purana agent) is named with the Gaṅgā and Yamunā in the river hymn RV 10.75.5; ŚB 1.4.1.14 places Videgha Māthava on the Sarasvatī before the eastward migration. The goddess and the river are kept as separate ids here and joined by an IDENTIFIED_WITH assertion qualified by the Ṛgveda.

nodes.name: Vasiṣṭha
nodes.summary: Ṛgvedic poet-priest to whose family maṇḍala 7 is attributed; priest of the Bharata king Sudās in the Battle of the Ten Kings, and in the Rāmāyaṇa the family priest of Daśaratha and rival of Viśvāmitra.
nodes.details: RV 7.33 (verified) makes him son of Mitra and Varuṇa, born “from the mind of Urvaśī” (7.33.11), and tells of his and Māna’s (Agastya’s) birth from a jar (7.33.13); RV 7.18 and 7.33.3–5 describe the Vasiṣṭhas’ prayers bringing Indra’s help to Sudās. In the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa he is the brahman priest at Hariścandra’s rite (AB 7.16). In the Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa (Bālakāṇḍa) his wish-granting cow is coveted by king Viśvāmitra, the root of their famous enmity; the Mahābhārata also tells Vasiṣṭha–Viśvāmitra episodes (Ādiparvan).

nodes.name: Viśvāmitra
nodes.summary: Ṛgvedic poet of the Kuśika clan to whom maṇḍala 3 — including the Gāyatrī (RV 3.62.10) — is attributed; he adopts Śunaḥśepa in the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa and, in the Rāmāyaṇa, takes the young Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa to protect his sacrifice.
nodes.details: RV 3.33 (dialogue with the rivers Vipāś and Śutudrī) and RV 3.53 (verified: “viśvāmitrasya rakṣati brahmedam bhārataṁ janam”, 3.53.12; Viśvāmitra conveyed Sudās, 3.53.9). AB 7.17–18: he renames the freed Śunaḥśepa Devarāta and adopts him; those of his hundred sons who refuse are cursed. Epic tradition makes him a kṣatriya king who attains brahminhood through austerity and the father of Śakuntalā (Mahābhārata).

sources.edition: TITUS, on the basis of Aufrecht 1879

nodes.name: Agastya
nodes.summary: Ṛgvedic poet to whom RV 1.165–191 are attributed, husband of Lopāmudrā (RV 1.179), who becomes in the Rāmāyaṇa the forest sage who arms Rāma, and in Tamil tradition (as Akattiyar) the founder of Tamil grammar and a culture-hero of the south.
nodes.details: RV 7.33.10–13 links his birth with Vasiṣṭha’s (Māna “rose from the jar”), whence the epithets Maitrāvaruṇi and Kumbhayoni; RV 1.165.15 calls the poet “Mānya”. The Mahābhārata (Āraṇyakaparvan) tells of Agastya and Lopāmudrā, the digestion of the demon Vātāpi and the drinking of the ocean; in the Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa (Araṇyakāṇḍa) Rāma visits his hermitage and receives weapons. Tamil tradition (attested in medieval commentarial literature) makes Akattiyar the first grammarian of Tamil and links him with the Potiyil hill; this is a separate, regional tradition and its relation to the Vedic poet is a matter of identification, not of evidence for a historical migration (Zvelebil).
openQuestions: Earliest Tamil source naming Akattiyar as grammarian (the regional agent may hold this).

nodes.name: Aṅgiras
nodes.summary: Primeval seer and eponym of the Āṅgirasa priestly clan; in the Ṛgveda the Aṅgirases are ancestral “fathers” who with Indra or Bṛhaspati opened the Vala cave and found the cows, and in the Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad Aṅgiras teaches the higher knowledge to Śaunaka.
nodes.details: RV 1.62.2 (“arcanto aṅgiraso gā avindan”), 10.14.6 (Aṅgirases, Atharvans and Bhṛgus as fathers), 10.108.10 (Saramā names the “terrible Aṅgirases”). The Atharvaveda is called Atharvāṅgirasaḥ. Patronymics such as Āṅgirasa (Ghora Āṅgirasa) mark clan membership, not necessarily direct descent.

nodes.name: Bhṛgu
nodes.summary: Ancestor of the Bhārgava priestly clan; in the Ṛgveda the Bhṛgus establish Agni among men, and in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa and Taittirīya Upaniṣad Bhṛgu Vāruṇi is the son and pupil of Varuṇa.
nodes.details: RV 1.58.6 (“dadhuṣ ṭvā bhṛgavo mānuṣeṣv ā”), 10.14.6. ŚB 11.6.1.1: Bhṛgu Vāruṇi thought himself superior to his father Varuṇa in knowledge and is shown the other world; TU 3.1–6: Varuṇa teaches him brahman. In the Mahābhārata the Bhārgavas are prominent from the Paulomaparvan onward; V. S. Sukthankar argued (1936) that Bhārgava redactors shaped the epic — an influential but debated hypothesis.

sources.quote: bhṛgurha vai vāruṇiḥ  varuṇam pitaraṃ vidyayātimene

nodes.name: Atri
nodes.summary: Ṛgvedic seer whose family (the Ātreyas) is credited with maṇḍala 5; RV 5.40 tells how Atri found the Sun hidden by Svarbhānu’s darkness. In the Rāmāyaṇa Rāma visits Atri and his wife Anasūyā.

sources.quote: gūḻhaṁ sūryaṁ tamasāpavratena turīyeṇa brahmaṇāvindad atriḥ

nodes.name: Yājñavalkya
nodes.summary: The pre-eminent teacher of the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad and an authority of the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, who wins the debate at Janaka’s sacrifice, teaches Janaka and his wife Maitreyī, and to whom the “white” formulas of the Śukla Yajurveda are attributed.
nodes.details: BU 3 (verified) shows him claiming Janaka’s thousand cows and answering eight challengers including Gārgī Vācaknavī (3.6, 3.8) and Uddālaka Āruṇi (3.7); BU 4.1–4 his teaching of Janaka; BU 2.4 and 4.5 his parting instruction to Maitreyī; BU 6.3.7 names him the pupil of Uddālaka Āruṇi; BU 6.5.3 attributes the white yajus to him. The later Yājñavalkya Smṛti carries his name (attribution, not authorship).

sources.edition: Kāṇva recension (GRETIL; checked against Limaye & Vadekar 1958)

earliestText.label: c. 8th–6th c. BCE (late Brāhmaṇa period; approximate)

nodes.name: Gārgī Vācaknavī
nodes.summary: A woman philosopher who twice questions Yājñavalkya at Janaka’s court (BU 3.6, 3.8), pressing him on what the worlds are “woven upon” until he warns her not to ask too much; her second questioning elicits the teaching of the imperishable (akṣara).
nodes.details: BU 3.6.1: “atha hainaṃ gārgī vācaknavī papraccha”; 3.8.8: “etad vai tad akṣaraṃ gārgi brāhmaṇā abhivadanti …”. After 3.8 she tells the assembled brahmins none of them will defeat Yājñavalkya.

sources.edition: Kāṇva recension (GRETIL; checked against Limaye & Vadekar 1958)

earliestText.label: parts possibly still being composed c. 4th–2nd c. BCE

nodes.name: Maitreyī
nodes.summary: One of Yājñavalkya’s two wives, described as a discourser on brahman (brahmavādinī), who on his departure asks for the teaching of immortality instead of wealth (BU 2.4; 4.5).
nodes.details: BU 2.4.5: “ātmā vā are draṣṭavyaḥ śrotavyo mantavyo nididhyāsitavyo maitreyi”; BU 4.5.1: “tayor ha maitreyī brahmavādinī babhūva; strīprajñaiva tarhi kātyāyanī”.

sources.edition: Kāṇva recension (GRETIL; checked against Limaye & Vadekar 1958)

earliestText.label: parts possibly still being composed c. 4th–2nd c. BCE

nodes.name: Uddālaka Āruṇi
nodes.summary: A leading Kuru-Pañcāla teacher of the early Upaniṣads who instructs his son Śvetaketu with the refrain “tat tvam asi” (CU 6), questions Yājñavalkya at Janaka’s court (BU 3.7) and, by the lineage in BU 6.3.7, was Yājñavalkya’s own teacher.
nodes.details: He also appears as a learner from kṣatriyas: Pravāhaṇa Jaivali teaches him the five fires (CU 5.3–10; BU 6.2), and the Kauṣītaki Upaniṣad (1.1) has Citra Gāṅgyāyani teach Āruṇi. Kaṭha Upaniṣad 1.11 calls Naciketas’s father “Auddālaki Āruṇi” — a patronymic (“son/descendant of Uddālaka”) whose relation to this figure is unresolved.

sources.edition: Kāṇva recension (GRETIL; checked against Limaye & Vadekar 1958)

earliestText.label: c. 7th–6th c. BCE (pre-Buddhist; “give or take a century”)

nodes.name: Śvetaketu
nodes.summary: Son and pupil of Uddālaka Āruṇi who returns proud from twelve years of Vedic study and is taught by his father that the self is the subtle essence of all (“tat tvam asi, śvetaketo”, CU 6); in CU 5.3 and BU 6.2 he cannot answer Pravāhaṇa Jaivali’s questions on the afterlife.

sources.edition: Kāṇva recension (GRETIL; checked against Limaye & Vadekar 1958)

earliestText.label: c. 7th–6th c. BCE (pre-Buddhist; “give or take a century”)

nodes.name: Satyakāma Jābāla
nodes.summary: The boy of the Chāndogya (4.4) who, not knowing his father, truthfully reports his mother Jabālā’s words and is accepted as a pupil by Hāridrumata Gautama for that truthfulness; he later teaches Upakosala (CU 4.10–15).
nodes.details: Not to be confused with Satyakāma Śaibya, a pupil of Pippalāda in the Praśna Upaniṣad (1.1).

sources.quote: satyakāmo ha jābālo jabālāṃ mātaram āmantrayāṃ cakre

earliestText.label: c. 7th–6th c. BCE (pre-Buddhist; “give or take a century”)

nodes.name: Janaka of Videha (Upaniṣadic king)
nodes.summary: The king of Videha in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa and Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad who holds a sacrifice with lavish gifts, sets a prize of a thousand cows for the most learned brahmin, and becomes Yājñavalkya’s student.
nodes.details: BU 3.1.1 (verified): “janako ha vaideho bahudakṣiṇena yajñeneje”; ŚB 11.6.3.1 has a parallel. BU 2.1.1 records that people ran about crying “Janaka, Janaka” — his patronage was proverbial. Identity caution: the Rāmāyaṇa’s Janaka of Mithilā, father of Sītā (`char:janaka`, epic agent), shares the name and kingdom, and later tradition treats “Janaka” as a dynastic title; the Vedic texts say nothing of Sītā, and this dataset does not assert identity (see `claim:janaka-videha-sita-father`).

sources.edition: Kāṇva recension (GRETIL; checked against Limaye & Vadekar 1958)

earliestText.label: c. 8th–6th c. BCE (late Brāhmaṇa period; approximate)

nodes.name: Naciketas
nodes.summary: The boy of the Kaṭha Upaniṣad whose father, angered by his questioning, gives him to Death; waiting three nights at Yama’s house, he receives three boons and refuses all worldly gifts in favour of the knowledge of what lies beyond death.
nodes.details: The frame story is older than the Upaniṣad (Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa 3.11.8; recall). A later retelling is the Nāciketa episode of the Mahābhārata (Anuśāsanaparvan; recall).

sources.quote: tasya ha naciketā nāma putra āsa

earliestText.label: last few centuries BCE (Olivelle’s group of verse Upaniṣads; numeric range approximate)

nodes.name: Ghora Āṅgirasa
nodes.summary: A teacher of the Āṅgirasa clan who, according to Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.17.6, taught Kṛṣṇa son of Devakī a doctrine likening a man’s life to a soma sacrifice, after which Kṛṣṇa “became free from thirst”.

sources.quote: tad dhaitad ghora āṅgirasaḥ kṛṣṇāya devakīputrāyoktvovāca

earliestText.label: c. 7th–6th c. BCE (pre-Buddhist; “give or take a century”)

nodes.name: Kṛṣṇa Devakīputra (Chāndogya)
nodes.summary: The pupil of Ghora Āṅgirasa named in a single sentence of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad (3.17.6) — “Kṛṣṇa, son of Devakī” — the only Vedic occurrence of that name-pair; whether he is the epic and Purāṇic Kṛṣṇa is disputed.
nodes.details: Proponents of identity (Bhandarkar 1913; Raychaudhuri 1920) point to the same name and mother and to ethical themes (austerity, generosity, non-injury, truthfulness — CU 3.17.4) resembling the Gītā. Sceptics note that nothing else in the passage connects him with the Yādavas, Mathurā or Vāsudeva, that “Kṛṣṇa” and “Devakī” were not unique names, and that the Chāndogya’s student has no divine status. Kept as a separate id; see `claim:krishna-devakiputra-identity` (material agent).
openQuestions: Can any independent evidence connect the Chāndogya’s pupil with the Vṛṣṇi hero Vāsudeva?

earliestText.label: c. 7th–6th c. BCE (pre-Buddhist; “give or take a century”)

nodes.name: Purūravas
nodes.summary: A mortal king, called “son of Iḍā” (aiḍa), who loses his apsaras wife Urvaśī; their dialogue is RV 10.95 and the full story ŚB 11.5.1. In Purāṇic genealogy he is the first king of the Lunar dynasty.

sources.quote: iti tvā devā ima āhur aiḻa

nodes.name: Urvaśī
nodes.summary: An apsaras who lives with the mortal Purūravas on conditions he breaks, then leaves him (RV 10.95; ŚB 11.5.1); RV 7.33.11 also links her with Vasiṣṭha’s birth. She is a celebrated heroine of later literature, notably Kālidāsa’s Vikramorvaśīya.

nodes.name: Vṛtra
nodes.summary: The serpent (ahi) or “obstruction” who encloses the waters and is slain by Indra (RV 1.32). Yāska records two readings — a cloud (nairuktas) or an asura son of Tvaṣṭṛ (aitihāsikas); later texts make Vṛtra a brahmin-born asura whose killing brings Indra guilt, and the Bhāgavata a devotee of Viṣṇu.

nodes.name: Śunaḥśepa
nodes.summary: Son of the brahmin Ajīgarta, sold to prince Rohita as a substitute victim for Varuṇa; bound to the stake at Hariścandra’s rājasūya, he is freed by praising the gods and adopted by Viśvāmitra as Devarāta (AB 7.13–18).
nodes.details: RV 1.24.12–13 already mentions Śunaḥśepa, bound and calling on Varuṇa; the Anukramaṇī attributes RV 1.24–30 to him (recall). The Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa (Bālakāṇḍa) retells the story with king Ambarīṣa and the sage Ṛcīka in place of Hariścandra and Ajīgarta, making Viśvāmitra Śunaḥśepa’s maternal uncle.

sources.edition: TITUS, on the basis of Aufrecht 1879

sources.quote: śunaḥśepo yam ahvad gṛbhītaḥ so asmān rājā varuṇo mumoktu

nodes.name: Saramā
nodes.summary: Indra’s messenger who tracks the cows stolen by the Paṇis and demands them back in the dialogue hymn RV 10.108; later tradition makes her the bitch of the gods, mother of Yama’s two dogs (Sārameya, RV 10.14.10).
nodes.details: RV 10.108.2: “indrasya dūtīr iṣitā carāmi”. In the Mahābhārata (Ādiparvan, Pauṣyaparvan) Saramā curses Janamejaya after his brothers beat her son (recall).

nodes.name: Brahman
nodes.summary: In the Ṛgveda (neuter bráhman) the potent sacred formulation of the poet-priest; in the Upaniṣads the ultimate reality, the ground from which beings arise and into which they return, often identified with the self (ātman).
nodes.details: Key Upaniṣadic loci (verified): BU 1.4.10 (“ahaṃ brahmāsmi”), BU 2.3.6 (“neti neti” as the description of brahman), CU 3.14.1 (“sarvaṃ khalv idaṃ brahma”), TU 3.1.1 (the definition by origin, sustenance and dissolution), Kena 1–4, Māṇḍūkya 2 (“ayam ātmā brahma”), Aitareya 3.3 (“prajñānaṃ brahma”). These sentences become the “great sayings” (mahāvākyas) of Advaita Vedānta. The concept is central in the Bhagavad Gītā (e.g. brahma-nirvāṇa) and the Brahma Sūtra.

sources.edition: Kāṇva recension (GRETIL; checked against Limaye & Vadekar 1958)

earliestText.label: c. 7th–6th c. BCE (pre-Buddhist; “give or take a century”)

nodes.name: Ātman
nodes.summary: The self — originally the body or breath, then the inner essence of a person — which the early Upaniṣads make the object of liberating knowledge and identify with brahman.
nodes.details: BU 1.4.1 (“ātmaivedam agra āsīt puruṣavidhaḥ” — in the beginning this was the self alone, in the form of a person), BU 2.4.5 (“ātmā vā are draṣṭavyaḥ …”), BU 4.4.5 (“sa vā ayam ātmā brahma”), CU 6.8.7 (“tat tvam asi”), Kaṭha 2.18–19 (the self is unborn and undying), Māṇḍūkya 2. The Bhagavad Gītā (2.19–20) reuses the Kaṭha verses on the unkillable self.

sources.edition: Kāṇva recension (GRETIL; checked against Limaye & Vadekar 1958)

earliestText.label: c. 7th–6th c. BCE (pre-Buddhist; “give or take a century”)

nodes.name: Ṛta
nodes.summary: The Ṛgvedic principle of cosmic, ritual and moral order and truth, guarded above all by Varuṇa and Mitra; in later thought its role is largely taken over by dharma.
nodes.details: RV 10.190.1 (“ṛtaṃ ca satyaṃ cābhīddhāt tapaso ’dhy ajāyata” — order and truth were born from kindled heat), RV 10.85.1 (“ṛtenādityās tiṣṭhanti”). Cognate with Avestan aša. The word dhárman also occurs in the Ṛgveda (e.g. RV 10.90.16 “dharmāṇi prathamāni”), and post-Vedic dharma absorbs much of ṛta’s scope.

sources.quote: ṛtaṁ ca satyaṁ cābhīddhāt tapaso ’dhy ajāyata

nodes.name: Yajña
nodes.summary: Vedic sacrifice — offerings into the fire with recitation, chant and formula — the central religious act of the Saṃhitās and Brāhmaṇas, which the Brāhmaṇas identify with Prajāpati and with Viṣṇu (“yajño vai viṣṇuḥ”).
nodes.details: RV 10.90.16: “yajñena yajñam ayajanta devāḥ” (with the sacrifice the gods sacrificed to the sacrifice). ŚB 1.1.2.13 and 14.1.1.6 identify Viṣṇu with the sacrifice. The Upaniṣads reinterpret the rite inwardly (e.g. CU 3.17, life as a soma sacrifice); the Bhagavad Gītā (3–4) generalises yajña to all action offered without attachment. Living śrauta performance continues in a few lineages (e.g. the 1975 Agnicayana in Kerala).

nodes.name: Om
nodes.summary: The sacred syllable recited at the beginning and end of Vedic recitation; the Upaniṣads make it an object of meditation and a symbol of brahman (CU 1.1.1; Kaṭha 2.15–17; the whole Māṇḍūkya).
nodes.details: CU 1.1.1: “om ity etad akṣaram udgītham upāsīta”. Kaṭha 2.15: “om ity etat”. Māṇḍūkya 1: Om is all this, past, present and future, and what is beyond the three times. In BU 3.9.1 Yājñavalkya’s “om” is an affirmation (“yes”). The Bhagavad Gītā (8.13; 17.23–24) continues the Upaniṣadic use.

sources.quote: om ity etad akṣaram udgītham upāsīta

earliestText.label: c. 7th–6th c. BCE (pre-Buddhist; “give or take a century”)

nodes.name: Karma
nodes.summary: Action — first, in the Brāhmaṇas, ritual action — which the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad makes the determinant of one’s future: “as one acts, so one becomes” (BU 4.4.5); the earliest explicit statements of the doctrine of moral retribution in Indian texts.
