comparisons.title: Kṛṣṇa across the Mahābhārata, Gītā, Harivaṃśa, Viṣṇu Purāṇa and Bhāgavata Purāṇa
comparisons.subject: char:krishna
comparisons.question: How is Kṛṣṇa presented — hero, partial descent, or the supreme Lord himself — and how much of his cowherd childhood is told?

rows.statement: A Vṛṣṇi prince, ally and charioteer of the Pāṇḍavas, called a portion (aṃśa) of Nārāyaṇa (1.61.90) and born from Nārāyaṇa’s black hair (1.189.31). He reveals a cosmic form at the Kaurava court (5.129) and dies from a hunter’s arrow (16.5). His childhood exploits (Pūtanā, Govardhana) are only alluded to, in Śiśupāla’s mocking speech (2.38.4–9).
Kṛṣṇa speaks as the Lord who “whenever dharma declines” takes birth age after age to protect the good (6.26.7–8) and shows Arjuna his universal form (6.33). No childhood narrative.

sources.quote: yadā yadā hi dharmasya glānir bhavati bhārata

rows.statement: Viṣṇu resolves to descend; Kṛṣṇa is born to Devakī as Yaśodā bears a daughter (48.11), grows up in Vraja, subdues Kāliya (55–56), lifts Govardhana (61–62), sports at night with the cowherd women (63.24–35), kills Kaṃsa (76) and founds Dvārakā (85–86): the first connected childhood narrative.

Viṣṇu plucks a white and a black hair, which become Balarāma and Kṛṣṇa (5.1.60–64: “this eighth embryo will be my hair”); the life of Kṛṣṇa follows the Harivaṃśa closely — birth (5.3), Govardhana (5.11), the night with the gopīs (5.13.15–48), Kaṃsa’s death (5.20).

After listing the descents, it declares “these are portions and parts of the Puruṣa, but Kṛṣṇa is the Lord himself” (1.3.28), though 2.7.26 still speaks of him appearing with a portion as “white-and-black-haired”. Book 10 greatly expands the childhood, culminating in the rāsa with the gopīs (10.29–33).

sources.quote: ete cāṃśakalāḥ puṃsaḥ kṛṣṇas tu bhagavān svayam

comparisons.note: The “hair” motif (MBh 1.189.31; ViP 5.1.60; BhP 2.7.26) and the Bhāgavata’s “bhagavān svayam” (1.3.28) are the textual poles of the later debate on whether Kṛṣṇa is an avatāra of Viṣṇu or their source (Gauḍīya view). See Matchett 2001.

comparisons.title: The Rāma story in Vālmīki and in the Mahābhārata’s Rāmopākhyāna
comparisons.subject: char:rama
comparisons.question: Which parts of the Rāma story does each version tell, and how do they differ?

rows.statement: Seven books: frame with Vālmīki, Nārada and the krauñca (1.1–4); births as portions of Viṣṇu (1.17); Viśvāmitra, Tāṭakā, Ahalyā, the bow and the four weddings (1.24–72); Paraśurāma (1.73–75); exile (Book 2); abduction (3.40–49); vānara alliance and Vālin (Book 4); Hanumān in Laṅkā (Book 5); war, fire ordeal and Brahmā’s hymn (6.103–106); consecration (6.116); Rāvaṇa’s back-story, Hanumān’s childhood, banishment, Śambūka, the twins and Sītā’s return to the earth (Book 7).

Told by Mārkaṇḍeya to console Yudhiṣṭhira. Opens with Rāvaṇa’s Paulastya genealogy and boon (3.258–259); Brahmā says Viṣṇu has descended and has the gods beget monkey allies, and sends the gandharvī Dundubhī as Mantharā (3.260). Omits the Viśvāmitra episodes, Ahalyā, the bow contest and the marriages (Sītā is simply Janaka’s daughter made by Tvaṣṭṛ, 3.258.9); compresses the exile; Lakṣmaṇa kills Kumbhakarṇa (3.271.16) and Indrajit (3.273); after Rāvaṇa’s death Sītā is vindicated by divine testimony without a fire-entry (3.275.10–36). No Uttarakāṇḍa material: no banishment, no twins.

comparisons.note: Whether the Rāmopākhyāna abridges Vālmīki (majority view) or preserves an older/independent telling is unresolved; see assertion text:ramopakhyana DERIVED_FROM text:valmiki-ramayana.

comparisons.title: Sītā’s birth
comparisons.subject: char:sita
comparisons.question: How was Sītā born and whose daughter is she?

rows.statement: Janaka found her rising from the furrow as he ploughed a field and named her Sītā; she is “not born of a womb” (ayonijā).
The Uttarakāṇḍa adds that she is the ascetic Vedavatī, reborn in the Tretā age to destroy Rāvaṇa.
“Janaka was king of Videha; Sītā was his daughter (ātmajā), whom Tvaṣṭṛ himself fashioned to be Rāma’s beloved queen.” No furrow-birth.
In the Jain telling Sītā is born to Janaka and his queen as twin of Bhāmaṇḍala (recall; not checked against the text).

comparisons.title: Sītā’s ordeal and banishment
comparisons.subject: char:sita
comparisons.question: After Rāvaṇa’s death, how is Sītā’s fidelity tested, and is she later banished?

rows.statement: Rāma publicly repudiates her; she has Lakṣmaṇa build a pyre and enters the fire calling Agni to witness (6.104.18–26); Brahmā hymns Rāma as Nārāyaṇa and Sītā as Lakṣmī (6.105); Agni returns her unharmed (6.106.1–3) and Rāma accepts her.

Uttarakāṇḍa: because of citizens’ gossip (7.44), Rāma has Lakṣmaṇa leave the pregnant Sītā near Vālmīki’s hermitage (7.46–47); she bears Lava and Kuśa (7.58); asked for a fresh oath at the horse sacrifice, she calls on the earth goddess Mādhavī, who takes her down on a throne (7.88.10–14).

Rāma tells Sītā to go, unwilling to take back a woman who lived in another’s house; she swears by the elements; Vāyu, Agni and Varuṇa declare her innocent, Brahmā reveals that Nalakūbara’s curse had protected her, and Daśaratha appears. No fire-entry; no banishment.
The real Sītā is placed in Agni’s keeping before the abduction and a “shadow” (māyā) Sītā is carried off; the fire ordeal restores the real Sītā (recall; a motif taken up by Tulsīdās).
Kampaṉ’s poem ends with the coronation; the Uttarakāṇḍa banishment is not part of his work (later supplements exist) (recall).

comparisons.note: Unreconciled: the fire-entry is Vālmīki-specific among the Sanskrit epic tellings; the banishment is confined to the Uttarakāṇḍa.

comparisons.title: Who kills Kumbhakarṇa?
comparisons.subject: char:kumbhakarna
comparisons.question: Who kills Rāvaṇa’s brother Kumbhakarṇa?

rows.statement: Rāma kills him (“having killed Kumbhakarṇa … Bharata’s elder brother rejoiced”).
Lakṣmaṇa burns him with the Brahmā weapon (“taṃ brahmāstreṇa saumitrir dadāha”).

comparisons.title: Karṇa’s parentage and status across the parvans
comparisons.subject: char:karna
comparisons.question: How do different parts of the Mahābhārata tell of Karṇa’s birth and social status?

rows.statement: The aṃśāvataraṇa makes him “a portion of Divākara” (1.61.89). The maiden Kuntī invokes the Sun with Durvāsas’s mantra, bears a son with armour and earrings, abandons him, and “the husband of Rādhā” takes him up (1.104.8–14).

At the tournament Kṛpa asks his mother, father and lineage; Duryodhana makes him king of Aṅga; when Adhiratha arrives Bhīma calls him a sūta’s son unfit for Aṅga; Kuntī secretly recognises him (1.127.22).

A long retelling: Sūrya warns him in a dream; Kuntī’s boon from Durvāsas; the basket set adrift on the Aśvanadī that drifts to the Carmaṇvatī, Yamunā and Gaṅgā (3.292.6–26); the childless Rādhā and Adhiratha adopt him (3.293); he gives Indra his armour and earrings for the spear (3.294).

Kṛṣṇa tells him that a kānīna son belongs to the mother’s husband, so “by dharma you are Pāṇḍu’s son” and the eldest Pāṇḍava, and offers him the throne (5.138.8–9, 11–27); Kuntī asks him to join his brothers and he promises to spare all but Arjuna (5.142–144).
After the war Kuntī reveals that Karṇa was her son; the Pāṇḍavas mourn him.

Yudhiṣṭhira grieves for his “elder brother Karṇa” (12.1.37); Nārada tells how Karṇa, posing as a Bhārgava brahmin, studied under Rāma Jāmadagnya and was cursed by him and by a brahmin (12.2–3); Yudhiṣṭhira curses all women never to keep a secret (12.6.10).
Kuntī confesses to Vyāsa that she cast the secretly born child into the water.

comparisons.note: Unreconciled: “sūtaputra” status (Ādi) versus legal Pāṇḍava status argued by Kṛṣṇa (Udyoga); McGrath (2004) discusses Karṇa as the epic’s alternative hero.

comparisons.title: Draupadī’s five husbands: the justifications in the Ādiparvan
comparisons.subject: char:draupadi
comparisons.question: What reasons does the Mahābhārata itself give for Draupadī’s marriage to all five Pāṇḍavas?

rows.statement: Kuntī, not seeing what her sons have brought, tells them to “enjoy it together”, and her word must be kept.
Objection within the text: Drupada calls it adharma, contrary to world and Veda; Dhṛṣṭadyumna cannot decide because of the subtlety of dharma.

Yudhiṣṭhira cites the Purāṇic precedent of Jaṭilā Gautamī, wife of seven sages, and the authority of the mother’s (guru’s) word. (A second precedent, Vārkṣī wife of the ten Pracetas, appears only in star passage *1910 after 1.188.14, not in the constituted text.)

Vyāsa privately tells Drupada that the Pāṇḍavas are five former Indras condemned by Śiva to human birth, and Draupadī is Śrī destined to be their common wife; he grants Drupada divine sight to see them.
A sage’s daughter, unable to find a husband, asked Śiva five times for a husband and was granted five in her next birth — told again by Vyāsa to the Pāṇḍavas at Ekacakrā (1.157.6–16).
The catalogue of incarnations says a part of Śrī was born in Drupada’s line from the altar, to captivate five men.

comparisons.note: Five distinct justifications (maternal command, precedent, divine plan, karmic boon, incarnation) stand side by side without harmonisation; Hiltebeitel (2001) reads them as a deliberate layering.

comparisons.title: Vidura’s origin: internal variation
comparisons.subject: char:vidura
comparisons.question: Whose incarnation or son is Vidura?

rows.statement: Son of Vyāsa by a servant woman, “Dharma in the form of Vidura, through the curse of that great-souled one”.
Explains the curse: Aṇī-Māṇḍavya, impaled though innocent, curses Dharma to be born of a śūdra woman.
The aṃśāvataraṇa says: “know Vidura, best of the wise, born in this world as … the son of Atri”, without mention of Dharma.

comparisons.title: Who restores Draupadī’s garment?
comparisons.subject: narr:draupadi-humiliation
comparisons.question: When Duḥśāsana pulls at Draupadī’s garment in the assembly hall, what makes it endless?

rows.statement: No agent is named: as he pulled, “another garment of the same kind appeared, many times over” (tadrūpam aparaṃ vastraṃ prādurāsīd anekaśaḥ).
Many manuscripts insert Draupadī’s prayer to Kṛṣṇa — “govinda dvārakāvāsin kṛṣṇa gopījanapriya …” — so that Kṛṣṇa (or Dharma) supplies the garments; the vulgate (Ganguli’s Sabhā Parva) follows this.

sources.locator: Sabhā Parva, Dyūta sub-parvan (vulgate; section number not checked)

comparisons.note: A clear case where the Critical Edition’s constituted text and the popular/vulgate tradition differ on a famous detail.

comparisons.title: Lists of Viṣṇu's manifestations, text by text
comparisons.subject: concept:avatara
comparisons.question: Which manifestations of Viṣṇu does each text list, in what number and order?

rows.statement: Foretells Varāha, Narasiṃha, Vāmana, Rāma Bhārgava (Tretā), Rāma Dāśarathi (Tretā–Dvāpara junction) and Kṛṣṇa at Mathurā (Dvāpara–Kali junction), and names Haṃsa and Hayaśiras as past manifestations. The constituted text has no Matsya, Kūrma or Kalki; the familiar ten-list beginning with Haṃsa is a vulgate reading.

Pauṣkara (lotus), Vārāha, Nārasiṃha, Vāmana, Dattātreya, Jāmadagnya, Rāma Dāśarathi, Kṛṣṇa (Māthura) and the future Kalki Viṣṇuyaśas (31.148); Vedavyāsa and the phrase 'ten manifestations of Vāsudeva' occur only in starred passages.

Gives no numbered list: Varāha raises the Earth 'as he took fish, tortoise and other forms in earlier kalpas' (1.4.8); Viṣṇu as tortoise (1.9.86) and in woman's form (1.9.107); the man-lion (1.20.32); Viṣṇu born fourfold as Rāma and his brothers (4.4.49); Kṛṣṇa as an aṃśa (4.24.27).

sources.edition: Critical edition, M. M. Pathak (Vadodara 1997–99); GRETIL e-text by P. Schreiner

rows.statement: Twenty-two: the Kumāras, Varāha, Nārada, Nara-Nārāyaṇa, Kapila, Dattātreya, Yajña, Ṛṣabha, Pṛthu, Matsya, Kūrma, Dhanvantari, Mohinī, Narasiṃha, Vāmana, Paraśurāma, Vyāsa, Rāma, Balarāma, Kṛṣṇa, Buddha, Kalki; avatāras are innumerable (1.3.26); these are portions, 'but Kṛṣṇa is Bhagavān himself' (1.3.28).
A second catalogue (Brahmā to Nārada) of about twenty-four, adding Suyajña, Hayaśīrṣa, Hari who saves Gajendra, Haṃsa and Manu, and treating Balarāma and Kṛṣṇa together.

1.1 reproduces the Bhāgavata's twenty-two almost verbatim (Buddha 'jinasuta' for BhP's 'añjanasuta'); 1.86.10–11 gives ten: Matsya, Kūrma, Varāha, Nṛhari, Vāmana, Rāma (Bhārgava), Rāma Dāśarathi, Kṛṣṇa, Buddha, Kalki.

Because of Bhṛgu's curse Viṣṇu has three divine manifestations (a portion of Nārāyaṇa born of Dharma, Narasiṃha, Vāmana) and seven human ones: Dattātreya, Māndhātṛ, Jāmadagnya, Rāma Dāśarathi, Vedavyāsa, Buddha and Kalki — no Matsya, Kūrma, Varāha or Kṛṣṇa in this count (the fish is Janārdana at 1.28).

sources.edition: Calcutta: Caukhamba Vidyabhavan 1954; GRETIL e-text (O. Hellwig), adhy. 1–176

rows.statement: Narrates the avatāras in order (Matsya, Kūrma, Varāha, Narasiṃha, Vāmana, Paraśurāma, Rāma, Kṛṣṇa via the Harivaṃśa, Buddha, Kalki) and calls them the 'ten' (16.12); its iconographic list (49) has Balarāma with plough and pestle in place of Kṛṣṇa.

sources.edition: Rajendralal Mitra ed. (Bibliotheca Indica 1870–79); GRETIL e-text

comparisons.note: The 'standard ten' (with Kṛṣṇa or Balarāma eighth and Buddha ninth) is a later convention; earlier and contemporaneous texts count three, six, nine, ten, twenty-two or 'innumerable'. Rows are not reconciled.

comparisons.title: Manu and the fish: the flood story from the Śatapatha to the Bhāgavata
comparisons.subject: narr:matsya-flood
comparisons.question: Who is the fish, who is saved, why, and where does the boat come to rest?

rows.statement: A small fish found in Manu's washing water asks protection and warns of a flood; Manu ties his boat to its horn and is carried to the 'northern mountain'; alone, he sacrifices and from the offering a woman (Iḍā) is born. The fish is not identified with a god.

Told by Mārkaṇḍeya: Manu Vaivasvata, performing austerities at Viśālā Badarī, saves a little fish which outgrows jar, pond, Gaṅgā and ocean; with the seven sages and all seeds he is towed to the Himālayan peak Naubandhana; the fish declares 'I am Prajāpati Brahmā' (3.185.48). The tale is called 'the purāṇa named Mātsyaka' (3.185.53).

King Manu, son of Ravi, practises yoga on the Malaya; the fish is recognised as Vāsudeva/Keśava/Janārdana (1.25–28); the flood comes at the end of the Cākṣuṣa manvantara (2.14); a serpent serves as the rope (2.18); the whole Purāṇa is the fish's teaching to Manu.

sources.edition: Calcutta: Caukhamba Vidyabhavan 1954; GRETIL e-text (O. Hellwig), adhy. 1–176

rows.statement: The demon Hayagrīva steals the Vedas from sleeping Brahmā's mouths (8.24.8); Satyavrata, a royal sage devoted to Nārāyaṇa and lord of the Draviḍas, catches the fish in the Kṛtamālā (8.24.12–13); Viṣṇu as the fish teaches him, slays Hayagrīva and recovers the Vedas (8.24.57); Satyavrata becomes Vaivasvata Manu in this kalpa (8.24.58).
Manu Vaivasvata at the Kṛtamālā; the fish is addressed as Viṣṇu–Nārāyaṇa–Janārdana; a flood after seven days; the boat tied to the golden one-horned fish with a great serpent.

sources.edition: Rajendralal Mitra ed. (Bibliotheca Indica 1870–79); GRETIL e-text

comparisons.note: The Purāṇic identification of the fish with Viṣṇu is absent from the Śatapatha and contradicted by the Mahābhārata's Brahmā. The Śatapatha row is from Eggeling's translation (not re-checked online in this session).

comparisons.title: From Rudra to the Liṅgodbhava: portrayals of Śiva
comparisons.subject: deity:shiva
comparisons.question: How is the god Rudra–Śiva characterised and ranked in successive texts?

rows.statement: Rudra is a fierce archer-god, 'the strongest of the strong', implored to spare offspring and cattle and praised as the best of physicians; a god among many, not supreme.

Rudra is the one god who does not tolerate a second (3.2), creator and protector, who generated Hiraṇyagarbha (3.4), whose benign form is 'śivā' (3.5); he is called Śiva, all-pervading (3.11; 4.14). A theistic supreme god.

rows.locator: MBh (CE), various (e.g. Sauptika and Anuśāsana parvans)
rows.statement: Śiva is a mighty, ambivalent god: destroyer of Dakṣa's sacrifice, giver of weapons to Arjuna, praised with a thousand names; Vaiṣṇava passages subordinate him to Nārāyaṇa.

In the Liṅgodbhava Brahmā (swan) and Viṣṇu (boar) fail to find the ends of the fiery liṅga; Śiva is supreme over both. The text prescribes the image: Candraśekhara within the liṅga, swan above, boar below.
The same pillar myth with an added episode: Brahmā claims to have seen the top, citing a falling ketakī flower as witness, and is punished for the lie.

sources.edition: Venkatesvara Press ed. (Bombay c. 1920), books 1 and 7; GRETIL e-text

rows.statement: Śiva as the lord of a Pāśupata-coloured universe, his marriage to Pārvatī, the birth of Skanda and the subjugation of Andhaka; the text maps Śaiva holy places such as Vārāṇasī.

comparisons.note: The rows show a trajectory from a feared Vedic god to a supreme deity; no single line of development is implied.

comparisons.title: The Goddess from Umā Haimavatī to the Devī Bhāgavata
comparisons.subject: deity:devi
comparisons.question: How does each text present the Goddess?

rows.statement: A beautiful woman, Umā Haimavatī, appears to Indra and reveals that the mysterious being (yakṣa) was Brahman. She is a revealer of knowledge; her relation to Śiva is not stated.

Viṣṇu sends Nidrā to be born of Yaśodā; she will be Kauśikī, dwell eternally on the Vindhya, slay Śumbha and Niśumbha, love meat-offerings and be worshipped on the ninth day; the Āryā hymn proper stands outside the constituted text (starred/appendix).

A supreme Goddess, formed from all the gods' radiance (DM 2), slays Madhu–Kaiṭabha (through Viṣṇu), Mahiṣa and Śumbha–Niśumbha, emits Kālī/Cāmuṇḍā and the Mothers, is hymned as Nārāyaṇī and promises to return whenever demons arise.

sources.edition: GRETIL e-text (SANSKNET); Devī Māhātmya = MkP 81–93 in this edition

rows.statement: The Goddess is the ground of all being who creates Brahmā, Viṣṇu and Śiva; the DM battles are retold (book 5); the Devī Gītā (7.31–40) gives her Vedāntic teaching to Himālaya.

comparisons.note: Coburn's phrase 'crystallization' marks the DM as the point where earlier goddesses are understood as one Goddess.

comparisons.title: How long are the yugas? Manu, the Mahābhārata, the Purāṇas and Āryabhaṭa
comparisons.subject: concept:yuga
comparisons.question: What durations does each source give for the four yugas, and in what kind of years?

rows.statement: Kṛta 4,000 years + dawn 400 + dusk 400; Tretā 3,000 + 300 + 300; Dvāpara 2,000 + 200 + 200; Kali 1,000 + 100 + 100; the 12,000 together are 'a yuga of the gods'; a year is a day-night of the gods (1.67); a thousand such yugas are Brahmā's day; a manvantara is 71. Manu does not convert into human years.

sources.edition: GRETIL e-text, text of Kullūka (Shastri 1983) with Medhātithi variants

rows.statement: Verses nearly identical to Manu 1.64–78 give the same 4,000/3,000/2,000/1,000 scheme with dawn and dusk and call the whole 'the twelve thousand known as a yuga' (12.224.28), without stating divine years.

The caturyuga is 12,000 divine years (1.3.11); 4, 3, 2, 1 thousand with sandhyās of as many hundreds (1.3.12–13). A manvantara is 852,000 divine years = 306,720,000 human years (1.3.19–21), i.e. 360 human years per divine year (equivalently 4,320,000 human years per caturyuga). ViP 4.24.33 states that Kali lasts 360,000 human years, and 4.24.34 '1,200 divine years'.

sources.edition: Critical edition, M. M. Pathak (Vadodara 1997–99); GRETIL e-text by P. Schreiner

rows.statement: Four yugas of 12,000 divine years; 4, 3, 2, 1 thousand with twice as many hundreds for the junctions; a thousand caturyugas are Brahmā's day; a Manu rules a little over 71.

A divine year is 360 solar years (3.7); a yuga of 12,000 divine years is divided into four equal quarters (yugapāda), not 4:3:2:1; Brahmā's day is 1,008 yugas (3.8); 3,600 years of the Kali had elapsed in Āryabhaṭa's 23rd year (3.10).

comparisons.note: Traditional chronology. González-Reimann argues that the divine-year multiplier arose to reconcile the epic 12,000-year cycle with astronomical periods. The arithmetic equivalences (×360) are the editor's, stated as implied by ViP 1.3.19–21.

comparisons.title: The churning of the ocean in four tellings
comparisons.subject: narr:samudra-manthana
comparisons.question: Who supports Mount Mandara, what happens to the poison, what emerges, and how is the nectar kept from the asuras?

rows.statement: Ananta uproots Mandara; the king of tortoises Akūpāra bears it; Vāsuki is the rope; Soma, Śrī, Surā, a white horse, the Kaustubha and Dhanvantari with the nectar emerge; Nārāyaṇa as Mohinī takes the nectar; Rāhu is beheaded; Nara and Nārāyaṇa win the battle. No poison episode in the constituted text.

Set in the Kṛta age; Mandara and Vāsuki; Dhanvantari, sixty crores of apsarases, Vāruṇī (taken by Aditi's sons, hence 'suras'), Uccaiḥśravas, the Kaustubha and the nectar; a war in which the sons of Aditi destroy the sons of Diti. No tortoise and no poison in the constituted text.

Caused by Durvāsas' curse on Indra; Viṣṇu himself as tortoise bears Mandara and in other forms pulls the serpent and presses the summit; Surabhi, Vāruṇī, the Pārijāta, apsarases, the moon (taken by Maheśvara), Dhanvantari and Śrī emerge; the nāgas take the poison; Viṣṇu in a woman's form gives the nectar to the gods.

sources.edition: Critical edition, M. M. Pathak (Vadodara 1997–99); GRETIL e-text by P. Schreiner

rows.statement: Viṣṇu as tortoise; Śiva drinks the hālāhala out of compassion (8.7.43); Lakṣmī chooses Mukunda (8.8.24); Mohinī distributes the nectar (8.9); Śiva later sees Mohinī and is infatuated (8.12).

comparisons.note: Critical-edition texts of the two epics lack episodes (Kūrma as Viṣṇu; Śiva and the poison) that the vulgate texts and the Purāṇas contain.

comparisons.title: Who are the eighteen? Purāṇa lists and verse counts
comparisons.subject: col:mahapuranas
comparisons.question: Which Purāṇa stands in the fourth (Śaiva/Vāyu) place, and what extents are given?

rows.statement: Brāhma (first), Pādma, Vaiṣṇava, Śaiva, Bhāgavata, Nāradīya, Mārkaṇḍeya, Āgneya, Bhaviṣya, Brahmavaivarta, Laiṅga, Vārāha, Skānda, Vāmana, Kaurma, Mātsya, Gāruḍa, Brahmāṇḍa; 'mahāpurāṇa' only in starred insertion 3.6.23*8.

sources.edition: Critical edition, M. M. Pathak (Vadodara 1997–99); GRETIL e-text by P. Schreiner

rows.statement: Same membership with Śaiva in fourth place; counts: Brāhma 10,000, Pādma 55,000, Vaiṣṇava 23,000, Śaiva 24,000, Bhāgavata 18,000, Nārada 25,000, Mārkaṇḍeya 9,000, Āgneya 15,400, Bhaviṣya 14,500, Brahmavaivarta 18,000, Laiṅga 11,000, Vārāha 24,000, Skānda 81,100, Vāmana 10,000, Kaurma 17,000, Mātsya 14,000, Sauparṇa 19,000, Brahmāṇḍa 12,000 = 400,000.

Fourth is the Vāyavīya, 'joined with Rudra's greatness', 24,000 verses; Brāhma 13,000, Āgneya 16,000, Brahmāṇḍa 12,200; describes the Bhāgavata as beginning with the Gāyatrī and including Vṛtra's slaying (53.20–21).

sources.edition: Calcutta: Caukhamba Vidyabhavan 1954; GRETIL e-text (O. Hellwig), adhy. 1–176

rows.statement: Keeps Śaiva fourth, then after Gāruḍa names the Vāyavīya and 'the eighteenth, called Brahmāṇḍa' (aṣṭādaśaṃ samuddiṣṭaṃ brahmāṇḍam iti saṃjñitam) — either a nineteenth title or an identification of the Vāyavīya with the Brahmāṇḍa.
Brāhma, Pādma, Vaiṣṇava, Vāyavīya, Bhāgavata, Nāradīya, Mārkaṇḍeya, Āgneya, Bhaviṣya, Brahmavaivarta, Laiṅga …
Brāhma, Pādma, Vaiṣṇava, Śaiva, Bhāgavata …; the Śaiva is fourth and 'accomplishes all aims'.

sources.edition: Venkatesvara Press ed. (Bombay c. 1920), books 1 and 7; GRETIL e-text

comparisons.note: The disagreement on the fourth place (Śaiva vs Vāyu) is preserved; Matsya's 24,000 for the Vāyavīya equals BhP's figure for the Śaiva.

comparisons.title: Rāma's ancestors: Raghu, Aja and the Vālmīki genealogy
comparisons.subject: lin:suryavamsha
comparisons.question: Who are the father and grandfather of Daśaratha, and where do Raghu, Nahuṣa and Yayāti stand?

rows.statement: … Dilīpa Khaṭvāṅga → Dīrghabāhu → Raghu → Aja → Daśaratha → Rāma, Lakṣmaṇa, Bharata, Śatrughna (Viṣṇu born fourfold). Nahuṣa and Yayāti belong to the Lunar line (4.8–10).

sources.edition: Critical edition, M. M. Pathak (Vadodara 1997–99); GRETIL e-text by P. Schreiner

rows.statement: Khaṭvāṅga → Dīrghabāhu → Raghu ('pṛthuśravāḥ') → Aja → Daśaratha.

Ikṣvāku → Vikukṣi → Bāṇa → Anaraṇya → Pṛthu → Triśaṅku → Dhundhumāra → Yuvanāśva → Māndhātṛ → Susaṃdhi → Dhruvasaṃdhi → Bharata → Asita → Sagara → Asamañja → Aṃśumat → Dilīpa → Bhagīratha → Kakutstha → Raghu → Kalmāṣapāda → Śaṅkhaṇa → Sudarśana → Agnivarṇa → Śīghraga → Maru → Praśuśruka → Ambarīṣa → Nahuṣa → Yayāti → Nābhāga → Aja → Daśaratha.
Vaivasvata Manu has nine sons (Ikṣvāku, Nṛga, Dhṛṣṭa, Śaryāti, Nariṣyanta, Nābhāga-Diṣṭa, Karūṣa, Pṛṣadhra, Vasumān).

sources.edition: Critical edition, M. M. Pathak (Vadodara 1997–99); GRETIL e-text by P. Schreiner

rows.statement: Vaivasvata Manu has ten sons (Ikṣvāku, Nabhaga, Dhṛṣṭa, Śaryāti, Nariṣyanta, Nābhāga, Diṣṭa, Tarūṣa, Pṛṣadhra, Vasumān).

comparisons.note: Homonymous kings (Nahuṣa, Yayāti, Nābhāga) in Vālmīki's list are kept as separate ids (char:nahusha-vr, char:yayati-vr, char:nabhaga-vr). Pargiter (1922) attempted to harmonise the lists; this table does not.

comparisons.title: How did the seats of the Goddess arise?
comparisons.subject: narr:shakti-pitha-origin
comparisons.question: Is Satī's body divided, and how many seats are there?

rows.statement: No dismemberment: at Dakṣa's sacrifice Satī names 108 tīrthas and the names she bears there (e.g. Viśālākṣī at Vārāṇasī), then burns herself and is reborn as Pārvatī.

sources.edition: Calcutta: Caukhamba Vidyabhavan 1954; GRETIL e-text (O. Hellwig), adhy. 1–176

rows.statement: Śiva wanders with Satī's corpse; gods enter it and it falls in pieces; the yoni falls at Kāmarūpa, which becomes the pre-eminent pīṭha (Kāmākhyā).
Viṣṇu cuts the corpse and its parts fall at sacred sites; a list of 108 seats of the Goddess similar to the Matsya's follows.

comparisons.note: Sircar (1973) traces the growth of pīṭha lists from four to fifty-one and 108; the corpse-dismemberment motif appears to be later than the Matsya's naming of tīrthas.

comparisons.title: How Sītā is abducted
comparisons.subject: narr:abduction-of-sita
comparisons.question: What exactly does Rāvaṇa take, and does he touch Sītā?

rows.locator: VR Araṇyakāṇḍa, abduction sargas (exact CE sarga not checked)
rows.statement: Rāvaṇa approaches in the guise of a mendicant, reveals himself and seizes Sītā bodily — the description has him grasp her by the hair and the thighs — and carries her off through the sky in his chariot.

Rāvaṇa does not touch Sītā: he digs up and lifts the ground on which her hermitage stands and carries her away with it. Commentators connect this to a curse that he would die if he forced an unwilling woman.
Before the golden-deer episode Rāma, knowing the future, tells Sītā to enter the fire and leave an illusory Sītā (māyā-Sītā) in her place; it is this double that Rāvaṇa carries off.

rows.locator: RCM Araṇyakāṇḍa, caupāīs before dohā 24 (common numbering)
rows.statement: While Lakṣmaṇa is away, Rāma tells Sītā to dwell in the fire until he has destroyed the rākṣasas; she enters the fire, leaving her own reflection (nija pratibimba), “of the same character, form and modesty.” Not even Lakṣmaṇa knows. Rāvaṇa abducts the reflection.
Rāvaṇa, a vidyādhara king, carries Sītā off to Laṅkā but does not force her; Jain tellings attribute his restraint to a vow taken before a Jain monk not to take a woman against her will.

comparisons.note: Ramanujan (1991) and the essays in Richman (1991) use divergences like these to argue for many “tellings” rather than one original with deviations. The rows are not ranked; they show how each telling protects (or does not protect) Sītā’s inviolability by different means.

comparisons.title: Who are Sītā’s parents?
comparisons.subject: char:sita
comparisons.question: How is Sītā born, and whose daughter (or sister) is she?

rows.locator: VR Bālakāṇḍa (Janaka’s account to Viśvāmitra; exact CE sarga not checked)
rows.statement: Janaka of Mithilā finds her in a furrow while ploughing the sacrificial ground; she is not born of a womb (ayonijā) and he raises her as his daughter.

She is the daughter of King Dasaratha of Bārāṇasī and his chief queen, sister of Rāma-paṇḍita and Lakkhaṇa; on their return from the Himalaya she is made queen consort. In the closing identification she is the mother of Rāhula in the Buddha’s last life.
She is the daughter of Janaka and Videhā, born as a twin with Bhāmaṇḍala, who is carried off at birth and raised among the vidyādharas.
She is born to Rāvaṇa’s queen Mandodarī; because she is foretold to cause Rāvaṇa’s ruin she is abandoned in a casket and found in Janaka’s realm, where she is raised.
She is born to Mandodarī (popular accounts of the text add that Mandodarī had drunk a pot of sages’ blood collected by Rāvaṇa) and is found by Janaka in a field being prepared for a sacrifice.
Nang Sida is born as Thotsakan’s daughter; because of an ill omen she is set adrift and is found and raised by King Chanok (Janaka). She is an incarnation of Laksami.
Nang Sida is the daughter of Thôtsakane (Rāvaṇa) and Nang Chanta, an incarnation of Nang Souxada.
Siti Dewi is presented in the summaries consulted as the adoptive daughter of Maharisi Kali; the details of her birth in the Laud-based text were not checked.

comparisons.note: Two clusters stand out: tellings in which Sītā is found in the earth (Vālmīki and many Hindu tellings) and tellings in which she is Rāvaṇa’s own daughter (Guṇabhadra’s Jain line, the Adbhuta, Thai and Lao tellings), with the Buddhist jātaka making her Rāma’s sister. The table does not decide which is earlier.

comparisons.title: Hanumān’s character
comparisons.subject: char:hanuman
comparisons.question: Who is Hanumān — what kind of being, what kind of devotee, and does he marry?

rows.statement: A vānara, son of the Wind god, minister of Sugrīva, eloquent and learned, who leaps the ocean to find Sītā; no wife is mentioned.

rows.locator: RCM Sundarakāṇḍa passim; Uttarakāṇḍa before dohā 120(ka) for “rāma te adhika rāma kara dāsā”
rows.statement: The paradigmatic servant-devotee (dāsa) of Rāma. The Mānas also states in Kākabhuśuṇḍi’s discourse that “Rāma’s servant is greater than Rāma” — a general claim about devotees that later Hanumān devotion applied to him.

A vidyādhara prince — son of Pavanañjaya and Añjanā — not an animal; the monkey is his clan’s banner emblem. He marries (several wives in the Jain tradition) and at the end renounces the world as a Jain monk.

A brilliant white monkey warrior with a frankly amorous nature: he falls in love with the mermaid Suvannamaccha (Thotsakan’s daughter), fathering Macchanu, and in one episode takes Thotsakan’s form to sleep with his queen.
The Hanuman–Sovann Maccha romance during the building of the causeway is one of the most loved episodes of Khmer performance.

comparisons.note: Lutgendorf (2007) traces how a vānara minister became, in North India, a celibate god and the archetypal devotee, while Jain and Southeast Asian tellings made him a married or amorous hero. None of these is treated here as the “real” Hanumān.

comparisons.title: Rāvaṇa’s portrayal
comparisons.subject: char:ravana
comparisons.question: What kind of being is Rāvaṇa, how is he judged, and who kills him?

rows.statement: A ten-headed rākṣasa king of Laṅkā, son of the sage Viśravas, mighty through ascetic boons, learned yet given to lust and arrogance; he abducts Sītā and is killed by Rāma.

A vidyādhara king of the rākṣasa lineage and a devout Jain, called ten-faced because his face was reflected in a necklace of nine gems; he is killed by Lakṣmaṇa (as Vāsudeva), not by Rāma, and is destined to become a future tīrthaṅkara.
A figure of tragic grandeur — majestic, heroic and cultured even in his fatal error — who does not touch Sītā; readers have long seen Kampaṉ’s Rāvaṇa as a tragic hero rather than a mere villain.
Rāvaṇa, lord of Laṅkā, invites the Buddha to his island and questions him on the dharma; he is a pious seeker, and no abduction is narrated.
Thotsakan, the ten-faced king of Laṅkā, is Sida’s father; he keeps his heart outside his body, and dies when Hanuman crushes it as Phra Ram’s arrows strike.
Hapmanasouane is Phra Lam’s cousin, and is compared with Devadatta or Māra, the adversaries of the Buddha.

comparisons.title: Kṛṣṇa and Rādhā
comparisons.subject: char:radha
comparisons.question: Is Rādhā named, and what is her relation to Kṛṣṇa?

rows.statement: No gopī is named Rādhā. In the rāsa episode Kṛṣṇa disappears with one favoured, unnamed gopī, whom later commentators (e.g. Viśvanātha Cakravartī) identify as Rādhā.

rows.locator: one verse (often cited as 1.89, Weber — unverified)
rows.statement: A single Prakrit verse speaks of Kṛṣṇa and Rādhā (Rāhiā) as lovers — the earliest known literary mention, in an anthology whose date is disputed (before 640 CE).
The cowherd girls’ round-dance enacts Kṛṣṇa (Māyavaṉ), Balarāma and Kṛṣṇa’s beloved Piññai — a Tamil cowherd beloved who is not named Rādhā.
Āṇṭāḷ’s girls wake Nappiṉṉai, Kṛṣṇa’s consort, to intercede for them; Rādhā does not appear.
Rādhā is the heroine: the poem follows her longing, jealousy, the messages of her friend and her reunion with Kṛṣṇa, who is her lover, not her husband.
Rādhā is the supreme goddess, mūlaprakṛti and Kṛṣṇa’s eternal śakti in Goloka; the text also narrates her marriage to Kṛṣṇa performed by Brahmā.
Rādhā is Kṛṣṇa’s hlādinī-śakti (power of bliss); Caitanya is Kṛṣṇa who has taken on Rādhā’s emotion and golden complexion in order to taste her love.
Śaṅkaradeva’s Ekaśaraṇa devotion centres on Kṛṣṇa alone; Rādhā is not worshipped alongside him in this tradition.

comparisons.note: The table shows Rādhā absent (Bhāgavata), marginal (Gāhā Sattasaī), central as beloved (Gītagovinda), supreme goddess (Brahmavaivarta) and theological principle (Caitanya Caritāmṛta), alongside Tamil tellings with a different beloved (Piññai / Nappiṉṉai) and an Assamese tradition that deliberately leaves her out.

comparisons.title: Who kills Rāvaṇa?
comparisons.subject: narr:lanka-war
comparisons.question: Who defeats the king of Laṅkā (or his double), and how?

rows.statement: Rāma kills Rāvaṇa in single combat with a divine weapon (the Brahmāstra).
Rāma kills Rāvaṇa; the poem makes the battle a display of Rāma’s divine līlā.
Lakṣmaṇa kills Rāvaṇa, as in all Jain universal history the Vāsudeva kills the Prativāsudeva; Rāma, a non-violent Baladeva, later becomes a monk and attains liberation.
After the ten-headed Rāvaṇa is dead, his thousand-headed brother Sahasra-Rāvaṇa strikes Rāma down; Sītā takes the form of Mahākālī and destroys him.
Śāraḷā Dāsa narrates a further war against a thousand-headed Rāvaṇa of Vilaṅkā; who strikes the final blow was not checked.
Phra Ram’s arrows cannot kill Thotsakan until Hanuman obtains and crushes the heart that Thotsakan has kept outside his body.
There is no Rāvaṇa and no war: the story ends with the return from exile and Rāma-paṇḍita’s long reign.

comparisons.title: Murukaṉ and Skanda across texts
comparisons.subject: deity:murugan
comparisons.question: How is the Tamil god Murukaṉ presented, and when does he carry Skanda’s attributes?

rows.statement: Cēyōṉ, “the red one,” presides over the hill (kuṟiñci) landscape, one of four deities assigned to landscapes; no mythology is given. The commentator Nacciṉārkkiṉiyar glosses him as “red Murukaṉ.”
Eight surviving poems praise Cevvēḷ (Murukaṉ) at Tiruparaṅkuṉṟam near Madurai and know the northern myth of his birth.

A guide-poem leading the devotee to Murukaṉ at six places; he has six faces and twelve arms, rides the peacock, wields the vēl and is linked to the Kṛttikā mothers — Skanda iconography in a Tamil poem.
Hill-dwellers dance the kuṉṟakkuravai for Murukaṉ, who is also linked to possession-dance (veṟiyāṭṭu) of the Vēlaṉ priest.
A full Tamil Skanda Purāṇa: birth from Śiva’s fiery seed, the war against Cūrapatmaṉ, and marriages to Teyvāṉai (Indra’s daughter) and the Tamil hunter girl Vaḷḷi.
In the Sanskrit epic Skanda is born of Agni (and Svāhā) or of Śiva, raised by the Kṛttikās, and made general of the gods; there is no Tamil Vaḷḷi.

sources.locator: Āraṇyakaparvan, Skanda episode (CE adhyāyas not checked)

comparisons.note: Read in sequence these rows support the scholarly account of convergence (Zvelebil 1973; Clothey 1978): a Tamil hill god acquires Skanda’s myth and iconography by the late Caṅkam period. The identification is recorded as IDENTIFIED_WITH, not as a merger.

comparisons.title: Vedic accounts of the beginning
comparisons.subject: narr:nasadiya
comparisons.question: What was there in the beginning, and how did the world come forth?

rows.statement: In the first age of the gods, being was born from non-being (asataḥ sad ajāyata); the regions were born from the “upward-stretched one”, Dakṣa from Aditi and Aditi from Dakṣa.

The world comes from a sacrifice: the gods sacrifice the thousand-headed Man (Puruṣa), who is “all this, what has been and what will be”; from his parts come the verses, animals, the four social classes, the moon, sun, Indra, Agni and the worlds.

sources.quote: puruṣa evedaṁ sarvaṁ yad bhūtaṁ yac ca bhavyam

rows.statement: A Golden Embryo (Hiraṇyagarbha) arose in the beginning as the one lord of what exists and upheld earth and sky; the great waters, bearing an embryo, gave birth to Agni; the refrain asks “to which god shall we offer?” and the last verse names Prajāpati.

There was neither non-being nor being; the One breathed windlessly by its own power; desire (kāma), the first seed of mind, arose; poets found the bond of being in non-being — and the one who oversees it in the highest heaven perhaps knows, or perhaps does not.

sources.quote: so aṅga veda yadi vā na veda

rows.statement: In the beginning there was only the self (ātman) in the form of a person; seeing nothing else it said “I am”; it was afraid, then desired a second, split itself into husband and wife and, taking pairs of animal forms, produced all creatures; whoever knows “I am brahman” becomes this whole world.

sources.edition: Kāṇva recension (GRETIL; checked against Limaye & Vadekar 1958)

rows.statement: In the beginning there was only Being (sat), one without a second; some say non-being came first, but “how could being come from non-being?”; Being thought “let me become many” and emitted heat, which emitted water.

comparisons.note: Five or six distinct models — emergence from non-being, cosmic sacrifice, a first-born lord, a self-questioning origin beyond knowledge, a self that divides itself, and Being without a second. ChU 6.2 explicitly rejects the “non-being first” view voiced in RV 10.72.2. The rows are not harmonised.

comparisons.title: The standing of Indra from the Ṛgveda to the Bhāgavata
comparisons.subject: deity:indra
comparisons.question: How powerful and how wise is Indra?

rows.statement: Indra is the most-praised god (about a quarter of the hymns), the soma-strengthened slayer of Vṛtra who released the waters; the refrain of RV 10.86 says “Indra is above all”.
Indra fails to recognise the yakṣa, which vanishes before him; Umā Haimavatī tells him it was brahman. Because he came nearest and first knew it as brahman, Indra is said to surpass the other gods.

Indra, sent by the gods, lives as a student with Prajāpati; after successive wrong answers he stays a total of 101 years before being taught the bodiless self, while the asura Virocana leaves content with the first teaching.

sources.quote: ekaśataṃ ha vai varṣāṇi maghavān prajāpatau brahmacaryam uvāsa

rows.statement: Indra is a teacher: he tells king Pratardana that he is breath (prāṇa), the self consisting of intelligence.

Kṛṣṇa persuades the cowherds to honour Mount Govardhana instead of holding the customary sacrifice to Indra; the angry Indra sends torrential rain, Kṛṣṇa lifts the mountain to shelter Vraja, and Indra submits to him.

comparisons.note: The rows show a shift from supreme warrior to learner and, in Kṛṣṇa devotion, a humbled god; they do not show that Indra’s worship ceased. The Bhāgavata row is from recall (narrative: `narr:govardhana`).

comparisons.title: Rudra from the Ṛgveda to the Śvetāśvatara
comparisons.subject: deity:rudra
comparisons.question: Who is Rudra, and how is he addressed?

rows.statement: A fierce, tawny, many-formed archer, father of the Maruts, whose wrath is feared and whose remedies heal; from Rudra, “lord of this world”, lordship does not depart.

sources.quote: īśānād asya bhuvanasya bhūrer na vā u yoṣad rudrād asuryam

rows.statement: When the gods reached heaven by sacrifice, the god who rules over cattle was left behind (hence “Vāstavya”); he claims and receives a share of the offering.

sources.quote: atha yo ’yaṃ devaḥ paśūnāmīṣṭe sa ihāhīyata

rows.statement: A new-born boy, crying, asks Prajāpati for names and receives eight — Rudra, Sarva, Paśupati, Ugra, Aśani, Bhava, Mahān Deva, Īśāna — identified with water, plants, wind, lightning, rain-cloud, moon and sun as forms of Agni.

Homage to Rudra’s wrath and arrows and to his innumerable forms — lord of cattle, of paths, of thieves, dweller on mountains — including “homage to the auspicious and the more auspicious” (namaḥ śivāya ca śivatarāya ca).

sources.edition: TITUS, on the basis of Weber 1871–72

rows.statement: There is one Rudra, without a second, who rules these worlds, creates and withdraws all beings; he is the all-pervading Śiva, the Maheśvara whose māyā is nature; knowing him as Śiva one attains peace.

sources.quote: eko hi rudro na dvitīyāya tasthe

comparisons.note: The sequence shows śiva moving from epithet (TS 4.5.8) to the name of the supreme lord (ŚvU). Historians also invoke non-Vedic contributions to Śiva; those are outside these rows.

comparisons.title: Viṣṇu in Vedic texts
comparisons.subject: deity:vishnu
comparisons.question: What is Viṣṇu’s character and rank in the Vedic corpus?

rows.statement: Viṣṇu measured the earthly realms and propped up the upper dwelling in three wide strides; in his highest step is a spring of honey.
The patrons always see Viṣṇu’s highest step like an eye fixed in heaven; with Indra he strides widely in the exhilaration of soma. He receives only a handful of hymns (about five or six).

sources.quote: tad viṣṇoḥ paramam padaṁ sadā paśyanti sūrayaḥ

rows.statement: Viṣṇu is the sacrifice and a dwarf; the asuras grant the gods as much earth as he lies upon, and through him the gods win the whole earth.
“The sacrifice is Viṣṇu”; the sacrificer’s steps re-enact the strides through earth, air and sky.
Reaching the goal of the gods’ session first, Viṣṇu becomes “the best of the gods”; being the sacrifice and the sun, he cannot contain his glory, and his own bow cuts off his head.
The disciplined traveller reaches the end of the road, “that highest step of Viṣṇu”.

comparisons.note: Minor in Ṛgvedic hymn-count, Viṣṇu is identified with the sacrifice and called best of the gods in the Śatapatha, and his “highest step” becomes an Upaniṣadic image of the goal — precursors of, but not yet, the supreme Viṣṇu–Nārāyaṇa of later theism.

comparisons.title: Who is the fish that saves Manu?
comparisons.subject: narr:manu-fish
comparisons.question: Who or what is the fish in the flood story?

rows.statement: An unnamed fish (matsya) that comes into Manu’s hands with the washing water; it asks to be reared, predicts the flood and tows the ship by its horn to the northern mountain. No god is named.
The fish finally reveals itself as Brahmā, the lord of creatures (Prajāpati), and charges Manu with creating all beings.
The fish is Viṣṇu (Janārdana) in his fish form, who saves king Manu and teaches him; the Purāṇa takes its name from this frame.
Hari takes the fish form to save the royal sage Satyavrata, future Vaivasvata Manu, and to recover the Vedas.

comparisons.note: Only the Śatapatha row was checked online; the epic and Purāṇic rows are from recall and give coarse locators.

comparisons.title: Two versions of Pravāhaṇa Jaivali’s teaching
comparisons.subject: narr:five-fires
comparisons.question: How do the Bṛhadāraṇyaka and Chāndogya tell the episode and the doctrine?

rows.statement: Śvetaketu comes to the assembly (pariṣad) of the Pañcālas and cannot answer the king’s five questions; his father Gautama goes to the king and asks for the teaching, which “never before dwelt in any brahmin” (6.2.8); the five fires are yonder world, rain-cloud, this world, man and woman; knowers go by the path of the gods and do not return, sacrificers go by the path of the fathers and return, and those who know neither path become worms, insects and biting creatures. The king quotes the seer’s verse on the two paths (= RV 10.88.15).

sources.edition: Kāṇva recension (GRETIL; checked against Limaye & Vadekar 1958)
sources.quote: yatheyaṃ vidyetaḥ pūrvaṃ na kasmiṃś cana brāhmana uvāsa

rows.statement: Śvetaketu comes to the assembly (samiti) of the Pañcālas; the king says that because this knowledge had never before gone to brahmins, rule in all worlds belonged to the kṣatriya (5.3.7); the five fires are yonder world, rain-cloud, earth, man and woman; those of pleasant conduct quickly reach a pleasant birth (brahmin, kṣatriya, vaiśya), those of foul conduct a foul one (dog, pig, caṇḍāla); a third state is that of tiny creatures who repeatedly “are born and die”.

sources.quote: tasmād u sarveṣu lokeṣu kṣatrasyaiva praśāsanam abhūd iti

comparisons.note: The Chāndogya ties rebirth explicitly to conduct (caraṇa) and to social birth; the Bṛhadāraṇyaka emphasises the two paths and quotes the Ṛgveda. Both make a kṣatriya the source of the doctrine.

discoveries.title: Vāsudeva and Saṅkarṣaṇa were worshipped from Bactria to the Deccan before the epics reached their final form
discoveries.body:
Four independent kinds of evidence cluster within roughly a century and a half: coins of the Greco-Bactrian king Agathocles found at Aï Khanoum (c. 190–180 BCE) showing two deities with a plough and a wheel; the Besnagar pillar on which Heliodorus, envoy of an Indo-Greek king, calls himself a Bhāgavata and Vāsudeva the “god of gods”; the Hāthībāḍā–Ghosuṇḍī inscriptions in Rajasthan naming Saṅkarṣaṇa and Vāsudeva together; and the Nāṇeghāṭ inscription of the Sātavāhana queen Nāganikā invoking them in the western Deccan.

The patrons were a Greek king, a Greek envoy, a local ruler and a Deccan queen. Whatever the date of the Mahābhārata’s final redaction, devotion to these two figures was already geographically and socially wide.
discoveries.caveat: The inscriptions name Vāsudeva and Saṅkarṣaṇa, not “Kṛṣṇa”; identifying the coin figures and the inscriptional gods with the epic Kṛṣṇa and Balarāma is scholarly interpretation (class 5). None of this dates the Kṛṣṇa narratives or proves any event in them.

discoveries.title: Two grammarians are among the earliest witnesses that Kṛṣṇa’s and Bali’s stories were told and performed
discoveries.body:
Pāṇini’s rule 4.3.98 (vāsudevārjunābhyāṃ vun) forms words for devotees of Vāsudeva and of Arjuna — evidence that both were objects of bhakti when the rule was framed, usually dated c. 5th–4th c. BCE. Two centuries or so later, Patañjali’s Mahābhāṣya on 3.1.26 describes performers who “have Kaṃsa killed” and “have Bali bound” before the audience’s eyes, and on 2.2.24 and 2.2.34 alludes to Kṛṣṇa with Saṅkarṣaṇa and to a prāsāda of Rāma and Keśava.

Read alongside the Ṛgveda’s three strides of Viṣṇu (1.154) and the Śatapatha’s dwarf who wins the earth (ŚB 1.2.5, with no Bali), the grammarians supply a textual stage of the Vāmana–Bali story between the Veda and the Purāṇas.
discoveries.caveat: These are grammatical examples: they attest that stories and cults were current, not the contents or date of any surviving epic or Purāṇa. Patañjali names neither Viṣṇu nor Vāmana in the Bali example, and reading “Rāma” as Balarāma is interpretation.

sources.locator: Mahābhāṣya on Aṣṭādhyāyī 3.1.26, vārttika 6 (Kielhorn ed. II.34–36)
sources.quote: kaṃsavadham ācaṣṭe kaṃsaṃ ghātayati … balibandham ācaṣṭe baliṃ bandhayati

discoveries.title: The oldest physical witness to the Mahābhārata is a table of contents found in a Buddhist anthology on the Silk Road
discoveries.body:
The Spitzer manuscript — Sanskrit fragments recovered at Kizil in the Tarim Basin in 1906 and now divided between Berlin and London — contains a list of the Mahābhārata’s parvans. Radiocarbon dating puts it around 130 CE (80–230 CE); palaeography suggests c. 200–230. It is roughly a millennium older than any surviving manuscript of the epic’s text.

The list was copied far from the Gaṅgā plain, in a Buddhist philosophical compilation, which says something about how widely the epic’s structure was known by the 2nd–3rd century.
discoveries.caveat: A parvan list shows that a work of that shape existed, not the wording of its text; the list’s gaps may reflect the purpose of the list rather than the epic’s contents.

discoveries.title: A 7th-century inscription dates itself by the Bhārata war — and fixes the latest possible date of Kālidāsa
discoveries.body:
The Aihole praśasti of Pulakeśin II, composed by Ravikīrti, is dated both in the Śaka era (556, i.e. 634/635 CE) and as 3,735 years after the Bhārata war — a reckoning that corresponds to the traditional Kali-yuga epoch of 3102 BCE, which Āryabhaṭa had already used in 499 CE. The same poem names Kālidāsa and Bhāravi as poets of renown.

One stone thus shows a traditional cosmological era in practical use by a Deccan court, and gives literary history a firm terminus ante quem for two poets.
discoveries.caveat: The epoch is a traditional, astronomically computed reckoning. Its use in 634 CE is evidence for how 7th-century elites counted time, not for when — or whether — the war took place.

sources.quote: attained to the fame of Kâḷidâsa and of Bhâravi

sources.edition: Critical edition, M. M. Pathak (Vadodara 1997–99); GRETIL e-text by P. Schreiner

discoveries.title: A verse of the Devī Māhātmya was carved in stone in 608 CE
discoveries.body:
The Dadhimatī Mātā inscription (Gupta year 289, 608 CE) quotes a verse beginning sarva-maṅgala-māṅgalye, found in the Devī Māhātmya (Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa 91.9). It gives that hymn a secure latest date — rare for a Purāṇic text. Nearly two centuries earlier the Gangdhar inscription (423/424 CE) records a “terrifying abode of the divine Mothers” built beside a temple of Viṣṇu.

Together they put organised Goddess worship on the epigraphic record well before the oldest manuscripts of the texts that celebrate it.
discoveries.caveat: The quotation shows that one verse existed by 608 CE, not that the whole Devī Māhātmya did in its present form.

discoveries.title: The Kuṣāṇa “Śiva” on coins is labelled with an Iranian name
discoveries.body:
Gold coins of Wima Kadphises and Kaniṣka show a deity with a bull and Śaiva-looking attributes, but the Bactrian legend reads ΟΗϷΟ (Oesho), which many numismatists derive from the name of the Iranian wind god Vāyu (Vēš). The graph keeps Oesho as its own record with two disputed IDENTIFIED_WITH assertions — to Śiva and to Vāyu — and the evidence for and against.

The case shows why identity must be an assertion rather than a merge: the same image can belong to two traditions at once, or be a deliberate synthesis.
discoveries.caveat: This is a live scholarly dispute; the dataset records both readings and does not decide it.

discoveries.title: The most-cited “earliest image of Śiva” is the least secure item in the graph
discoveries.body:
The Mohenjo-daro seal that John Marshall in 1931 called “proto-Śiva” is the oldest object in the dataset associated with Śiva — c. 2350–2000 BCE. It is also modelled as a disputed claim: Doris Srinivasan’s iconological assessment and later work argue that the horned, seated figure does not support the identification, and the Indus script remains undeciphered.

For this reason the atlas never lets a disputed link set an “earliest attestation”: Śiva’s earliest dated material record in the computed profile is the Gudimallam liṅga, itself carrying a range of dates.
discoveries.caveat: Absence of a secure identification is not evidence that no continuity exists; it means the seal cannot carry the weight popular accounts place on it.

discoveries.title: In the Mahābhārata the fish that saves Manu is Brahmā, not Viṣṇu
discoveries.body:
The flood story runs from the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa (1.8.1, where an unnamed fish saves Manu) to the Purāṇas. In the critical Mahābhārata (3.185.48) the fish reveals itself as Prajāpati Brahmā. Only in the Matsya and Bhāgavata Purāṇas does it become Viṣṇu’s first avatāra, and the Bhāgavata adds the demon Hayagrīva who steals the Veda.

The theological identity of the rescuer changed as the story moved between bodies of literature; the graph keeps each version separate and joins them with a DERIVED_FROM assertion rather than a merge.
discoveries.caveat: A later Vaiṣṇava reading may preserve older oral tradition; textual sequence is not proof of origin.

sources.quote: ahaṃ prajāpatir brahmā matparaṃ nādhigamyate / matsyarūpeṇa yūyaṃ ca mayāsmān mokṣitā bhayāt

discoveries.title: There is no single early list of Viṣṇu’s ten avatāras
discoveries.body:
The constituted text of the Mahābhārata’s Nārāyaṇīya lists Varāha, Narasiṃha, Vāmana, Paraśurāma, Rāma and others — but no Fish, no Tortoise and no Kalki. The Agni Purāṇa’s ten include Balarāma rather than Kṛṣṇa; the Bhāgavata counts twenty-two; the Matsya includes figures such as Māndhātṛ and Vyāsa.

The familiar ten is a convention that crystallised late. Every AVATARA_OF edge in the graph is qualified by the text that makes it, so the lists can be compared rather than flattened.
discoveries.caveat: Vulgate texts and other passages of the same works sometimes count differently; the comparison uses the critical or e-text editions cited.

sources.edition: Rajendralal Mitra ed. (Bibliotheca Indica 1870–79); GRETIL e-text

discoveries.title: In the critical Viṣṇu Purāṇa, the word “mahāpurāṇa” is an insertion
discoveries.body:
The critical text of the Viṣṇu Purāṇa (3.6.21–23) lists eighteen purāṇas. The half-verse that calls them mahāpurāṇas and adds the upapurāṇas appears only as a starred insertion (3.6.23*8), recorded in the apparatus rather than the constituted text.

The category “the Eighteen Mahāpurāṇas” — the frame through which the corpus is usually introduced — is itself something the manuscripts show being added.
discoveries.caveat: An insertion in one text attests manuscript variation, not a date for the term; other Purāṇas use it.

sources.edition: Critical edition, M. M. Pathak (Vadodara 1997–99); GRETIL e-text by P. Schreiner

discoveries.title: The critical Mahābhārata has no prayer to Kṛṣṇa when Draupadī is disrobed
discoveries.body:
In the constituted text (2.61.40–41) Draupadī’s garments simply keep appearing as Duḥśāsana pulls. Her famous appeal to Govinda “who dwells in Dvārakā” survives only in star passages (*542–*547) relegated to the apparatus of the Critical Edition.

The graph records Draupadī DEVOTEE_OF Kṛṣṇa at this point as disputed, with the comparison table showing exactly what each source states.
discoveries.caveat: The Critical Edition reconstructs the archetype shared by the manuscripts it used; it does not show the prayer is late everywhere, and many living tellings centre on it.

discoveries.title: The Mahābhārata tells its own Rāma story — with Lakṣmaṇa killing Kumbhakarṇa and no fire ordeal
discoveries.body:
The Rāmopākhyāna (MBh (CE) 3.257–275) retells the Rāma story differently from Vālmīki: Lakṣmaṇa, not Rāma, kills Kumbhakarṇa (3.271.16, against VR (CE) 6.55.128–129); Sītā is cleared by the gods’ testimony and a curse on Rāvaṇa rather than by entering fire; there is no banishment. Yet it already presents Rāma as Viṣṇu descended (3.260.5).

Two Sanskrit tellings of the same story, in two great texts, disagree on who kills whom — exactly the kind of difference the comparison tables exist to show.
discoveries.caveat: Whether the Rāmopākhyāna abridges Vālmīki or preserves an independent version is disputed.

sources.quote: tadartham avatīrṇo 'sau manniyogāc caturbhujaḥ / viṣṇuḥ praharatāṃ śreṣṭhaḥ

discoveries.title: The Upaniṣad that first makes Śiva the supreme lord is built from older Rudra verses
discoveries.body:
The Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad reuses Ṛgvedic and Yajurvedic material verbatim — the Śatarudrīya of the Taittirīya Saṃhitā (ŚvU 3.5), a Ṛgvedic verse to Rudra (RV 1.114.8 = ŚvU 4.22) and the Puruṣa hymn (RV 10.90.1–2 = ŚvU 3.14–15) — while applying śiva and maheśvara to one supreme lord.

The passage from Vedic Rudra to the Śiva of devotion is visible here in the texture of a single text, not only in a sequence of texts.
discoveries.caveat: Whether śiva is a name or an epithet in these verses is debated; the identification of Rudra with Śiva is recorded as the Upaniṣad’s assertion.

sources.quote: puruṣa evedaṃ sarvaṃ yad bhūtaṃ yac ca bhavyam
puruṣa evedaṁ sarvaṁ yad bhūtaṁ yac ca bhavyam
yā te rudra śivā tanūr aghorāpāpakāśinī

sources.edition: TITUS, on the basis of Weber 1871–72
sources.quote: yā́ te rudra śivā́ tanū́r ágʰorā́pāpakāśinī
vīrān mā no rudra bhāmito vadhīr
mā nas toke tanaye mā na āyau
sarvavyāpī sa bhagavāṃs tasmāt sarvagataḥ śivaḥ

discoveries.title: The Gaṅgā is almost absent from the Ṛgveda
discoveries.body:
The river at the heart of later sacred geography appears once by name in the Ṛgveda, in the river list of 10.75.5 (with the adjective gāṅgya at 6.45.31). The Sarasvatī has hymns of its own. In the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa (1.4.1) Agni’s eastward journey runs from the Sarasvatī to Videha beyond the Sadānīrā.

The sacred map of the earliest texts and the sacred map of the temple atlas are different maps.
discoveries.caveat: Absence of mention in one corpus is not absence of the river from the composers’ world; the migration reading of ŚB 1.4.1 is interpretive.

discoveries.title: Vedic prose already names the Mahābhārata’s frame figures
discoveries.body:
The Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa (13.5.4) names Janamejaya Pārikṣita, who performed the horse sacrifice, with brothers Bhīmasena, Ugrasena and Śrutasena — the trio the epic names at its opening — and Bharata Dauḥṣanti, “whom the apsaras Śakuntalā bore”.

The epic’s royal frame draws on names already present in Vedic memory of the Kuru realm.
discoveries.caveat: That the Brāhmaṇa’s Janamejaya and the epic’s are the same figure is inferred from names and lineage, not proven; and a shared name says nothing about the historicity of the epic’s war.

discoveries.title: Both oldest Upaniṣads credit the doctrine of rebirth to a king — and tell it differently
discoveries.body: The “five fires” teaching on the fate of the dead is given to the brahmin Uddālaka Āruṇi by the Pañcāla king Pravāhaṇa Jaivali in both the Bṛhadāraṇyaka (6.2) and the Chāndogya (5.3–5.10). Only the Chāndogya ties rebirth to conduct and to birth in a social class; the Bṛhadāraṇyaka quotes a Ṛgvedic verse instead.
discoveries.caveat: This is a literary attribution, not evidence that the doctrine originated among kṣatriyas.

sources.edition: Kāṇva recension (GRETIL; checked against Limaye & Vadekar 1958)
Kāṇva recension (GRETIL; checked against Limaye & Vadekar 1958)

discoveries.title: Whose daughter is Sītā? The answer depends on the tradition
discoveries.body:
In Vālmīki she is found in a furrow and raised by Janaka. In the Buddhist Dasaratha Jātaka she is Rāma’s sister and becomes his queen. In Vimalasūri’s Jain Paumacariya she is Janaka’s natural daughter with a twin brother, Bhāmaṇḍala. In Guṇabhadra’s Jain telling, the Adbhuta Rāmāyaṇa, the Thai Ramakien and the Lao Phra Lak Phra Lam she is born to Rāvaṇa’s household and set adrift because of an omen.

The graph records each parentage as a separate kinship assertion qualified by its text, so the genealogy view shows all of them at once.
discoveries.caveat: Several rows still carry “awaiting check” locators; no line of descent between the tellings is implied, and no version is treated as the authentic one.

sources.quote: the daughter’s name was the lady Sītā

discoveries.title: In later devotional tellings, the Sītā whom Rāvaṇa abducts is a reflection
discoveries.body:
Vālmīki’s Rāvaṇa seizes Sītā. Kampaṉ’s Rāvaṇa lifts the earth on which her hermitage stands, so as not to touch her. In the Adhyātma Rāmāyaṇa and Tulsīdās’s Rāmcaritmānas the real Sītā enters fire before the abduction and an illusory Sītā (Māyā-Sītā) is taken; the ordeal by fire restores the original.

The change follows the theology: as Rāma becomes Brahman itself, his consort cannot be touched by the demon.
discoveries.caveat: The motif is older than the Mānas and is not unique to it; the theological explanation is a scholarly reading.

sources.quote: तुम्ह पावक महुँ करहु निवासा। जौ लगि करौं निसाचर नासा ॥

discoveries.title: A Thai royal ceremony is named after two Tamil temple hymns
discoveries.body:
The Bangkok court Brahmans’ new-year rite Triyampawai–Trippawai takes its name from Māṇikkavācakar’s Tiruvempāvai and Āṇṭāḷ’s Tiruppāvai — Tamil hymns to Śiva and to Viṣṇu sung in the month of Mārkaḻi. Tamil texts in Thai and Grantha scripts survive, and the hymns have been recorded being chanted.

It is a living thread from South Indian bhakti to a Southeast Asian court, distinct from the better-known Rāmāyaṇa route.
discoveries.caveat: This does not date the transmission, or show that the officiants understand the Tamil they recite.

discoveries.title: A 16th-century poet produced a critical edition of a Marathi classic
discoveries.body:
The Jñāneśvarī carries its own dated colophon (Śaka 1212, 1290 CE, under the Yādava king Rāmacandra) and a second note, dated 1584, in which Eknāth says he restored the text because variant readings had corrupted it.

The problem of textual corruption — and an attempt to solve it — appears in a vernacular tradition three centuries before modern critical editions.
discoveries.caveat: The e-text used is a modern edition; the colophons themselves should be checked against early manuscripts.

sources.quote: एकाजनार्दनें अत्यादरीं| गीता- ज्ञानेश्वरी प्रतिशुद्ध केली

discoveries.title: The oldest Tamil grammar names Māyōṉ and Cēyōṉ as lords of landscapes — their equation with Viṣṇu and Skanda is a later gloss
discoveries.body:
The Tolkāppiyam names Māyōṉ (“the dark one”) and Cēyōṉ (“the red one”) as presiding over the forest and mountain landscapes of love poetry. The commentator Nacciṉārkkiṉiyar glosses them as Viṣṇu and Murukaṉ, and Murukaṉ’s identification with the Sanskrit Skanda is a further convergence.

The graph keeps Murukaṉ and Skanda as two records joined by an assertion qualified by tradition — the convergence is part of the history, not an assumption.
discoveries.caveat: The date of the relevant part of the Tolkāppiyam is itself disputed.

discoveries.title: 17 of the 45 temples with founding legends have no surviving fabric older than 1500 CE
discoveries.body:
Of the 45 temples in the atlas whose tradition gives a founding story, 17 have no surviving fabric dated before 1500 CE — among them the Kāśī Viśvanātha (1780), Kalighat and Somnath (rebuilt 1951). Across all 103 dated temples, 16 have a surviving phase from before 600 CE, and several of those — Deogarh, Udayagiri, Bhitargaon, Tigawa — are monuments no longer in regular worship.

Many of the places most central to living practice have been rebuilt repeatedly, while some of the oldest fabric survives where worship lapsed. The atlas therefore keeps two dates on every temple: the tradition’s and the building’s.
discoveries.caveat: A late building is not a late cult: inscriptions, texts and earlier phases may attest worship long before the surviving fabric. The counts describe the 103 temples of this dataset only, and one early date (Muṇḍeśvarī) is disputed.

discoveries.title: One 18th-century queen stands behind the present fabric of several “ancient” shrines
discoveries.body:
Ahilyābāī Holkar of Indore built the present Kāśī Viśvanātha temple (1780) and the Viṣṇupada at Gaya (1787), renovated Aundha Nāganātha, built a separate Somanātha temple (1783), and is credited — disputedly — with rebuilding Grishneshwar.

Four of these are counted among the twelve jyotirliṅgas; the buildings pilgrims enter are largely hers.
discoveries.caveat: These are rebuildings and renovations of existing sacred sites, not foundations; the Grishneshwar attribution is disputed.

discoveries.title: The twelve jyotirliṅgas are a fixed list with unfixed places
discoveries.body:
Four of the twelve positions have rival claimant temples — Vaidyanātha (Deoghar or Parli), Nāgeśvara (Dwarka, Aundha or Jageshwar), and others — and at least seven of the fifteen claimant temples in the atlas are buildings of 1700 or later.

The network is real as a devotional list; its geography is contested in ways the map makes visible.
discoveries.caveat: Several memberships rest on recall-level sources; a late building does not mean a late cult.

discoveries.title: Conquest carried a temple design from Kanchi to Pattadakal
discoveries.body:
After the Cālukya king Vikramāditya II took the Pallava capital Kanchi, his queen Lokamahādevī built the Virūpākṣa at Pattadakal (c. 740–745), whose Drāviḍa design follows Kanchi’s Kailāsanātha. A century earlier the Pallava Narasiṃhavarman I had taken the Cālukya capital Vātāpi.

The atlas’s DERIVED_FROM edge between two temples records an argument about influence, with its evidence class.
discoveries.caveat: Stylistic dependence is a scholarly argument (class 5), not a documented commission.

discoveries.title: One Vaiṣṇava family at Eran kept its cult under a change of empire
discoveries.body:
At Eran, Dhanyaviṣṇu’s family raised a pillar under the Gupta Budhagupta (484/85 CE) and then the colossal Varāha under the Hūṇa ruler Toramāṇa (c. 510), dating the new foundation by Toramāṇa’s first regnal year.

The inscriptions show local patrons sustaining a Vaiṣṇava cult across a political rupture.
discoveries.caveat: The family link for the Budhagupta pillar rests on an edition cited from recall (material:188).

discoveries.title: The epics were carved in stone in Java and Cambodia as monumental programmes
discoveries.body:
Prambanan’s Rāmāyaṇa and Kṛṣṇa reliefs belong to a temple tied to the Śivagṛha inscription of 856 CE — the same period as the Old Javanese Kakawin Rāmāyaṇa (c. 856–930). Angkor Wat, built under Sūryavarman II (c. 1113–1150), carries the churning of the ocean, the Kurukṣetra battle and the war in Laṅkā in its galleries.

The largest surviving narrative programmes of these stories in stone stand outside South Asia.
discoveries.caveat: The link between Prambanan and the Śivagṛha inscription is an argument (de Casparis), since the inscription was found apart from the temple; “largest” is a statement about what survives.

sources.locator: Angkor (site page not reachable during research)

discoveries.title: Rāma and Sītā are attested in more distinct texts in this graph than any deity
discoveries.body:
Counting distinct texts in which a figure is directly attested, Rāma (23), Sītā (21) and Kṛṣṇa (21) lead; Śiva and Viṣṇu are the strongest bridges in the network (highest betweenness), connecting otherwise separate corpora, temples and inscriptions.

Narrative figures travel across languages and religions — Hindu, Jain, Buddhist, Southeast Asian — where a deity’s cult is more often carried by temples and inscriptions than by retellings.
discoveries.caveat: Network counts measure this dataset — which reflects what was researched — and are never evidence of religious importance or of historical truth.

sacred.name: Pādma mahākalpa (past)
sacred.description: Traditional chronology: the great kalpa called Pādma that closed the first half (parārdha) of Brahmā's hundred-year life, according to the Viṣṇu Purāṇa.

sources.edition: Critical edition, M. M. Pathak (Vadodara 1997–99); GRETIL e-text by P. Schreiner
sources.quote: ekam asya vyatītaṃ tu parārdhaṃ brahmaṇo 'nagha / tasyānte 'bhūn mahākalpaḥ pādma ity abhiviśrutaḥ

sacred.note: Brahmā's full life (para) is a hundred of his years (ViP 1.3.5). Traditional reckoning as stated in the cited texts; it is not a historical or scientific chronology and is not drawn on the same axis as scholarly dates.

sacred.name: Vārāha kalpa (current day of Brahmā)
sacred.description: Traditional chronology: the present day of Brahmā, the first kalpa of the second parārdha, named after the Boar (ViP 1.3.28); a day of Brahmā is a thousand caturyugas (Manu 1.72; ViP 1.3.15; BhP 3.11.22), followed by a night of equal length.

sources.edition: Critical edition, M. M. Pathak (Vadodara 1997–99); GRETIL e-text by P. Schreiner
GRETIL e-text, text of Kullūka (Shastri 1983) with Medhātithi variants

sacred.note: Human-year figure computed as 1,000 × 4,320,000 using the 360:1 ratio implied by ViP 1.3.19–21; Manu gives only divine yugas. Āryabhaṭa instead makes a day of Brahmā 1,008 yugas (AB 3.8). Traditional reckoning as stated in the cited texts; it is not a historical or scientific chronology and is not drawn on the same axis as scholarly dates.

sacred.name: Svāyambhuva manvantara (1st)
sacred.description: Traditional chronology: the first of the fourteen manvantaras of the present kalpa, under Svāyambhuva Manu (ViP 3.1.6), in which Dhruva, son of Uttānapāda, lived (ViP 1.11).

sources.edition: Critical edition, M. M. Pathak (Vadodara 1997–99); GRETIL e-text by P. Schreiner

sacred.note: Each manvantara is 'a little over seventy-one' caturyugas (ViP 1.3.18; BhP 3.11.24); ViP 1.3.19–21 gives 852,000 divine and 306,720,000 human years 'without the excess'. Traditional reckoning as stated in the cited texts; it is not a historical or scientific chronology and is not drawn on the same axis as scholarly dates.

sacred.name: Cākṣuṣa manvantara (6th)
sacred.description: Traditional chronology: the sixth manvantara, at whose end the deluge of the Matsya story occurs according to the Matsya Purāṇa (2.14) and the Bhāgavata (1.3.15); the Bhāgavata also places the churning of the ocean in this period (recall).

sources.edition: Calcutta: Caukhamba Vidyabhavan 1954; GRETIL e-text (O. Hellwig), adhy. 1–176
Critical edition, M. M. Pathak (Vadodara 1997–99); GRETIL e-text by P. Schreiner

sacred.note: The Bhāgavata (8.24.58) instead says Satyavrata became Vaivasvata Manu 'in this kalpa', placing the Matsya episode at a kalpa's end; the texts are not harmonised here. Traditional reckoning as stated in the cited texts; it is not a historical or scientific chronology and is not drawn on the same axis as scholarly dates.

sacred.name: Vaivasvata manvantara (7th, current)
sacred.description: Traditional chronology: the present, seventh manvantara of Vaivasvata (Śrāddhadeva) Manu, son of Vivasvat, with Purandara as Indra and the seven sages Vasiṣṭha, Kaśyapa, Atri, Jamadagni, Gautama, Viśvāmitra and Bharadvāja (ViP 3.1.30–32; BhP 8.13.1–5); Vāmana is born in it (BhP 8.13.6).

sources.edition: Critical edition, M. M. Pathak (Vadodara 1997–99); GRETIL e-text by P. Schreiner

sources.quote: manur vivasvataḥ putraḥ śrāddhadeva iti śrutaḥ / saptamo vartamāno yaḥ

sacred.note: Traditional reckoning as stated in the cited texts; it is not a historical or scientific chronology and is not drawn on the same axis as scholarly dates.

sacred.name: Sāvarṇika manvantara (8th, future)
sacred.description: Traditional chronology: the coming eighth manvantara, whose Manu Sāvarṇi will be King Suratha by the Goddess's boon; the Devī Māhātmya is framed as 'in the Sāvarṇika manvantara' (MkP colophons) and the Viṣṇu Purāṇa describes the future manvantaras (3.2).

sources.edition: GRETIL e-text (SANSKNET); Devī Māhātmya = MkP 81–93 in this edition
Critical edition, M. M. Pathak (Vadodara 1997–99); GRETIL e-text by P. Schreiner

sacred.note: Traditional reckoning as stated in the cited texts; it is not a historical or scientific chronology and is not drawn on the same axis as scholarly dates.

sacred.name: Mahāyuga (caturyuga)
sacred.description: Traditional chronology: the cycle of Kṛta, Tretā, Dvāpara and Kali, totalling 12,000 divine years (Manu 1.71; ViP 1.3.11; BhP 3.11.18); computed as 4,320,000 human years where one divine year = 360 human years.

sources.edition: GRETIL e-text, text of Kullūka (Shastri 1983) with Medhātithi variants
Critical edition, M. M. Pathak (Vadodara 1997–99); GRETIL e-text by P. Schreiner

Traditional reckoning as stated in the cited texts; it is not a historical or scientific chronology and is not drawn on the same axis as scholarly dates.

sacred.name: Twenty-eighth mahāyuga of the Vaivasvata manvantara (current)
sacred.description: Traditional chronology: the present caturyuga, the twenty-eighth of the seventh manvantara: the Matsya places Vedavyāsa's birth in the twenty-eighth Dvāpara (47.245), and the Viṣṇu Purāṇa lists twenty-eight Vyāsas of successive Dvāparas (3.3, recall).

sources.edition: Calcutta: Caukhamba Vidyabhavan 1954; GRETIL e-text (O. Hellwig), adhy. 1–176
sources.quote: aṣṭame dvāpare viṣṇur aṣṭāviṃśe parāśarāt / vedavyāsas tadā jajñe

sources.edition: Critical edition, M. M. Pathak (Vadodara 1997–99); GRETIL e-text by P. Schreiner

sacred.note: Traditional reckoning as stated in the cited texts; it is not a historical or scientific chronology and is not drawn on the same axis as scholarly dates.

sacred.name: Kṛta (Satya) yuga
sacred.description: Traditional chronology: the first and best age, dharma standing on four feet: 4,000 divine years with dawn and dusk of 400 each = 4,800 (Manu 1.69; ViP 1.3.12–13), i.e. 1,728,000 human years at 360:1. The Rāmāyaṇa sets the churning of the ocean 'formerly in the Kṛta age' (VR CE 1.44.14); tradition places Narasiṃha's killing of Hiraṇyakaśipu in this age (the Matsya's '4th yuga' wording at 47.237 is ambiguous).

sources.edition: GRETIL e-text, text of Kullūka (Shastri 1983) with Medhātithi variants
Critical edition, M. M. Pathak (Vadodara 1997–99); GRETIL e-text by P. Schreiner

sources.quote: pūrvaṃ kṛtayuge rāma diteḥ putrā mahābalāḥ

sacred.note: The placement of Narasiṃha in Kṛta is traditional (class 6); texts differ. Traditional reckoning as stated in the cited texts; it is not a historical or scientific chronology and is not drawn on the same axis as scholarly dates.

sacred.name: Tretā yuga
sacred.description: Traditional chronology: the second age: 3,000 divine years with junctions of 300 each = 3,600 (1,296,000 human years). The Nārāyaṇīya places Rāma Bhārgava in Tretā (MBh CE 12.326.77); the Matsya places Vāmana in the seventh Tretā (47.239) and Dattātreya, Māndhātṛ and Jāmadagnya in particular Tretās (47.241–243).

sources.edition: GRETIL e-text, text of Kullūka (Shastri 1983) with Medhātithi variants
Calcutta: Caukhamba Vidyabhavan 1954; GRETIL e-text (O. Hellwig), adhy. 1–176

sacred.note: Traditional reckoning as stated in the cited texts; it is not a historical or scientific chronology and is not drawn on the same axis as scholarly dates.

sacred.name: Junction of Tretā and Dvāpara (Rāma)
sacred.description: Traditional chronology: the Nārāyaṇīya foretells that 'at the junction of Tretā and Dvāpara' Viṣṇu will be Rāma Dāśarathi and slay Rāvaṇa (MBh CE 12.326.78–81); the Matsya places Rāma in the twenty-fourth yuga (47.244).

sources.quote: saṃdhau tu samanuprāpte tretāyāṃ dvāparasya ca / rāmo dāśarathir bhūtvā bhaviṣyāmi jagatpatiḥ

sources.edition: Calcutta: Caukhamba Vidyabhavan 1954; GRETIL e-text (O. Hellwig), adhy. 1–176

sacred.note: Traditional reckoning as stated in the cited texts; it is not a historical or scientific chronology and is not drawn on the same axis as scholarly dates.

sacred.name: Dvāpara yuga
sacred.description: Traditional chronology: the third age: 2,000 divine years with junctions of 200 each = 2,400 (864,000 human years); in each Dvāpara a Vyāsa divides the Veda (ViP 3.3, recall; MatsP 47.245).

sources.edition: GRETIL e-text, text of Kullūka (Shastri 1983) with Medhātithi variants
